sessions.title: QUASOS Challenge Winners Session

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: Attenuation Estimation Using Spatially Weighted Total Variation Regularization: Effects of Beamforming and Spectral Band Selection
papers.abstract: We applied a spatially weighted total variation method for attenuation estimation and evaluated different beamforming (Plane Wave DAS, Fixed Aperture DAS) and spectral bandwidth selection strategies on reference datasets. Fixed probe-centered bandwidths provided more accurate and stable estimates than adaptive peak-based selection, while differences between plane wave and fixed aperture were not conclusive.

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: Two-Stage Label-Efficient Deep Learning for Ultrasound Attenuation Estimation from RF Data
papers.abstract: Quantitative ultrasound attenuation estimation provides valuable tissue characterization biomarkers, but supervised deep learning methods require paired RF data and ground-truth attenuation maps that are difficult to obtain at scale. To address this limitation, a two-stage label-efficient framework is proposed for RF-based ultrasound attenuation estimation. First, a Masked Autoencoder is pretrained on label-free QUASOS Challenge RF data by reconstructing randomly masked RF regions, enabling target-domain RF representation learning without attenuation labels. Second, synthetic RF–attenuation pairs are generated using k-Wave with simulation parameters matched to the QUASOS RF distribution. The pretrained encoder is then fine-tuned with this synthetic supervision to estimate spatial attenuation maps. Evaluation is performed using held-out synthetic data with known labels and no-reference physics-consistency criteria on the provided challenge data. This framework supports scalable learning-based quantitative ultrasound attenuation mapping with reduced dependence on large labeled attenuation datasets.

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: Cepstrum-Stabilized Confidence-Weighted Algebra Attenuation Mapping
papers.abstract: Quantitative ultrasound attenuation imaging provides objective acoustic information, but conventional frequency-domain estimation is vulnerable to speckle-induced spectral fluctuation and low-signal regions. We propose a cepstrum-stabilized, confidence-weighted attenuation mapping framework to improve map stability while preserving layer-dependent contrast. A three-layer gelatin phantom with different Al₂O₃ concentrations was used. Reference-normalized log spectral ratios were computed from local sample and reference spectra, followed by cepstrum liftering to suppress spectral fluctuation. The stabilized estimates were incorporated into a confidence-weighted regularized optimization framework. Compared with a conventional frequency-shift-based method, the proposed framework produced a smoother attenuation map, clearer visualization of the intermediate low-contrast layer, increased layer CNR, and reduced within-layer CV. These preliminary results support its potential for robust attenuation mapping, although calibrated phantom validation is required.

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: Attenuation Coefficient Estimation Through Analytical Regularized Models in the Spectral-Log Difference Framework
papers.abstract: This work evaluates three reference-phantom spectral-log difference methods for ACS estimation in the QUASOS Attenuation Estimation category: RSLD, SWIFT, and RED. All methods estimate ACS in dB/cm/MHz from sample-to-reference spectral ratios while compensating diffraction and system effects. RSLD uses TV regularization, SWIFT introduces backscatter-thresholded spatial weights in the fidelity and regularization terms to reduce interface artifacts, and RED replaces the explicit prior with a 7×7 denoising regularizer. Full matrix capture data were beamformed, spectra were inspected per dataset, and all references for each group/probe were used. Blocks were 8×12 wavelengths with 80% overlap. Frequency bands were probe- and group-specific: 4–9 MHz for L11-5 and 2–7 MHz for L7-4, except in Group D, where 2–7 and 1–5 MHz were used. Hyperparameters were selected based on a coefficient of variation below 10% in uniform ACS regions. Results across layered and inclusion phantoms showed that SWIFT has a consistent ACS structure, lesion/layer detectability, and better interface handling.

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: Speed-of-Sound Estimation from Full-Matrix Capture Data via Short-Lag Spatial Coherence and Eikonal Refinement
papers.abstract: Local speed-of-sound (SoS) estimation from pulse-echo ultrasound supports tissue characterization and aberration correction. Full-matrix capture (FMC) records all transmit–receive element pairs, providing the propagation-path diversity needed to recover spatially varying SoS from a single transducer. Coherence-based methods select the SoS that maximizes receive-channel coherence, but straight-ray assumptions introduce bias at tissue boundaries where refraction is non-negligible. We describe a two-stage pipeline for per-pixel SoS estimation from FMC data, submitted to the QUASOS challenge with L7-4 and L11-5v linear array transducers.

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: PWI-Net – QUASOS Sound Speed Recovery from Transformed Latent Wavefields
papers.abstract: In this work, we apply a deep learning framework (PWI-Net) to estimate spatially varying speed of sound from plane-wave ultrasound data using the QUASOS Challenge dataset.

papers.topicName: Technical Challenge: Quantitative Ultrasound Estimation of Attenuation and Speed-of-Sound
papers.title: Differentiable Subsurface-Offset-Extended Reverse-Time Migration for Sound Speed Estimation and Aberration Correction in Medical Pulse-Echo Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Accurate estimation of tissue sound speed is essential for aberration correction in pulse-echo ultrasound imaging. Most existing sound speed estimation methods rely on ray-based delay models that minimize aberration delays between partial images. However, these approaches generally neglect refraction and diffraction effects. In this work, we introduce a differentiable subsurface-offset-extended reverse-time migration (RTM) framework for simultaneous sound speed estimation and aberration correction in pulse-echo ultrasound. By directly differentiating the subsurface-offset extension of RTM with respect to the sound speed profile, the method minimizes image inconsistency in an extended image domain while fully accounting for wave propagation effects.

sessions.title: MIS: Wearable & Tele-Ultrasound

papers.title: Low-Cost Cardiac Monitoring Using Cognitive Ultrasound
papers.abstract: In order to realize continuous monitoring using ultrasound, it is necessary to develop wearable ultrasound devices with low power consumption, low hardware cost, and a small form factor, without sacrificing diagnostic capabilities. In this work, we introduce a novel cognitive ultrasound algorithm for monitoring the left ventricular inner dimension (LVID) using only a single transmit event per estimate, adaptively steering a single focused beam towards informative regions of the tissue. This dramatically reduces the pulse repetition frequency and beamforming compute required to monitor the LVID compared to standard cardiac imaging pipelines.

papers.title: First Human Trial of during-the-Dive Imaging with a Programmable Ultrasound system, Progress Towards a Wearable Decompression Stress Monitor
papers.abstract: Decompression sickness can occur from ambient pressure reduction, which is attributed to bubble formation in cases of excess supersaturation, and the likelihood of injury can only be estimated after completion of hyperbaric exposure. To overcome this temporal limitation, an ultrasound system was packaged in custom housing, isolating it from the environment. Safe operation of the system was validated with a commercial phantom at 101 kPa and 191 kPa in a hyperbaric chamber, confirmed by temperature and oxygen measurements. After Institutional Review Board approval and informed consent, 12 participants conducted a hyperbaric chamber dive to 505 kPa for 20 minutes. Recordings of the subclavian vein and calf muscle were obtained pre-dive and during-the-dive. Two divers had circulating gas emboli during decompression. Calf muscle brightness was found to increase 1350 a.u. from pre-dive to decompression, exceeding phantom and test-retest measurements. We present the first ever operation of a programmable ultrasound system in a hyperbaric environment, with detection of bubbles in divers during decompression, which will inform the future development of a wearable diver monitor.

papers.title: UriSense: a 128-Element Wearable Ultrasound Platform for Bladder Monitoring
papers.abstract: UriSense is a 392-mW wearable B-mode ultrasound prototype for future low-power bladder monitoring. The system uses a 128-element PMUT transducer, two 64-channel transmitters, two low-power ultrasound analog front-ends acquiring 64 receive channels, an Artix-7 FPGA for control/buffering, and ESP32 Wi-Fi for data transmission. The main innovation is a sparse-receiver architecture that preserves a 128-element effective imaging aperture while physically acquiring only 64 receive channels. A compact encoder–decoder CNN reconstructs the missing 64 channels before beamforming, reducing AFE count, FPGA I/O, PCB complexity, wireless payload, and receiver-side power. With bladder-specific duty cycling, sparse reception, clock/power control, wireless burst transfer, and external processing, average power is reduced from >1 W continuous operation to 392 mW. In phantom imaging with commercial ATL 7-4 and PMUT transducers, CNN-assisted reconstruction increased ROI wall-to-background contrast by ~58% and improved anterior/posterior wall visualization compared with sparse reception alone.

papers.title: Wearable Ultrasound-Based Muscle-Specific Tremor Monitoring via Tissue Displacement Analysis in Essential Tremor Disease
papers.abstract: The world's most prevalent movement disorder, essential tremor (ET) disease, is characterized by involuntary oscillatory movements of the upper extremities. Conventional tools like IMUs and electromyography are unable to provide muscle-specific information, hindering exploration of individual muscle group involvement in overall limb tremor. In this work, we piloted a system of custom-made wearable ultrasound arrays (4-WUS) to directly image an ET subject's flexors, extensors, pronator, and supinator during postural wrist tremor. From the B-mode data, we extracted frame-to-frame tissue displacements for each muscle, and performed power spectral density analysis to derive individual activation frequencies between 4 to 4.5 Hz. These are notably higher than the reference IMU-derived gross tremor frequency (TF) of 3.1 Hz. Coherence analysis indicated a weaker relationship between flexors and other muscles at gross TF, with no notable inter-muscle phase differences likely due to muscle co-contraction. Our initial results show variation in individual muscle group activity from gross wrist behavior during tremor, supporting further exploration of 4-WUS for muscle-specific ET monitoring.

papers.title: Distributed Wearable Ultrasound for Longitudinal Monitoring of Neuromuscular Coordination
papers.abstract: Measuring neuromuscular coordination during dynamic tasks requires non-invasive, multi-site acquisition. Handheld musculoskeletal ultrasound is operator-dependent and impractical during activity. We developed a distributed wearable ultrasound (D-WUS) system using time-delay spectrometry with swept-frequency chirp signals, enabling multi-site M-mode imaging during movement. A 4-channel D-WUS system acquired bilateral vastus lateralis (VL) and vastus medialis oblique (VMO) signals using 20-ms chirps (3-5 MHz) at 50 lines/s. A factorization-PCA pipeline isolated dominant contraction signals; cross-correlation yielded bilateral symmetry indices (BSI). Over a 16-week NCAA Division I volleyball season, D-WUS metrics, countermovement jumps, and session RPE were collected from 30 athletes (462 athlete-weeks) via linear mixed-effects models. Higher training load was associated with decreased VL BSI (p = 0.033); reduced VL BSI predicted elevated eccentric peak force (p = 0.046), consistent with compensation when coordination degrades. D-WUS BSI tracked within-athlete neuromuscular state across a competitive season, supporting real-time and longitudinal monitoring during dynamic movement.

papers.title: Real-Time Interpretable Probe Contact Classification for Latency-Constrained Tele-Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Mixed reality (MR)-based human teleoperation enables remote expert guidance in ultrasound, but maintaining consistent probe–patient contact remains challenging under strict visuo-haptic latency constraints (<150 ms). Existing deep learning approaches are computationally intensive, opaque, and unsuitable for portable deployment. We propose an interpretable and lightweight tabular framework for real-time classification of contact quality. The method encodes acoustic transmission physics through a 21-sector polar grid to extract a compact 28-dimensional feature vector in 12.67 ms per frame. A 9,000-frame dataset of vascular and obstetric phantom acquisitions was used to evaluate classification of optimal contact, air gaps, and probe tilt. CatBoost achieved 99.67% accuracy and F1-score with 0.0022 ms inference time. Total latency remains well below 150 ms, enabling >30 FPS on portable devices. The model provides explainability by linking predictions to spatial intensity variations, supporting intuitive feedback for novice operators. This demonstrates the potential of interpretable models for real-time feedback in latency-constrained MR-guided human teleoperation in ultrasound.

sessions.title: MIM: Ultrasound and Photoacoustic Technologies for Healthcare Applications

papers.title: Revisiting the Concept of “phenotype” in Pediatric sarcomeric Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy Using Myocardial Stiffness and Strain Variations Assessed by Ultrafast Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Pediatric sarcomeric hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) carries significant risk, but genotype–phenotype relationships remain unclear. This study investigates myocardial mechanical properties using ultrafast ultrasound imaging, combining shear wave elastography (SWE) and strain analysis to assess myocardial stiffness and work. Sixty subjects were included: healthy volunteers (HV), genotype-positive/phenotype-positive HCM patients (G+/P+), and genotype-positive/phenotype-negative individuals (G+/P–). While diastolic myocardial stiffness was significantly higher in HCM patients compared with HV and G+/P–, it did not differentiate HV from G+/P– subjects. In contrast, one-beat myocardial work and stress–strain loop area differed significantly across all groups, enabling discrimination of G+/P– individuals from both HV and HCM patients. These findings suggest that combining SWE with strain-derived myocardial work provides sensitive markers of early myocardial alterations, potentially improving phenotypic characterization and risk stratification in HCM.

papers.title: Adaptive Robotic Ultrasound, Doppler, and Photoacoustic Imaging for Wrist Joints
papers.abstract: We present an adaptive robotic system for ultrasound (US), Doppler (DU), and photoacoustic (PA) imaging of wrist joints, addressing challenges posed by the wrist’s complex and curved anatomy. The system integrates a robotic arm, multimodal US/PA imaging, an OPO laser, and a water bath for acoustic coupling. During scanning, joint locations are initialized using an RGB-D camera, and the robot adaptively follows the tissue surface in a closed loop using boundaries extracted by a pre-trained model. Probe orientation and position are continuously updated using regression and predictive modeling to maintain an optimal probe–tissue distance. In a volunteer study, the adaptive system avoided collisions and significantly improved tracking accuracy, achieving 1.0 ± 0.5 mm positional error and 2.1 ± 5.6° angular error, compared to larger errors with RGB-D initialization. The adaptive approach also improved image quality, increasing CNR from 19 dB (without angular adaptation) to 25 dB and enhancing visualization of bone, soft tissue, and vascular features.

papers.title: High-Frequency Point-of-Care Nakagami Parameter Estimation for Assessing Steatosis in Ex-Vivo Liver Allografts on Normothermic Machine Perfusion
papers.abstract: Biopsy is the clinical standard for steatosis assessment in donor liver allografts on normothermic machine perfusion (NMP), but is invasive and lacks whole-liver coverage. We hypothesize that steatosis-induced changes in hepatic microstructure alter ultrasonic scatterer statistics in a manner detectable by the Nakagami parameter, enabling non-invasive severity grading. Parametric Nakagami maps were generated from 14 MHz beamformed RF data in 24 ex-vivo allografts on NMP, classified by biopsy as minimal (<10%) or mild-to-severe steatosis (≥10%). The Nakagami parameter was significantly higher in mild-to-severe compared to minimal steatosis (median [IQR]: 0.77 [0.66–0.84] vs. 0.60 [0.56–0.67]; Mann-Whitney U, p=0.014). ROC analysis yielded an AUC of 0.81 (95% CI: 0.60–0.96) at a Youden-optimal threshold of 0.63. These findings confirm the hypothesis and demonstrate good diagnostic accuracy of point-of-care QUS Nakagami parametric imaging for non-invasive, real-time steatosis grading in ex-vivo liver allografts on NMP, with potential to reduce reliance on biopsy and support transplant decision-making.

papers.title: Point-of-Care Photoacoustic and Ultrasound Imaging for Arthritis
papers.abstract: We present a point-of-care photoacoustic and ultrasound imaging system for arthritis that enables automated, reproducible assessment of disease activity. The system integrates ultrasound imaging, a tunable laser, a robotic platform, and a deep learning model for automatic segmentation of joint space and synovial regions. Trained on annotated data from 43 finger joints of patients, the model achieved a Dice score of 0.77±0.03 and IoU of 0.64±0.03. Six imaging biomarkers were quantified, including hyperemia, blood oxygenation, power Doppler, joint space echogenicity, joint space volume, and synovial volume. In a longitudinal study with biweekly imaging, hyperemia showed the strongest association with disease activity (R²=0.41), followed by oxygenation and Doppler signals. Biomarker trends closely tracked clinical scores, with hyperemia decreasing alongside treatment. Combined biomarker models further improved correlation with disease activity (R² up to 0.52), demonstrating the system’s potential for objective, longitudinal arthritis monitoring.

papers.title: Miniature Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasound Transducer Array for Three-Dimensional Endobronchial Photoacoustic Imaging
papers.abstract: Lung cancer remains a leading cause of cancer-related mortality globally, and early malignancy assessment is critical for improving survival. We present a 0.5 mm-diameter, 60-element PMUT array as a key step toward a miniaturized endobronchial photoacoustic imaging (EB-PAI) probe. The long-term goal is to use the PMUT array to form an EB-PAI probe that combines optical absorption contrast and ultrasound-scale imaging depth to enable high-resolution 3D imaging of structural and functional biomarkers for early-stage lung nodule assessment. We fabricated the miniaturized PMUT array, characterized its frequency response and sensitivity, and used it to image a black wire phantom. Future work will evaluate animal tumor models to assess the system’s potential for clinical translation.

papers.title: Real-Time Wearable Ultrasound-Based Gesture Recognition for Human-Machine Interaction
papers.abstract: This work presents a real-time, wearable ultrasound-based system for gesture recognition in human–machine interaction. While electromyography (EMG) remains the gold standard for sensing muscle activity, it is sensitive to noise and interference, motivating the use of ultrasound (sonomyography) to monitor muscle deformation. Unlike prior systems, which are often not wearable or wireless, this work focuses on a practical, low-power solution for real-world use. The proposed system integrates a wireless, battery-powered three-channel A-mode ultrasound platform with a wearable probe and forearm brace for consistent placement. It includes a full signal-processing pipeline, a lightweight 1D convolutional neural network for classification, and a simple game interface for demonstration. Evaluation shows gesture classification accuracies ranging from 80–100% on untrained test data, with real-time performance typically achieving 75–85%. Accuracy is highest when training and testing data are collected from consistent sensor positions, supporting the system’s feasibility for continuous use.

sessions.title: MSD: High-Frame-Rate and 3-D Ultrasound Imaging Technologies

papers.title: Design Framework for Ultrasound Coupling Structures Using Differentiable Physics
papers.abstract: Ultrasound coupling structures provide an acoustic path from a transducer to a target medium. Cones filled with water are commonly-used coupling structures and are designed using assumptions of the transducer beam geometry. However, wave behavior within a coupling volume can lead to unexpected focal distortions, or may be harnessed for acoustic concentration. With this in mind, we developed a full wave acoustic simulator for axisymmetric transducers, JAXisymmetric. This simulator was written with JAX, a computing library for gradient-based optimization via automatic differentiation. We first validated JAXisymmetric with the widely used k-Wave axisymmetric code (L2 norm: 3%) and with experiments (JAXisymmetric peak pressure error: 7%, k-Wave: 18%). We then implemented JAXisymmetric within a design framework to achieve two objectives in coupling shape optimization: 1: Minimize focal distortions 2: Concentrate pressure in a region of interest This work shows that coupling structure shape can be optimized to minimize focal distortions, or to create a desired focus. Our codes will be made open-source to enable users to design physics-based acoustic coupling structures.

papers.title: Human Circle of Willis Phantom for 3D Ultrasound Localization Microscopy
papers.abstract: 3D ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) resolves microvascular architecture at capillary scale but also shows potential for larger structures such as the Circle of Willis (CoW), where quantitative accuracy is limited by high microbubble concentrations causing signal overlap and speckle. Here, we present a realistic human CoW phantom for 3D ULM evaluation. A 3D model designed in Blender (v4.4) was printed in Elastic 50A resin and placed in a water-filled chamber. Flow was driven by two peristaltic pumps supplying the BA and ICAs. Two contrast conditions were tested: full-circuit perfusion and selective BA injection using SonoVue. A 1 MHz multi-lens probe (256 elements) acquired 4D ultrafast data (16 transmissions, 363 Hz) under baseline and left ICA occlusion. RF data were beamformed, SVD-filtered, and microbubbles localized and tracked for flow estimation. The phantom reproduced CoW dynamics, showing flow redistribution after occlusion, visualized via BA-injected microbubbles. Measured vessel radii and flow agreed with design values, demonstrating physiologically consistent compensatory pathways and the potential of this platform for 3D ULM biomarker development.

papers.title: Sign Coherence Beamforming for High Frame Rate Ultrasound
papers.abstract: A sign coherence beamformer is proposed to improve ultrafast ultrasound image quality while preserving the high throughput of field programmable gate array based parallel delay and sum beamforming. The method combines a sign multiplication coherence factor and a simplified sign coherence factor to suppress incoherent components using sign consistency and adjacent sign multiplication. It avoids covariance estimation, complex adaptive weighting, and square root operations. The beamformer was implemented in a parallel architecture using channel shifts and depth dependent aperture selection. Simulation, phantom, and carotid artery data were used for validation. Compared with delay and sum beamforming, the method improved image contrast and resolution. The FPGA implementation generated 128 × 2048 images at 10,557 frames/s, corresponding to 2.7 Gpixels/s, with moderate resource overhead.

papers.title: Windmill Readout with Top-Orthogonal-to-Bottom-Electrode (TOBE) Quad Arrays for Ultrafast Volumetric Imaging
papers.abstract: Ultrafast volumetric imaging has enabled groundbreaking innovations in super-resolution contrast imaging, shear-wave elastography, and more, however, clinical translation has been hindered by array technology. Both electrostrictive TOBE arrays and conventional Row-Column Arrays (RCAs) suffer from a requirement to use coherent compounding over many transmit events. When significant tissue motion is present, compounding leads to signal and resolution losses. A novel readout scheme is introduced that offers volumetric imaging with only a few transmit events, significantly faster than previous RCA methods. The approach requires a so-called TOBE QUAD array: an array composed of 4 TOBE arrays with readout from the outer edges. With only 4-16 transmit events, a high-quality volume is formed that is superior to an effective 32×32 fully-wired array (Fig. B). This can be done with any-sized TOBE array and can be done at a much faster rate than is possible with a conventional RCA. Whole aperture acquisitions are possible at 90 Vol/s. 16-transmit Windmill acquisition is possible at 180Vol/s with potential to increase to 800 Vol/s with next-generation biasing electronics.

papers.title: Air-Backed Curved Acoustic Reflectors for Elevational Beam Refocusing in Faster 3-D Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: 3-D ultrasound enables volumetric visualization but remains clinically inaccessible due to limitations of existing approaches. FASTER, a clip-on device for 3-D imaging on 1-D arrays via a rapidly tilting reflector, suffers from a divergent elevational beam that degrades resolution and a calibration procedure requiring two ultrasound systems and a water tank. We present FASTER-AIR, a two-stage diverge-and-refocus strategy that restores elevational focusing using a convex reflector followed by a concave fast-tilting reflector. The reflectors are 3-D-printed with thin walls and air-filled cores, leveraging the water-air impedance mismatch for high reflectivity. A 3-D-printed Beam Scope attachment with index tabs along the scan path enables water-tank-free, semi-automatic calibration. FASTER-AIR reduced elevational FWHM at 40 mm from 2.4 to 1.46 mm, -6 dB wire width from 2.98 to 1.39 mm, and improved anechoic-cyst CNR from 1.57 to 2.24. It also enables SIVV-based volumetric flow rate measurement, infeasible on FASTER due to its wide beamwidth, with excellent agreement with pump settings across 60-420 mL/min (Y = 1.006X + 0.172).

papers.title: Cluster-Based Sparse 2D Mut for Volumetric Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: This study investigates a clustered sparse 2D aperture for 3D ultrasound imaging as a compromise between image quality, channel count, and manufacturability. The proposed design arranges elements in dense 4×4 clusters sparsely distributed across the aperture and is compared with a classic sparse layout of similar aperture size and element count. Imaging performance was assessed using time-of-flight simulations, including point spread function resolution, sidelobe energy, contrast ratio, and gCNR in hyperechoic and anechoic cyst phantoms. Experimental validation was performed using a multiplexed matrix array configured to mimic sparse and clustered apertures. Results show that clustering preserves resolution, improves contrast ratio, and enhances global hyperechoic gCNR, while maintaining similar sidelobe energy and anechoic target detectability. Yield modeling with Poisson and Negative Binomial approaches indicates that clustered non-monolithic architectures may offer a fabrication advantage over large monolithic arrays. Overall, clustered sparse apertures show promise for practical 3D ultrasound imaging with improved manufacturability.

sessions.title: PNL: Nonlinear Physical Acoustics

papers.title: Potential-Informed Acoustic Holography for Patterned Acoustic Vortex Array Field Construction
papers.abstract: Acoustic vortex arrays hold great promise for parallel particle trapping in microfluidics and biomedicine. However, two key limitations persist: analytical methods are restricted to symmetric configurations, and conventional holographic optimization targets only pressure fields, overlooking that trapping force is governed by the Gor'kov potential. This mismatch prevents constructing arbitrarily patterned vortex arrays with stable potential wells. To address this, a potential-informed acoustic holography (PIAH) method is proposed, incorporating the Gor'kov potential into holographic inversion with two-stage gradient optimization combining field reconstruction and field–potential coupled losses to enable arbitrary vortex array construction while enforcing well stability and uniformity. Results show that PIAH successfully constructs patterned vortex array fields; compared with IASA, pressure fluctuation along vortex rings is reduced by about 60% and potential fluctuation by about 56%, confirming more stable trapping wells. In summary, PIAH offers a novel approach for constructing arbitrarily patterned vortex array fields with optimized potential wells.

papers.title: Adaptive Waveform Inversion with Source Estimation for Ultrasound Tomography
papers.abstract: Full-waveform inversion (FWI) in ultrasound tomography (UST) can produce high-resolution sound speed images but is highly sensitive to cycle skipping when low-frequency signals or accurate starting models are unavailable. Frequency-difference FWI (FD-FWI) recently emerged as a promising strategy for mitigating cycle skipping by synthesizing approximate low-frequency information, but its effectiveness remains limited in challenging scenarios. Adaptive waveform inversion (AWI), provides an alternative approach to circumvent cycle skipping by driving the estimated filter between simulated and measured signals to zero-lag. In this work, we investigate AWI with dynamic source estimation for UST and compare its performance with FD-FWI in breast and transcranial imaging simulations.

papers.title: Task-Oriented Acoustic Metamaterial Neural Encoder for Intensity-Only Compressive Object Reconstruction
papers.abstract: We propose a physics-guided Acoustic Neural Network–Digital Neural Network (ANN-DNN) framework for intensity-only compressive object reconstruction. Unlike conventional acoustic and near-field acoustic holography (NAH), which require dense phase-sensitive measurements and costly inverse solvers, our method directly reconstructs object shape from compact measurements through physical encoding. The main contribution is treating the acoustic metamaterial layer as a trainable encoder jointly optimized with a digital decoder. Composed of 3D cross-shaped unit cells with filling-ratio-tuned responses, the layer compresses a 64×64×2 complex field into a 4×4×1 intensity-only measurement, achieving 512-fold compression and 4× area reduction. The design targets 40 kHz ultrasound and stereolithography fabrication. The optimized encoder reconstructs object shapes from only 16 measurements and outperforms free-space encoding. IoU improves from 0.4988 to 0.6220 and correlation from 0.7467 to 0.8520. Under perturbation, IoU remains 0.5781 and correlation 0.8208. This paves the way for hardware-efficient ultrasonic imaging from compressed intensity-only measurements.

papers.title: Coupling the Bourret Approximation with Monte Carlo Simulation for Diffusion Characterization in Multiple Scattering Media
papers.abstract: Quantitative characterization of wave transport in heterogeneous media requires reliable estimates of effective medium parameters, yet full-wave simulations become more costly at high acoustic-impedance contrast. This work proposes a finite-domain transport framework coupling the Bourret approximation from multiple scattering theory with Monte Carlo (MC) and random walk (RW) simulations. Through the Dyson equation, Bourret gives the effective wavenumber and elastic mean free path. The associated angular scattering response defining the phase function is regularized by partial isotropization to reduce directional bias. These Bourret-derived values are then used in MC and RW simulations to extract the diffusion coefficient in finite media slabs. Compared with k-Wave, the diffusion coefficient from Bourret alone exhibits a significant error, but coupling Bourret to the MC-RW framework substantially improves agreement. This framework supports QUS-based inverse characterization of diffuse disease microstructure by linking measurable scattering observables to effective-medium transport quantities. Also, it can apply to the characterization of hepatic steatosis, fibrosis, and malignancy.

papers.title: Fast Nearfield Method Particle Velocity Expressions for a Circular Piston Compared with Rayleigh Integral and Numerical Differentiation Methods
papers.abstract: Particle velocity is required in addition to pressure for accurate evaluation of acoustic intensity, power, and radiation force, particularly in the nearfield, where diffraction and edge-wave structure strongly influence the local field. Although pressure and velocity potential formulations are well established for circular ultrasound transducers modeled as baffled circular pistons, direct expressions for transient and continuous-wave particle velocity components are generally unavailable. Numerical differentiation of the velocity potential provides a straightforward route to particle velocity, but steep nearfield gradients make this approach error-amplifying and unreliable. This motivates direct particle velocity formulations that preserve nearfield accuracy and that are computationally efficient.

papers.title: Accurate and Efficient Ultrasonic Wave Simulation Using Split-Exponential Integrator
papers.abstract: The forward modeling of wave equations is a fundamental problem in medical ultrasound imaging. Despite that many algorithms have been proposed to simulate the forward modeling, more advanced simulation tools continue to be desired for applications with an intricate environment. Here we propose a new modeling method based on the Fourier Pseudospectral Method and Split-Exponential Integration, running full-wave ultrasound simulation tasks on the OpenPros prostate dataset, and compare its performance with traditional methods like finite difference with lower or high orders, and well as the spectral-based k-wave methods. The test results have shown that the new method achieves a great balance between efficiency and accuracy, with potential to be widely applied to ultrasound waveforming problems.

sessions.title: MBB: Beam Design and Image Reconstruction Methods

papers.title: Acoustic Holography for Spherically Curved 2-D Arrays Using Ring-Bessel Propagation Model
papers.abstract: Conventional acoustic holography assumes a planar aperture, causing severe phase errors on spherically curved 2-D arrays. We present a differentiable framework extending the angular spectrum method (ASM) to curved geometries via a ring-decomposed propagation model. By dividing the surface into concentric rings treated as planar sources and applying coherent superposition, it preserves FFT efficiency while accurately capturing curved wavefronts. Phase optimization uses automatic differentiation with an adaptive multi-task loss employing homoscedastic uncertainty weighting. This jointly optimizes structural correlation, target intensity, contrast, and background suppression without manual tuning. Validations used Field II simulations and hydrophone measurements on a 128-element 1 MHz spherical sparse 2-D array. For an 8 × 4 mm target, the conventional method completely failed to shape the beam (1.67 × 1.82 mm). The proposed method successfully synthesized the beam in simulation (10.19 × 4.94 mm) and experiments (7.47 × 3.10 mm). Phase maps visually confirm active curvature compensation, proving this framework enables arbitrary beam shaping on spherical arrays.

papers.title: Trajectory-Controlled Curved Beamforming for Ultrasound Imaging in Obstructed Anatomies
papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging through bone and rib structures is often limited by acoustic impedance mismatches that disrupt wave propagation and degrade energy delivery beyond obstructed regions. To address this challenge, we investigate beamforming along prescribed curved trajectories, implemented through caustic beamforming, to enable acoustic energy to navigate around barriers rather than relying on straight-line propagation. Using k-Wave simulations with a bone-like obstruction, an aperture phase profile is synthesized to generate a parabolic curved path toward a fixed target. Compared to conventional focused steering under blockage, the proposed approach yields higher and more stable pressure at the target while maintaining a smoother and less distorted propagation pattern. These findings highlight the potential of curved trajectory beamforming, grounded in caustic physics, as a physically principled strategy for reliable energy delivery and improved ultrasound imaging in obstructed anatomies.

papers.title: An Inverse Aperture Operator Framework for Wavefield Correlation Imaging with Joint Angle Optimization
papers.abstract: Wavefield Correlation Imaging (WCI) leverages wavefield extrapolation to account for diffraction and refraction effects, offering a balance between accuracy and complexity compared to full waveform inversion. Nonetheless, recovering continuous receive wavefields from discrete element measurements is inherently ill-posed and not explicitly addressed in conventional WCI. This work proposed a model-based inverse formulation of WCI (MBI-WCI) that incorporates an aperture operator to consistently map continuous wavefields onto discrete sensor measurements, improving reconstruction quality, particularly for large-pitch arrays. Given the ill-posed nature of the problem, multiple transmit angles are jointly inverted and stabilized using Tikhonov regularization. Results in simulation and phantom experiments show that MBI-WCI preserves resolution while reducing sidelobes and artifacts, yielding improved contrast (CR, gCNR) compared to WCI and Delay-and-Sum. Moreover, this new framework enables advanced joint regularization strategies (i.e., exploiting structural similarities), with potential for high-quality imaging when using undersampled arrays.

papers.title: Decoupling Synthetic Aperture Processing via Data Re-Encoding
papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture enables powerful data processing by combining echoes from multiple transmissions for retrospective focusing and advanced spatial and temporal encodings. However, these approaches tightly couple processing with beamforming, making direct analysis and optimization challenging. We study an approach that decouples these effects by treating synthetic aperture as a re-encoding of data separate from focusing, with the goal of gaining insight into pulse sequencing and processing. The proposed approach builds on REFoCUS, which estimates a multistatic dataset from an arbitrary pulse sequence. Rather than performing pixel-wise multistatic beamforming, we recombine the data into an arbitrary transmit sequence using a separately chosen encoding matrix. These steps are combined into a single frequency-dependent matrix operation, termed re-encoding, enabling visualization of magnitude and phase interactions. This provides a flexible and interpretable framework for analyzing transmit and processing schemes. We demonstrate the use of this technique in four applications: multiline transmit, spatiotemporal encoding, acoustic window adjustment, and synthetic aperture sequencing.

papers.title: Laplace-Domain Beamforming for Ultrafast Plane-Wave Imaging
papers.abstract: Laplace-domain beamforming is proposed to improve the image quality in ultrafast plane-wave imaging with linear arrays. This type of beamforming overcomes the shortcomings of standard Fourier-domain beamforming by accounting for three spatial dimensions, the element height, and frequency-dependent absorption. These modifications yield a Laplace diffraction theorem that relates the lateral Fourier transform of the echo signals to the spatial Laplace transform of the object function. Phantom and in-vivo experiments proved the validity of this relation and, in comparison to Fourier-domain beamforming, showed improvements in spatial resolution, contrast, and image uniformity. The lateral and the axial resolution, for instance, improved by up to 13% and 23%, respectively. The computational costs were comparable. The proposed Laplace-domain beamforming, hence, is very beneficial and has the potential to improve ultrafast imaging.

papers.title: Power-Weighted Passive Acoustic Detection and Dynamic Differentiation: Mechanisms of Subspace Selection and Power Estimation
papers.abstract: Passive cavitation imaging (PCI) is widely used to monitor focused ultrasound (FUS) therapy. Passive Acoustic Detection and Dynamic Differentiation (PADAM) was recently introduced to separate cavitation sources via spectral structure across spatial principal components. However, its relationship to signal power and subspace organization is unclear. This work explores the mechanisms and extends the approach to power-based imaging. To achieve power estimation, we implement a hybrid beamforming approach where a PADAM image acts as a spectral-subspace filter over delay-sum-integrate (DSI) images, yielding power-weighted PADAM (p-PADAM), and we analyze frequency-dependent structure across eigen-subspaces derived from the spatial-covariance matrix to determine frequency correspondence of eigenvectors with spectral components. The method achieves spatial separation of stable and inertial cavitation with a CNR of 18.7, and we show that p-PADAM scales with independently measured DSI power selected in the frequency domain for harmonic components. These results define the structure underlying PADAM and establish p-PADAM as a promising approach to PCI in cavitation safety monitoring.

sessions.title: MSR: Pulses of resolution

papers.title: * INVITED * Multi-Lens Ultrasound Arrays Enable Large Scale three-Dimensional micro- Vascularization Characterization Over Whole Organs
papers.abstract: Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (ULM) enables super-resolution imaging of microvasculature but is largely limited to 2D. Extending ULM to 3D is crucial yet challenged by limited field of view, penetration, and system complexity. This work introduces a large-aperture array with acoustic lenses to reduce directivity, improving sensitivity and volumetric coverage. The approach is validated from simulations to in vivo studies, including transcranial imaging in primates, demonstrating strong potential for clinical whole-organ 3D ULM imaging.
keywords: 3D ULM / volumetric ultrafast ultrasound imaging / whole organ

papers.title: 4D Dynamic Coronary Ultrasound Localisation Microscopy in Ex Vivo Beating Mouse Heart Reveals Microvascular Perfusion Changes During the Whole Cardiac Cycle
papers.abstract: Coronary microcirculation is critical to myocardial perfusion, yet its micrometric dynamics in the beating heart remain inaccessible to current imaging tools. We developed a 4D ULM framework to capture coronary microvascular perfusion throughout the cardiac cycle in the ex vivo mouse heart. Using an 80×80 RCA probe (12.5 MHz) and an ultrafast sequence (28 plane waves, 1000 Hz), 3D images of Langendorff-perfused beating mouse hearts (N = 8, 40 mmHg) were acquired during continuous microbubble injection. Cardiac cycles were compounded into a representative cycle, with inter-cycle motion corrected at sub-wavelength accuracy via ICP registration and velocity regularization, yielding a 3D ULM map at each of 140 cardiac frames. The framework resolves vessels below 20 µm, revealing marked perfusion changes between systole and diastole, MB density varying from 305 to 736 MBs/mm³ and ~25% pulsatile velocity variation across micro- and larger vessels. This establishes a foundation for quantitative 4D ULM mapping of coronary microvascular function under physiological and pathological conditions.

papers.title: Label-Free High-Throughput Super-Resolution Tumor Microvascular Imaging
papers.abstract: High-resolution imaging of tumor microvascular structure and hemodynamics is important for cancer research because it can reveal tumor angiogenesis beyond the resolution of conventional ultrasound and enable longitudinal monitoring of vascular remodeling during treatment. However, current super-resolution ultrasound microvascular imaging methods, such as ultrasound localization microscopy, typically require microbubble contrast injections, long acquisitions, and computationally intensive localization and tracking, which limit their throughput for tumor imaging. To address these limitations, we propose a label-free, high-throughput super-resolution framework for tumor microvascular imaging using native blood-flow signals.

papers.title: Quantitative Microvessel Orientation Biomarkers for Assessing Axillary Lymph Node Metastasis in Breast Cancer
papers.abstract: Axillary lymph node (ALN) status is critical for breast cancer treatment planning but is commonly assessed using invasive biopsy. Ultrasound is the primary imaging tool for identifying suspicious ALNs, but its sensitivity remains limited. This study introduces quantitative microvessel orientation biomarkers from contrast-free ultrasound microvessel imaging to differentiate metastatic from reactive ALNs. Imaging was performed in 68 breast cancer patients with prebiopsy suspicious ALNs, including 34 metastatic and 34 reactive nodes confirmed by histopathology. Twelve orientation-related biomarkers were extracted in Cartesian and polar coordinates, including vessel count, penetration density, vessel diameter ratio, and polar-domain vessel distribution features. These biomarkers were combined into an orientation score ranging from 0 to 8, representing circumferential to penetrating vascular architecture. The orientation score alone achieved an AUC of 0.82 with sensitivity and specificity of 0.79. Combining it with clinical variables improved performance to an AUC of 0.86 and sensitivity of 0.91.

papers.title: Clinical Feasibility of Super Resolution Ultrasound and Volumetric Power Doppler Imaging of Prostate Cancer
papers.abstract: The correlation between prostate vascularity and malignancy risk is well established in prostate cancer. Current clinical imaging techniques, such as dynamic contrast-enhanced MRI, lack the specificity to distinguish between malignant growth, prostatitis, and benign prostatic hyperplasia, and often underestimate prostate cancer volume due to limited resolution. Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM), a super-resolution vascular imaging technique, addresses these limitations by providing microvascular-scale resolution to enable precise delineation of tumor boundaries. This is a prospective, single-arm pilot study of patients undergoing radical prostatectomy (RP) for prostate cancer to investigate ULM’s ability to provide insights into the tumor microvascular environment.

sessions.title: TMI: Multimodal Transducers and Applications

papers.title: * INVITED * Ultrasound-Based Multimodal Integrated Interventional and Wearable Platforms for Diagnosis and Treatment
papers.abstract: Biomedical ultrasound is widely used for medical imaging and intervention, but ultrasound alone is insufficient for precision diagnosis and therapy. To address this limitation, we developed ultrasound-based multimodal diagnosis-and-treatment platforms integrating optical and electrical modalities. By leveraging complementary contrast, penetration depth, and spatial resolution, these platforms enable comprehensive assessment of tissue structure, function, and molecular information, while supporting ultrasound-mediated targeted delivery and real-time treatment guidance. Based on these platforms, we developed an ultrasonic–optical–electrical interventional system for dynamic visualization and precise ablation of pancreaticobiliary lesions, an optical–ultrasonic wearable patch for continuous carotid monitoring, and an ultrasound-based in vivo targeted delivery system for functional carriers. Together, these studies establish multimodal interventional and wearable platforms that enable closed-loop coordination of multiscale diagnosis and multifunctional therapy, improving the precision and spatiotemporal synchronization of diagnosis and treatment.

papers.title: Fiber-Coupled Acousto-Optic Ultrasound Probe for Miniaturized in Vivo Photoacoustic Imaging
papers.abstract: Miniaturized photoacoustic imaging (PAI) probes are essential for disease diagnosis but remain difficult to scale due to bulky interconnects and signal degradation. This work presents a fiber-based acousto-optic architecture converting acoustic signals into optical intensity modulation, enabling compact readout via an optical fiber. The probe integrates a ScAlN bimorph pMUT with a ScAlN-cavity optical microresonator (OMR) defined by Bragg mirrors and transparent electrodes. Acoustic waves drive the pMUT, generating a voltage that modulates the OMR resonance. Operating at the maximum slope of the OMR reflectance curve converts this into detectable reflected light intensity changes. The devices were assembled on a PCB with the fiber-coupled OMR on one side and the pMUT facing the acoustic field on the other. Testing with a 5 MHz ultrasonic transducer demonstrated successful end-to-end signal transduction, achieving 0.36 mV/kPa sensitivity. Impedance matching between pMUT and OMR could improve sensitivity by up to 10×. These results establish proof-of-concept for pMUT-OMR integration, motivating acousto-optic arrays for endoscopic PAI applications such as bladder cancer assessment.

papers.title: Phase-Free Multi-Focus Axial Acoustic Field Synthesis via Inverse Design of Photoacoustic Emitters
papers.abstract: Programmable multi-focus acoustic field generation without electronic phase control remains challenging, especially when precise axial spacing and low crosstalk are both required. This work presents a target-driven inverse design framework for synthesizing manufacturable photoacoustic (PA) emitter arrays that generate controllable multi-focus axial acoustic fields. An axial-profile-first strategy was developed to map a desired multi-peak axial response directly to array geometry. A target profile with three focal depths was decomposed using hypothesis-guided nonnegative least-squares fitting, and each component was assigned to a curved-patch emitter family with tunable geometric parameters. Candidate arrays were ranked using a multi-objective cost function incorporating profile error, focal overlap, compactness, aspect ratio, and interleaving. The optimized design consisted of three interleaved curved-patch layers and was validated by point-source forward calculation and full-wave k-Wave simulation. Simulations showed three axial focal maxima at 3.4, 8.6, and 11.4 mm, confirming the feasibility of geometry-driven, phase-free multi-focus acoustic field synthesis.

papers.title: Fiber-Tip Optical Ultrasound Probe for Acoustic Detection Induced by Ultra-High Dose Rate (UHDR) Electron Beam
papers.abstract: Online dose mapping is essential for safe and accurate beam delivery in FLASH radiation therapy (RT). While ionizing radiation acoustic imaging (iRAI) enables real-time, deep tissue dose measurement and beam localization for RT, previous piezoelectric acoustic sensors have suffered from electronic noise and neutron damage from ultra-high dose rate radiation (UHDR) beam. We report an innovative single-element full-optical surface-micromachined optical ultrasound transducer (SMOUT) mounted on an optical fiber tip to detect acoustic waves induced by UHDR beam. The design and fabrication of the fiber-tip SMOUT probe have been demonstrated, and its optical and acoustic characteristics, as well as transmittance to the FLASH electron beam and imaging capability have been characterized. Experiments show the probe exhibits negligible disturbance to UHDR beams. After 1-D scanning the probe, the 2-D dose distribution of the UHDR beam can be mapped with high consistency. These findings highlight the potential of SMOUT based iRAI for mapping the dose distribution under UHDR beam, which is an important step toward practical implementation of iRAI-based online dosimetry in FLASH RT.

papers.title: Impact of Titanium Encapsulation and ECoG Electrodes on the Acoustic Field of an UltrasoundECoG Implant Prototype : An Experimental Study
papers.abstract: Our group developed a 64-channel ECoG device to restore movement in disabled patients. To close the sensorimotor loop, we aim to integrate intracranial ultrasound (IUS) for chronic sensory feedback. However, clinical implants require biocompatible enclosures (typically titanium), whose effect on ultrasound fields remains poorly characterized. We investigate how Ti encapsulation and platinum ECoG electrodes affect a PZT transducer's pressure field. A PZT transducer was tested in three configurations: (1) bare in water; (2) mounted in the Ti housing; (3) with a platinum electrode array and silicone layer added. Pressure fields were mapped via hydrophone. PZT-on-Ti compatibility was assessed by recording ECoG noise on 4 electrodes with and without 60 Vpp ultrasound. The unoptimized Ti casing attenuates ultrasound comparably to skull, yet platinum electrodes partially counteract this by focusing the beam, recovering near-bare-transducer pressures at ~2 mm depth. Resolution reached 2.43 mm (z) and 1.48 mm (x). ECoG recordings showed no signal degradation with PZT integration. These results support IUS as a viable sensorimotor loop closure strategy.

sessions.title: MTN: Neuromodulation and Brain Theranostics

papers.title: Noninvasive Dose Estimation and Efficacy Prediction of FUS-Triggered Drug Release in Epileptic Rats via Acoustic Droplet Vaporization
papers.abstract: Conventional epilepsy pharmacotherapy lacks spatial specificity and real-time monitoring. We developed a BBB-sparing theranostic platform using propofol-loaded nanodroplets (Pro-NDs, 95.2±1.0 μg/mL) synthesized via avidin–biotin conjugation and pressurized recondensation (size: 2.90 μm to 605.3 nm). The system integrates 2.1-MHz FUS with a 7.5-MHz probe for real-time acoustic droplet vaporization (ADV) monitoring. Pro-NDs showed robust stability (leakage <22.1% at 4 hr) and high biocompatibility. Under FUS (1.5, 2.0, 2.5 MPa), Pro-NDs exhibited significant pressure-dependent contrast and linear drug release (R²=0.99), peaking at 38.0±3.7%. In vivo, increasing pressure expanded vaporization volumes (up to3.96 mm²) and cumulative differential intensity (CDI) up to 3.7-fold vs. control. In PTZ-induced epileptic rats, FUS-triggered release suppressed seizure spikes by up to 52.4±7.4% at 2.5 MPa. Notably, CDI values highly correlated with spike inhibition (R²=0.96), enabling noninvasive efficacy prediction. Histology confirmed BBB integrity and zero tissue damage even at 2.5 MPa. This platform provides a safe, quantitative strategy for precision imaging-guided neuromodulation.

papers.title: Transcranial 4D Functional Ultrasound Imaging Combined with Focused Ultrasound neuromodulation Can Modulate and Monitor Brain Activity in Awake Behaving Mice
papers.abstract: Non-invasive tools that can modulate and monitor brain circuits are critical for understanding circuit function and enabling non-invasive brain-machine interfaces. Here, transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) neuromodulation is combined with 4D functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) into a single non-invasive tool for circuit modulation and monitoring. Four awake, head-fixed mice underwent simultaneous fUSI and tFUS neuromodulation during a reach-to-grasp task (1 reach/15 s). Reach and neuromodulation aligned activation maps were computed from power Doppler signal using generalized linear models. Activation was detected in the focal region, matching the expected focal width. At the highest pressure, reach attempts and velocity decreased by 34% and 27%, with partial recovery by 63 min and full recovery by 14 days. Velocity decreased with pressure, while reach attempts were unaffected at lower parameters but ceased entirely at the highest. H&E and Fluoro-Jade C histology showed no damage or neurodegeneration. These results establish ultrasound as a non-invasive platform for reversible circuit modulation and monitoring, enabling closed-loop ultrasound-based brain-machine interfaces.

papers.title: Transcranial Blood–Brain Barrier Opening with Real-Time, High-Resolution Ultrasound–Guidance Using a Diagnostic Probe
papers.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS) is a non-invasive method to open the blood-brain barrier, enabling drug delivery to the brain. Current systems offer limited insight into the underlying vasculature, leaving vascular dynamics around blood–brain barrier opening (BBBO) poorly characterized, thereby limiting safety and efficacy. To address these gaps, we introduce a single transducer, high frequency platform enabling accurate transcranial targeting, real time monitoring, and ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) to guide and assess BBBO. Results showed real-time feedback from cavitation imaging aligned with BBB opening regions. A temporary fivefold drop in Doppler signal during treatment was observed. ULM provided high-resolution mapping of microvascular activity, though no major changes in flow or microbubble count were observed before and after BBBO.

papers.title: Ultrasound-Guided FUS System for Targeted Gene Therapy for Brain Tumors
papers.abstract: While MB-FUS can enhance drug delivery to brain tumors, existing systems lack integrated real-time imaging, beam-steered targeting, and microbubble monitoring. Furthermore, delivery assessment methods lack noninvasive in vivo imaging for spatial and longitudinal tracking. We developed an ultrasound-guided FUS (USgFUS) platform (1.5 MHz, 128-element 2D array with integrated L12-5 imaging transducer) providing real-time tumor visualization via contrast-enhanced ultrasound, phased-array beam-steered therapy, and passive acoustic mapping of microbubble dynamics. To enable noninvasive longitudinal tracking, we employed in vivo PET imaging of 64Cu-radiolabeled AAV9 and fluorescent reporter expression to quantify vector biodistribution and transgene expression in the GL26 glioma mouse model. At 21 hours post-injection, 64Cu-AAV9 accumulation was 3.2-fold higher in FUS-treated tumors (p=0.004), with 6.4-fold increase in AAV genome copies via qPCR (p=0.0003). Enhanced delivery translated into 5.3-fold increased reporter expression at 17 days (p=0.0002). Our USgFUS platform with PET imaging enables precise, quantifiable AAV delivery and longitudinal monitoring for brain tumor gene therapy.

papers.title: MR-Guided Focused Ultrasound Blood Brain Barrier Opening Enables Targeted, Small Volume GABA Neuromodulation
papers.abstract: Array-based ultrasound devices can temporarily disrupt the blood–brain barrier (BBB) with high spatial specificity, enabling the targeted delivery of neuromodulatory agents to deep brain regions. Here, we evaluated whether small volume BBB opening (BBBO) guided by magnetic resonance acoustic radiation force imaging (MR-ARFI) could facilitate focal delivery of γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) to the putamen of macaque monkeys and modulate tactile-evoked fMRI responses.

papers.title: AI-Driven Vascular Neuro-Navigation for Targeted Focused Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Precise anatomical targeting is essential for focused ultrasound (FUS) neuromodulation, but current MRI-based or post-hoc histology approaches lack accessible real-time intraoperative feedback. We propose an AI-driven vascular neuro-navigation system that leverages Power Doppler (PD) imaging together with a SegFormer-based vision transformer to simultaneously predict anterior-posterior (AP) coordinates and segment brain regions from cerebrovascular patterns. Volumetric PD scans (15 MHz, 150 µm step) of 32 mice yielded 24,000 coronal slices, which were atlas-registered and SVD clutter-filtered to train a single-stream hierarchical transformer encoder with two MLP heads: a 264-bin AP classifier and a 23-class regional segmentation head. The model achieved an AP mean absolute error of 0.07 mm with 76.5% of samples within the 0.1 mm FUS targeting margin, and a mean Dice coefficient of 0.8964 across primary regions including somatosensory cortex (0.961), hippocampus (0.943), and thalamus (0.931). This system enables accessible, real-time, precision non-invasive neuromodulation by replacing costly MRI registration with vasculature-based navigation.

sessions.title: NSP: Signal Processing and Underwater Acoustics

papers.title: Physics-Informed Adaptive Inversion for Feature Recovery in Degraded Ultrasonic A-Scans
papers.abstract: Ultrasonic A-scan signals are often degraded by attenuation and coupling variability, obscuring critical features such as interface reflections and weak structural responses. Conventional methods based on fixed assumptions or denoising are not robust under varying acquisition conditions and often fail in low signal-to-noise ratio regimes. This work presents a physics-informed adaptive inversion framework for feature recovery from degraded ultrasonic A-scans. The method integrates parametric modeling of the acquisition process with sparsity-constrained reconstruction and incorporates an embedded deconvolution mechanism to jointly estimate system response and reflectivity. Experimental evaluation on controlled and real inspection data shows improved separability of closely spaced reflections by 14.7% and enhanced detection of low-amplitude reflections by 3 dB compared to conventional approaches. The method maintains reliable performance across varying signal qualities, with results in degraded cases validated against destructive testing.

papers.title: DINO-Based Vision Transformers for Ultrasonic Flaw Detection Without Pretraining
papers.abstract: This work proposes the use of the DINO (Self Distillation with No Labels) self-supervised learning algorithm for multi-class flaw detection in NDT applications. The DINO algorithm can be trained on a set of unlabeled ultrasonic signal data, thereby overcoming the limitation of lack of well-labeled field data or experiments. We implement a computationally efficient DINO framework which is designed with a vision transformer, test it on experimental ultrasonic NDT benchmark data and compare the performance against other supervised and self-supervised learning algorithms.

papers.title: Approximate Delay-and-Sum Beamforming for Diverging-Wave Imaging of Pipes
papers.abstract: Rapid nondestructive testing of liquid-filled steel pipes can be accomplished using diverging-wave (DW) ultrasound imaging, where an immersed phased-array probe emits several DW pulses at different steering angles and records the resulting backscattered signals. This work presents an approximate delay-and-sum beamforming method for simplified multimode image reconstruction of inspected pipe sections. The targeted application context is characterization of surface-breaking cracks in pipe walls, and we show that our approach yields sufficiently accurate images for subsequent defect localization and sizing.

papers.title: Experimental Validation of Enhanced Ultrasonic Testing Using Optimal Code–Based FDTR and Wiener Filtering
papers.abstract: Pulse compression is widely used in ultrasonic and radar systems to enhance axial resolution and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). Although longer codes improve SNR while preserving resolution, conventional matched filtering cannot fully decode signals in truncated ranges. To overcome this limitation, the optimal code–based Full Decoding of Truncated Ranges (FDTR) method enables complete decoding across all gates, including near-surface regions. However, in ultrasonic testing, system-induced distortion—mainly from transducer characteristics—degrades decoding accuracy and effective SNR. To address this issue, Wiener filtering is integrated into the FDTR framework to compensate for distortion and noise. Experimental results show that FDTR alone cannot clearly resolve closely spaced targets within truncated ranges. In contrast, the proposed hybrid approach successfully separates the targets, suppresses sidelobes, and improves peak localization. These results demonstrate enhanced defect detectability and reliable performance without requiring any modification to the hardware configuration.

papers.title: FPGA System Design for Edge Inference Using Air-Coupled Ultrasonic Array Sensing
papers.abstract: This work presents an FPGA-based edge inference system for real-time air-coupled ultrasonic array sensing. The proposed MPSoC platform integrates programmable acoustic focusing, multi-channel signal preprocessing, and on-chip CNN inference to enable low-latency shape recognition. Preliminary results show that the CNN-based approach provides clearer and more robust object recognition than traditional Delay-and-Sum beamforming.

papers.title: Class-Conditioned Target Source Extraction with Acoustic Signature Prototypes for Multi-Source Underwater Ship Noise Separation
papers.abstract: Underwater ship noise separation has largely been studied under two-source conditions due to two limitations of Blind Source Separation with Permutation Invariant Training (BSS-PIT): limited use of class-discriminative information and unstable N! permutation search as the source count grows. We propose a class-conditioned Target Source Extraction framework using Class-level Acoustic Signature (CAS) prototypes injected via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), reducing pairwise inter-class similarity from 0.83 to 0.35 in the embedding space. On the DeepShip benchmark, the proposed method achieves 4.2 dB SI-SNR at two sources, compared with 3.5 dB for BSS-PIT, and retains 0.7 dB at five sources, where BSS-PIT drops below the unseparated mixture (-1.3 dB). These results support class-level conditioning as a viable direction for underwater ship noise separation beyond BSS-PIT.

sessions.title: MCL: Clinical Session

papers.title: * INVITED * Ultrasound Imaging of Peripheral Nerve and Muscle: Clinical Applications
papers.abstract: Neuromuscular ultrasound (NMUS) is increasingly seen as an essential in providing care for diseases of nerve and muscle. The clinical application of B-mode imaging in the assessment of peripheral nerve trauma, nerve compression syndrome, polyneuropathies, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, and disorders of the muscle will be reviewed through case examples and current scientific evidence. The advantages and limitations of B-mode NMUS will be addressed alongside novel ultrasound imaging approaches, including shear wave elastography imaging and optoacoustic imaging.

papers.title: * INVITED * In vivo evaluation of safety and performance of a novel microbubble enhanced ultrasound pharmacomechanical procedure in animal models and initial human clinical trials
papers.abstract: Background: Venous thromboembolism is a common clinical event, reported to cause up to 100,000 deaths annually in the U.S. A novel, pharmaco-mechanical device (ST system) was designed to eliminate acute thrombus from the vasculature. Methods: The ST system* was evaluated for safety and performance in a swine model of iliac vein thrombosis. Safety was evaluated by examination of the treated vessels following necropsy. A pilot study using the ST system in patients with acute DVT was completed to determine the feasibility and safety of the system in clinical use. Results: In the animal model, MMS was performed on clot for an average of 18 minutes. Forward flow restoration was achieved in all cases. Necropsy revealed no significant damage to the vessel walls. In the clinical trial in patients with acute DVT, clot elimination was achieved to re-establish flow in all patients. Conclusions: In a porcine DVT model and an initial human feasibility trial, a new microbubble enhanced ultrasound device was found to significantly reduce thrombus burden while preserving the vein walls. This data supports evaluation of this novel technology in a pivotal prospective human clinical trial.

papers.title: * INVITED * Mapping the Future of Neurosonography: Where We Stand and What’s Next
papers.abstract: While conventional cranial ultrasound remains the bedside standard for neonatal neuroimaging, its traditional reliance on structural grayscale imaging fails to capture real-time functional and perfusion changes in the developing brain. To address this limitation, recent advancements have pushed neurosonography beyond anatomy into advanced functional domains, integrating techniques like contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) and microvascular imaging to track cerebral blood flow and hemodynamic fluctuations directly at the bedside. This talk will provide a comprehensive overview of the current shift from structural grayscale to advanced functional neurosonography in the clinic, while mapping out the critical translational breakthroughs, technical limitations, and collaborative industry partnerships needed to shape the future of neonatal neuroimaging.

sessions.title: MIS: Wave Propagation & Aberration Mitigation

papers.title: Fast, Open-Source Simulation of Ultrasound Scattering
papers.abstract: Mesh-free acoustic simulators, such as Field II and SIMUS, are widely used to design ultrasound sequences and synthesize realistic datasets. Publicly available implementations remain slow, limiting interactive sequence design and large-scale data generation. We present an open-source implementation of the SIMUS mesh-free, frequency-domain Fraunhofer model of ultrasound scattering. We re-architected the algorithm for GPU parallelism and memory access patterns via custom Metal and CUDA kernels, enabling significant speedups on Apple Silicon and NVIDIA GPUs For 1 000 000 scatterers under a 64-element phased array, simulation time drops from 320 s to 0.060 s (NVIDIA RTX 4090, 5278× speedup). We verified that our simulated pressure fields and RF signals numerically matched the reference implementation. Accelerated by commonly available hardware, this simulator vastly accelerates common workflows for the many researchers and engineers relying on mesh-free acoustic simulation.

papers.title: k-Space Finite-Difference Passive Acoustic Mapping for Accurate Source Localization in Strong Aberrating Media
papers.abstract: A k-space finite-difference propagation (k-FDP) method was developed for passive acoustic mapping in strongly heterogeneous media. Using PVC and perforated epoxy aberrators, hydrophone signals, and a 96-element array, sound-speed maps were used for phase correction. k-FDP reduced localization errors to 0.65 and 0.19 mm, outperforming heterogeneous angular spectrum (AS)-based methods, AS-GF and AS-FSS, by 71–85%, showing promise for cavitation monitoring in transcranial therapy.

papers.title: Transcranial Ultrasound Imaging via Eikonal-Based Aberration Correction and Automated Murine Skull Boundary Extraction
papers.abstract: Transcranial ultrasound is vital for non-invasive neurovascular monitoring but suffers from phase aberrations due to skull speed-of-sound (SoS) heterogeneity. Standard reconstruction assuming a uniform 1540 m/s SoS compromises SNR and resolution, causing severe distortion beneath the skull. We present an automated pipeline for murine skull boundary extraction and eikonal-based aberration correction. Initially, the superior skull surface is segmented from B-mode data using a gradient vector flow active contour to initialize a SoS map. An eikonal-based beamformer then reconstructs the image, enabling inferior boundary localization and SoS map refinement. The workflow was validated via $k$-Wave simulations using CT-derived ground truths and ex vivo mouse skull experiments with a needle target. Results show the final SoS map achieves high fidelity to ground truth with minimal interface discrepancies. While standard 1540 m/s beamforming fails to resolve the needle, the iterative refinement successfully restores target contrast and spatial resolution. This adaptive approach effectively compensates for phase aberrations, ensuring image integrity for intracranial targets.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Frequency Filtering Enhances Bone Interface Imaging in Quantitative Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Spatiotemporal frequency filtering is proposed to improve cortical bone interface imaging in quantitative ultrasound. In bone, incoherent scattering produces spatially decorrelated signals, while specular reflections from cortical interfaces remain highly coherent. Conventional delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming does not exploit this distinction, leading to reduced contrast and blurred interfaces. We introduce a frequency-wavenumber domain beamforming approach that selectively preserves low-frequency, low-wavenumber components associated with coherent reflections. The method was validated using simulations, a bone-mimicking phantom, and in vivo tibia measurements. Compared to DAS, the proposed approach improves contrast and contrast-to-noise ratio, particularly for weak or oblique reflections. Enhanced interface visibility also reduces variability in backscatter coefficient estimation. The method is compatible with real-time implementation via GPU-accelerated FFT and provides a robust foundation for downstream quantitative analysis in bone ultrasound.

papers.title: Contrast-Free Spectral Deconvolution with Short-Lag Spatial Coherence Beamforming for Vascular Ultrasound
papers.abstract: This work introduces a contrast-free variant of pulse inversion spectral deconvolution that replaces phase-inverted pulse pairs with two independent Gaussian derivative function kernels tuned to tissue and erythrocyte spectral bands, combined with short-lag spatial coherence beamforming. Results demonstrate the ability to enable more reliable contrast-free vascular imaging without microbubble contrast agents.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Cavitation Control via Eigen-Subspace Separation of Passive Acoustic Signals

sessions.title: MIM: Advanced Methods for Image Reconstruction and Analysis

papers.title: Ultrasound Speed-of-Sound Shift Imaging for Spatiotemporal Monitoring of Clot Formation and Lysis
papers.abstract: Monitoring blood clot formation and thrombolysis is important for treatment assessment. Tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) is widely used for thrombolysis, motivating quantitative monitoring of clot lysis efficacy. We present dense speed-of-sound shift imaging (DSI), a noninvasive ultrasound framework for spatiotemporal monitoring of clot formation and lysis using B-mode data from a single imaging transducer. The framework estimates interframe displacements with optical flow and reconstructs slowness-shift maps through a regularized inverse problem, from which relative speed-of-sound (SoS) shifts are derived. DSI captures spatially localized, temporally evolving SoS shifts across systems with increasing complexity, including fibrin clots and porcine blood. In fibrin, fibrinogen increases SoS shift magnitude, and thrombin accelerates clotting kinetics. In porcine blood, DSI successfully tracks both clotting and tPA-mediated thrombolysis, revealing the kinetic asymmetry between rapid clot formation and slower clot breakdown. These results support DSI as a simple ultrasound-based approach for quantitative monitoring of clot-related material dynamics using standard imaging data.

papers.title: Large-Scale Radiologist Evaluation of Iterative Model-Based Distributed Aberration Correction on 319 in Vivo Human Liver Acquisitions
papers.abstract: B-mode image defocusing presents a significant clinical challenge in the difficult-to-image population where increased fat layers introduce wavefront aberrations. Previously, we developed an iterative model-based method that enables simultaneous sound speed estimation and aberration correction. We now demonstrate strong clinical value in aberration correction through an ongoing image-analysis-based multi-task multi-reader ultrasound radiological study. Through this study, readers evaluate aberration-corrected images (using our iterative model) against conventional beamforming (1540 m/s sound speed assumption) on 319 in vivo liver acquisitions from 81 high-BMI subjects. Study results reveal a significant reader-preference towards aberration-corrected B-modes (84% preference) over conventional B-modes (11% preference) and an increase in diagnostic image visibility (18% percent increase). Furthermore, significant beneficial results occur such as changes in target size and shape, target clarity, and improved target border sharpness. These preliminary study results demonstrate objective clinical value for the future of iterative model-based distributed aberration correction.

papers.title: Pulse-Echo Sound-Speed Imaging Using Conditional Diffusion Models
papers.abstract: Speed-of-sound (SoS) is a quantitative biomarker for applications such as breast cancer, sarcopenia, and fatty liver disease. Analytical pulse-echo SoS imaging methods typically require extensive preprocessing, full channel data access, and carefully tuned regularization. Typical deep learning (DL) methods rely on large, carefully designed datasets, and often struggle to generalize from simulation to real data, hence remain insufficiently validated on clinical data. We propose a model-based DL framework for SoS imaging using conditional diffusion models, enabling training with limited data while yielding improved generalization.

papers.title: Real-Time Abdominal Ultrasound Scan View Recognition via Spatial Viewpoint Reasoning with HiCAT
papers.abstract: Abdominal ultrasound (US) scan views are standardized, but recognition remains difficult due to patient variability and image complexity, requiring expert operators. Conventional deep learning approaches relying on local appearance are unstable under such variability. In addition, explainable AI (XAI) is essential since freehand US lacks spatial alignment. We propose a Hierarchical Context Aggregation Transformer (HiCAT), which reformulates scan view recognition as a spatial viewpoint reasoning problem. HiCAT encodes input patches into multi-scale representations and applies cross-attention to integrate local and global features. Tokens are aggregated via multiple instance learning (MIL), enabling visualization of decision evidence through token weights.
