Temporal MIL is further applied to handle occlusion and motion artifacts. Evaluated on 35 subjects with 13 standard views, HiCAT achieved 96.9% accuracy, outperforming strong baselines by +4.6%. It also provides interpretable visual evidence and supports real-time inference (~144 Hz), demonstrating potential for reliable US guidance.

papers.title: Multi‑parameter Ultrasound Intelligent Diagnosis System for BI‑RADS 4 Breast Tumors Based on Segmentation‑Assisted Dual‑Dimensional Feature Fusion
papers.abstract: BI‑RADS 4 breast tumors have a wide malignancy risk (2–95%), causing high diagnostic uncertainty. This paper proposes a multi‑parameter ultrasound intelligent diagnosis system with segmentation‑assisted dual‑dimensional feature fusion, comprising USFD‑Net (segmentation) and FDC‑Net (classification). Using multi‑modal ultrasound data, the system introduces segmentation masks as spatial priors via a shallow LAAM module and cross‑fuses features via a deep SIMI module. On 1,528 pathologically proven BI‑RADS 4 tumors, USFD‑Net and FDC‑Net outperform existing methods; with segmentation‑assisted fusion, the classification model achieves 79.83% ACC, 84.76% AUC, and 76.88% F1. Grad‑CAM shows attention focused on tumor regions. Results confirm the strategy significantly improves diagnosis and provides new insights for heterogeneous multi‑task learning.

papers.title: Fourier-DeepONet-F: an Efficient Neural Operator for Robust Speed-of-Sound Reconstruction in Single-Patch Ultrasound Computed Tomography
papers.abstract: Wearable ultrasound computed tomography faces challenges of limited angles, ill-posedness, and computational intensity, hindering fast and accurate SoS reconstruction from a miniaturized patch. We propose Fourier-DeepONet-F, a neural operator that adapts to variable-position transducer arrays. Unlike conventional Fourier-DeepONet, it uses 2D coordinate trunk inputs, layer‑wise receiver dimension transformation, group normalization, and GeLU. We also contribute a synthetic dataset of 50k SoS‑ultrasound pairs simulated with k‑Wave using 32 transducers at varying positions. On our dataset, Fourier-DeepONet‑F reduces convergence time by 40% and inference time by 53% compared to Fourier-DeepONet, but preserving comparable image quality. It also shows significantly stronger generalization and robustness than InversionNet and NIO, reconstructing tiny inclusions in challenging scenarios. This approach holds clinical promise for enabling fast speed-of-sound imaging on wearable ultrasound devices, facilitating point-of-care screening and continuous health monitoring.

sessions.title: MSD: High-Performance Architectures and Real-Time Ultrasound Systems

papers.title: High-Throughput and Resource-Efficient FPGA Beamforming for Ultrasound Imaging Using Delay Approximation- Initial Results
papers.abstract: Ultrasound beamforming is computationally intensive due to high data rates and complex delay calculations, limiting real-time implementation on resource-constrained hardware. This work presents FPGA implementations of CFB-DAS and the diverging-beam BF2 using a Taylor-based delay approximation to reduce complexity. In CFB-DAS, 32 inputs are summed per cycle, while 64 inputs are computed in parallel per clock cycle to form a low-resolution sample, and 57 such samples are accumulated to generate a 32-bit output. Exact delay computation is infeasible on XC7ZU5EG-SFVC784; hence, a linear approximation reduces the operations to one multiply-add per channel. Experimental validation using AFE5832, XC7A100T, and a 5 MHz probe shows CFB-DAS achieves 1500 fps with 94% DSP, 95% FF, and 98% LUT reduction (22% BRAM), while BF2 achieves 26 fps with 88%, 97%, and 98% reductions (44% BRAM), with minimal LR/AR degradation.

papers.title: Real-Time Wide-Field-of-View Row-Column Imaging Using an Elliptical Lens
papers.abstract: Row-column arrays (RCAs) perform 3D imaging with low channel counts, but their field of view (FOV) is limited because emissions can only be steered electronically in the elevation direction. To overcome this limitation, we propose a simple elliptical-cylinder lens that transforms the laterally unsteered, planar emission into a spherical wavefront. Since spherical wavefronts have a simple time-of-flight function, this approach halves the number of ray-tracing calculations required. The simple design also enables the use of a fast, dual-stage beamforming algorithm. Evaluated using K-Wave simulations, the proposed lens increased the FOV by 50°, and real-time volumetric beamforming was demonstrated. Ultimately, by expanding the FOV without compromising processing speed or resolution, this lens might enable the integration of large-organ 3D ultrasound into routine clinical practice.

papers.title: A GPU-Based Real-Time Ultrafast Ultrasound Sensitive Imaging System for Human Placental Blood Flow Imaging
papers.abstract: We developed a GPU-based real-time ultrafast ultrasound system for placental blood flow imaging on a Verasonics Vantage NXT 256 research scanner. Using an ensemble length of 32 and spatiotemporal filtering, the system achieved real-time frame rates of 40-55 fps for B-mode imaging and 6-9 fps for power flow imaging, depending on imaging parameters. The results demonstrate that GPU-accelerated ultrafast imaging enables real-time, high-sensitivity placental blood flow visualization, showing the potential for clinical translation in early detection of placental abnormalities.

papers.title: Real‑Time GPU‑Accelerated f‑k Beamforming for High‑Frame‑Rate Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: This work introduces a high-performance, GPU-accelerated beamforming pipeline based on the frequency-wavenumber (f-k) Stolt mapping algorithm for plane-wave (PW) ultrasound. While f-k methods offer superior image quality, their computational demands have traditionally limited real-time use. We overcome this by implementing a modular Producer-Consumer architecture in CUDA, utilizing NVIDIA Inter-Process Communication (IPC) to stream RF data directly to GPU memory, reducing host-side bottlenecks. The pipeline includes apodization, evanescent-wave suppression, and Stolt interpolation, ensuring lossless, real-time synchronization. Performance was validated on both 64-channel ultraportable and 256-channel systems data using NVIDIA RTX 3070/5080 GPUs. Results show frame rates up to 10 kHz for 64×512-pixel images and a peak throughput of 749 MSamples/s for larger 256×2048 frames, with a 10 ms average latency. This scalable framework enables high-quality ultrafast imaging on diverse hardware, providing a foundation for advanced flow and functional ultrasound.

papers.title: A New Open and Scalable High-Channel-Count Medical Ultrasound Research Platform
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a new open medical ultrasound research platform that relies on a modular architecture based on unitary 64-channel boards that integrate both transmit and receive functionalities, enabling scalable configurations ranging from 64 to 1024 channels. The architecture ensures accurate channel synchronization, high data throughput (up to 1 GB/s per 64 channels), and efficient system integration within a compact footprint. Each channel includes a programmable pulser implemented as an arbitrary waveform generator, capable of generating complex excitation signals, extending the range of possible imaging and therapeutic applications. On the software side, the platform provides a flexible programming environment with high-level APIs compatible with Python, MATLAB and C++, supporting sequence design, data acquisition, and real-time beamforming. The system has been tested for various imaging modes including 3D B-mode and 3D Doppler imaging. The combination of scalable hardware and flexible software makes the proposed platform a versatile tool for advanced medical ultrasound research, targeting both academic laboratories and early-stage industrial developments.

papers.title: A Flexible Research Platform for Real-Time Multi-Probe Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Multi-probe ultrasound imaging enhances field of view and angular coverage but traditionally relies on multiple synchronized scanners and offline processing. To overcome these limitations, we present a dedicated multi-probe research platform enabling real-time acquisition, beamforming, and processing from a single scanner. The system integrates four 64-element CMUT arrays with a 256-channel ULA-OP 256 scanner. Modular mechanical supports provide flexible coplanar alignment, offering either an arc-shaped isocenter configuration of probes or independent roto-translation of each probe. A MATLAB GUI enables users to design custom transmit-receive sequences. Real-time processing, including DAS/FDMAS beamforming on shared or independent spatial grids, coherent compounding, and Doppler modalities, is accelerated by on-system DSPs and a GPU. Results demonstrate real-time dual-probe coherent B-mode imaging. Sustainable pulse repetition frequencies range from 500 Hz (2048x384 grid) to 7600 Hz (512x64 grid). By eliminating offline bottlenecks, this platform facilitates the real-time development and testing of advanced multi-probe techniques like vector velocity imaging and elastography.

sessions.title: PPN: Phononics & Nonlinear Physical Acoustics

papers.title: * INVITED * Microwave phononic integrated circuits for sensing and analog computing
papers.abstract: Phononic (acoustic-wave) integrated circuits offer unique advantages for sensing and analog computing beyond conventional electronic and optical platforms. In this talk, I will highlight our recent advances in a mid-infrared detector based on phononic-crystal oscillators, achieving picowatt-per-root-hertz sensitivity while maintaining bandwidths exceeding 10 kHz. I will then discuss our frequency-domain analog computing approach based on nonlinear phononic devices. Finally, I will outline a vision for phononic integrated circuits as a unified and versatile platform for sensing, computation, and quantum information processing.

papers.title: A 3D Printed Polymeric Ultrasonic Metamaterial with Underwater Acoustic Bandgaps
papers.abstract: An acoustic bandgap (ABG) is a frequency range over which acoustic wave propagation is suppressed by an engineered metamaterial (MM). Such ABGs can be tailored to block, guide, or concentrate ultrasonic waves, enabling underwater applications in filtering, beam shaping, and sensing. Metal 3D printing has previously been reported to fabricate 3D MMs. However, it often involves substantial manufacturing complexity and can be cost prohibitive. In this study, a polymeric and potentially disposable ultrasonic MM is designed and fabricated using widely employed fused deposition modeling to generate underwater ABGs, offering an alternative for a range of applications.

papers.title: Nonlinear Coefficients in PZT and lead-Free Piezoelectric Transducers Determined from Constant Current Amplitude Admittance Measurements
papers.abstract: Piezoelectric materials are widely used in high power devices such as ultrasonic actuators and motors, but their nonlinear vibration behavior is not sufficiently quantified. This limitation is critical when comparing lead based and lead free materials, as reliable evaluation under high power conditions is required. Conventional constant voltage amplitude measurements produce hysteresis and jump phenomena near resonance, making stable curve fitting and parameter extraction difficult. Therefore, a method for accurate and stable evaluation of nonlinear behavior is needed. In this study, nonlinear coefficients are determined using constant current amplitude admittance measurements, which provide stable resonance curves without hysteresis or jumps. Nonlinear vibration is modeled by introducing a cubic strain term into the stress strain relationship, and the third order elastic coefficient is obtained through curve fitting based on a transfer matrix approach. Experiments confirmed that the method enables stable parameter determination and reveals differences in nonlinear behavior between materials, indicating the need for improved modeling.

papers.title: Measurement of Acoustic Pressure in Water Generated by an ELIPS
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the acoustic pressure distribution in water generated by an Elliptical reflector for high-Power ultraSound (ELIPS), a high-power ultrasonic transducer characterized by many available driving frequencies. Previous evaluations of ELIPS have been limited to vibration velocity measurements at the tip of the thin waveguide. In this study, acoustic pressure in water was measured using an FOPH to minimize disturbance to the acoustic field. The waveguide tip was inserted approximately 1 mm into water and driven at 0.50, 1.0, 1.4, and 1.7 MHz. Acoustic pressure distributions were obtained over a region extending 3 mm along the axis and ±0.7 mm radially, with a spatial resolution of 0.1 mm. The results were compared with numerical simulations. Acoustic pressures on the order of several MPa were observed at all frequencies, with a maximum of 6.6 MPa at 1.7 MHz. Good agreement between experimental and simulation results was obtained up to 1.4 MHz. In addition, axial directivity increased with frequency. These findings demonstrate the capability of ELIPS to generate high acoustic pressure in water and highlight its potential as a high-intensity ultrasonic source.

papers.title: Observation of Topological Pump Rejection in Nonlinear Acoustic Vortices
papers.abstract: Nonlinear mixing of structured waves obeys orbital-angular-momentum (OAM) selection rules, yet using this topology to spatially decouple the high-frequency pumps from the generated low-frequency field has not been experimentally demonstrated. Here we report the observation of topological pump rejection (TPR) in nonlinear acoustic vortices. Two equal-charge ultrasonic vortices retain a topologically enforced on-axis pump null, while their quadratic interaction generates a vortex-free difference-frequency wave that remains finite on-axis. Full-field amplitude and phase measurements confirm this coexistence of a singular pump field and a trivial generated field. Increasing the pump charge broadens both the low-pump-exposure window and the near-uniform region of the generated field. Remarkably, the effect persists from 500 Hz to 8 kHz and under broadband transient modulation in experiments, showing that TPR is not restricted to monochromatic driving. In airborne acoustics, this immediately enables wideband low-frequency directional delivery with reduced co-localized ultrasonic pump exposure.

sessions.title: MBB: Array Design and Volume Beamforming

papers.title: Spatial Multi-Rate De-Aliasing with Multi-Row, Multi-Pitch Arrays for Fundamental Grating-Lobe Suppression in Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Grating lobes are a fundamental barrier, particularly to high-frequency and 2-D ultrasound arrays, where meeting the spatial Nyquist limit imposes pitch constraints that are difficult to fabricate and that exacerbate inter-element crosstalk. Existing mitigations, such as aperiodic layouts or adaptive apodization, reduce artifact amplitudes but do not eliminate the underlying spatial aliasing. We extend time-domain multi-rate de-aliasing to the spatial domain by pairing a spatial de-aliasing algorithm with a multi-row, multi-pitch array that places two sub-Nyquist pitches on adjacent rows within a single aperture, thereby capturing correlated echoes whose overlapping spatial spectra are separated by the algorithm to recover unaliased channel data. Validated with Field II simulations and in vitro phantom measurements from a 5 MHz two-row array configured for sub-Nyquist sampling, the framework achieved ~10 dB and ~7 dB of grating-lobe suppression, respectively. Unlike conventional methods that only mitigate artifact amplitudes, this approach fundamentally resolves spatial aliasing, providing a deterministic design pathway for advanced multidimensional arrays.

papers.title: Heuristic Design of Linear Hybrid Ultrasound Arrays
papers.abstract: Hybrid Arrays (HA) utilize separate transmit (TX) and receive (RX) hardware to improve SNR and reduce complexity, but they present significant challenges in beamforming and layout design under realistic manufacturing constraints. This work introduces a novel heuristic method formulated as an Answer Set Programming (ASP) problem to optimize 1D HA designs by maximizing the size and continuity of the Virtual Aperture (VA). The resulting Virtual-Aperture-Continuous Arrays (VACA) allow for apodization strategies implemented directly in the VA domain. Comparative simulations against random arrays (RA) show that VACAs with VA-based apodization achieve a 4.5% improvement in gCNR and 10% better API. In-vivo carotid artery imaging further validates these results; while RAs fail to resolve artery walls, VACA designs clearly display them. Specifically, VA-based apodization offers the highest resolution, though it introduces some near-field artifacts. This approach demonstrates a robust framework for designing high-performance hybrid arrays within practical hardware limitations.

papers.title: High-Resolution Volumetric Ultrasound Imaging via 3D Null Subtraction Beamforming with Matrix Array Aperture Design
papers.abstract: We present a 3D Null Subtraction Imaging (NSI) framework that uses 2D apodization masks to simultaneously improve resolution and suppress sidelobes in volumetric ultrasound with matrix arrays. Tested a 1024-element (32×32) array on a 256-channel system with 4:1 multiplexing, using three aperture designs: fully-addressed circular, Fermat spiral sparse, and a novel spiral "no-reuse" aperture that eliminates channel conflicts. 3D NSI reduced azimuth/elevation FWHM by ~20% (36% area reduction) and improved contrast ratio, while requiring <3× DAS compute overhead. The no-reuse design achieved 16× faster than conventional multiplexed imaging. In vivo carotid images confirmed improved vessel delineation. 3D NSI is a computationally efficient, real-time capable beamforming method for high-quality volumetric imaging on hardware-constrained systems.

papers.title: Microbeamformer Delay Error-Based Receive Apodization for 4D Ultrafast Volumetric Imaging
papers.abstract: Microbeamforming (µBF) reduces the number of system channels required for volumetric ultrasound imaging by grouping transducer elements into sub-apertures (SAPs) that are pre-beamformed on receive. However, intra-SAP delay profiles are typically fixed according to predefined receive focal points, resulting in suboptimal reconstruction of voxels outside the receive focal zone. In this study, we introduce a BF delay errors-based receive apodization method (µDEA) to mitigate this limitation by down-weighting receive-channel contributions from voxels that are poorly matched to the fixed intra-SAP delay profile. The results demonstrate that μDEA substantially improves spatial resolution, with lateral FWHM reductions of 48.4% and 46.6% at 20 and 60 mm depths, respectively. This resolution improvement supports future in vivo evaluation of μDEA for 4D ultrafast volumetric ultrasound imaging

papers.title: Improving the Elevational Focusing of Fast Orthogonal Row-Column Electronic Scanning (FORCES) Imaging with Retrospective Transmit Beamforming (RTB)
papers.abstract: FORCES imaging utilizes electrostrictive RCAs to enable high-quality, electronically scannable 2D ultrasound imaging everywhere within a 3D volume. While FORCES achieves full lateral and axial dynamic transmit and recieve focusing, elevational focusing is limited to a fixed transmit focus. This results in poor elevational resolution and out-of-plane artifacts, particularly near the probe. We propose FORCES RTB to achieve dynamic elevational transmit focusing throughout the imaging plane. By treating the focal arc of each acquisition as a virtual source, we utilize decoded synthetic aperture data from up to 16 stacked images to perform dynamic transmit focusing in the elevational direction. FORCES and FORCES RTB are compared using a 128 × 128 element TOBE array. Comparisons on wire and cyst phantoms show improvements. 50 mm from the focal zone, RTB achieved an elevational FWHM of 4.7 mm, compared to 28.7 mm for standard FORCES. In cyst phantoms, RTB doubled the gCNR from 0.15 to 0.30 at 60 mm from the focus. FORCES RTB effectively reduces out-of-plane artifacts and enhances elevational resolution.

papers.title: Fast 3D Ultrasound Beamforming Utilizing 4D Tensor Completion
papers.abstract: Conventional 3D ultrasound beamforming is commonly performed using line-by-line delay-and-sum (DAS), where each scan line is sequentially formed across the imaging volume. While this method is well established, it becomes computationally demanding for high-resolution volumetric imaging and limits achievable frame rates. In hardware implementations such as FPGA-based systems, these constraints further motivate the transition from sequential line-based processing to pixel-based beamforming, which offers greater flexibility for parallel computation. The objective of this work is to develop a fast 3D beamforming framework by utilizing sparse beamforming. We propose a two-stage reconstruction framework for fast 3D beamforming. First, only a randomly selected sparse subset of pixels within the imaging volume is reconstructed using pixel-based DAS beamforming, thereby significantly reducing the number of beamforming operations. In the second stage, the missing pixels are recovered using 4D tensor completion (TC) utilizing rank minimization, where the data are modeled as a tensor spanning three spatial dimensions and time (3D+t).

sessions.title: MTC: Cardiovascular, Vascular & Tissue Dynamics

papers.title: Shear Wave elastography and Biaxial Mechanical Testing Independently Suggest Isotropy of Tissue Stiffness in Normotensive Human Right Ventricular Myocardium
papers.abstract: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is commonly associated with right ventricular (RV) pressure overload and failure. Small animal studies of PH using biaxial mechanical testing (BMT) show isotropy of RV tissue stiffness before, and anisotropy after, chronic RV pressure overload, but the corresponding (an)isotropy of stiffness in the human RV is unknown. Further, BMT, the gold standard for RV tissue stiffness assessment, cannot be translated to the clinic. We assess the anisotropy of stiffness in excised normotensive human RV myocardium using both BMT and shear wave elastography, which is noninvasive and can be applied in the clinic. Excised hearts from six human decedents without history of PH were tested within 24 hours of death. For each heart, the RV free wall was removed. A rotational scan of SWE was performed, then a sample was excised from the SWE location and BMT was performed with strain measured by ultrasound using a row-column array. Four of five RVs exhibited isotropy by SWE while one exhibited anisotropy. All six BMT tests exhibited isotropy. These results suggest isotropy of stiffness in normotensive human RV myocardium similar to that seen in small animals.

papers.title: A Novel Quantitative Ultrasound Method for Assessment of Myocardial Microstructure in Cardiac Amyloidosis
papers.abstract: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is a systemic disease characterized by myocardial amyloid deposition resulting in alterations in myocardial structure and function. Conventional echocardiography has limited sensitivity for detecting early tissue changes, often necessitating cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR). Quantitative ultrasound (QUS) assesses tissue microstructure through analysis of radiofrequency (RF) data. Echocardiography was performed to acquire RF frames from the parasternal long-axis view. The basal interventricular septum was segmented for QUS analysis. CMR parameters including late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) burden and extracellular volume (ECV) were collected. Effective scatterer diameter (ESD) and effective acoustic concentration (EAC) were computed from the backscatter coefficient. The envelope-detected signal was fit to the Homodyned K distribution to compute α and k. CA patients had higher LGE burden and ECV compared to controls (p≤0.003). There was statistically significant difference in the parameter k (p = 0.04) when comparing CA patients to control subjects. ESD, α, and k correlated with LGE (R≥0.72,p≤0.04) and α correlated with ECV (R=0.77,p=0.02).

papers.title: A Flexible Ultrasound Array Patch for Simultaneous, Calibration-Free Monitoring of Carotid Pulse-Wave Velocity and Blood Pressure
papers.abstract: We present a lightweight flexible ultrasound array patch that enables calibration-free cuffless blood-pressure (BP) monitoring with concurrent vascular-stiffness assessment at the carotid artery. The patch integrates eight 1-3 piezoelectric composite elements at 5 MHz with 4 mm pitch, serpentine FPCB interconnects, and Ecoflex encapsulation, forming a 30 × 5 mm sensing core (~1 g). A decoupled-backing structure, relocating the backing layer above the negative electrode via silver-paste contact, reduces damping and enhances SNR. Carotid wall motion is extracted from M-mode ultrasound using a Kalman tracker, and local pulse-wave velocity (PWV) is computed from inter-element pulse-foot delays. Motion, waveform, and PWV features are fed into a PWV-adaptive framework, in which PWV serves as both an input variable and a stratification cue for systolic and diastolic BP estimation. On 100 measurements from 30 healthy volunteers under leave-one-subject-out cross-validation, the framework achieves R² of 0.978 and 0.909 with mean absolute errors of 2.7 and 3.4 mmHg for SBP and DBP, while simultaneously providing direct local carotid PWV as an indicator of arterial stiffness.

papers.title: Cardiac Natural Mechanical Waves Speed and Trajectories Estimated with 3D Ultrafast Ultrasound Imaging As a Biomarker of Primary Mitral Regurgitation
papers.abstract: Using 3D ultrafast ultrasound imaging, the atrial kick wave speed and its trajectory were estimated on 10 primary mitral regurgitation patients. In addition to the wave speed, a marker of rigidity, new biomarkers based on wave trajectories are assessed and compared to 8 healthy volunteers.

papers.title: Longitudinal Multimodal Ultrasound Imaging of Vascular and Microstructural Remodeling During Wound Healing
papers.abstract: Impaired wound healing in diabetic conditions remains poorly understood at the tissue scale. We present a multimodal ultrasound framework combining B-mode and Power Doppler imaging for simultaneous, longitudinal assessment of vascular and microstructural remodeling in a murine wound model. Full-thickness excisional wounds were monitored over 28 days in healthy (C57BL/6) and diabetic (db/db) mice using a 30 MHz transducer. Quantitative analysis integrated vascularity indices with intensity- and texture-based features to characterize tissue organization throughout healing. Diabetic mice exhibited a delayed and reduced vascular response, with perfusion confined near the wound surface and lower temporal variability compared to controls. Structurally, diabetic tissue showed higher echogenicity and more homogeneous texture, reflecting altered scatterer organization. These findings demonstrate that multimodal ultrasound can jointly track perfusion dynamics and tissue reorganization in a spatially resolved manner, revealing distinct healing signatures between healthy and impaired conditions and establishing its potential for chronic wound assessment and therapeutic monitoring.

papers.title: Ultrasound Backscatter Tensor Imaging Using Row-Column Addressed Arrays
papers.abstract: Accurate fiber-orientation estimation is essential for identifying pathological changes in neural, muscular, and myocardial tissues. Magnetic resonance diffusion tensor imaging enables this, but is limited by high cost and poor portability. Ultrasound backscatter tensor imaging provides a more accessible alternative; yet most approaches rely on 2D fully sampled arrays with high hardware complexity. To address the high hardware complexity associated with these systems, low-channel-count solutions have recently attracted increasing attention, among which row-column-addressed arrays (RCA) have emerged as a promising approach. In this work, we explore the feasibility of 2D fiber orientation estimation using RCA.

sessions.title: TMI: Wearable Ultrasonic Transducers

papers.title: A Flexible Transparent Ultrasonic Array for Wearable Acousto-Optic Sensing of Vasculature
papers.abstract: A flexible transparent ultrasonic transducer (FTUT) array is developed for wearable acousto-optic vascular sensing. Conventional wearable devices lack comprehensive vascular assessment, and existing transparent arrays are rigid or have poor element density and imaging performance. This work introduces a 128-element FTUT array with a 0.3 mm pitch and 6 MHz center frequency, featuring optimized multilayer matching and backing layers to overcome acoustic impedance mismatch, improve transmission and bandwidth, and enhance flexibility. The array achieves ultrasonic performance comparable to commercial probes. Photodetectors and VCSEL lasers are integrated behind the transparent array for pulse waveform, pulse wave velocity, and photoacoustic measurements. High optical transparency allows efficient light transmission. Ultrasound imaging (coherent plane-wave compounding on Verasonics Vantage 256) enables conformal carotid artery imaging and vessel diameter tracking for blood pressure estimation. Integrated VCSELs also support compact photoacoustic imaging, demonstrating multimodal wearable vascular sensing.

papers.title: A Wearable Dual-Plane Ultrasound Patch for Automated Whole-Bladder Imaging and Volumetry
papers.abstract: This work presents a wearable dual-plane ultrasound patch for automated, continuous bladder imaging and volumetry. The patch integrates three 64-element linear arrays, including two vertically aligned arrays for an extended sagittal view and one horizontal array for transverse imaging, enabling whole-bladder assessment without manual probe manipulation. A time-division scanning strategy allows rapid acquisition of multi-plane ultrasound data. To reconstruct complete sagittal bladder images, a feature-based image stitching algorithm is introduced, followed by automated bladder contour detection and volume estimation. The patch also incorporates a 2 mm self-adhesive hydrogel layer to provide stable acoustic coupling and hands-free skin attachment, supporting continuous monitoring. In healthy volunteers, the system successfully imaged both large and small bladder volumes, including cases where a commercial convex probe could not capture the entire bladder. Estimated bladder volumes agreed well with commercial devices, demonstrating the potential of this wearable system for long-term, automated bladder monitoring.

papers.title: Accuracy Enhancement of Wearable Ultrasound Bladder Volume Measurement via Optimized MEMS Chip Arrangement
papers.abstract: This study proposes a wearable ultrasound method for accurate bladder volume measurement using an optimized piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducer (PMUT) chip arrangement. Conventional handheld ultrasound scanners are mainly used for intermittent assessment, while catheter-based monitoring is invasive and may affect patient comfort and safety. To address the accuracy limitations of wearable bladder monitoring, this work compares four measurement strategies using an FDA-approved handheld bladder volume scanner as the reference standard: clinical B-mode ultrasound estimation, B-mode contour fitting, an orthogonal PMUT patch layout, and a nine-point PMUT patch layout. PMUT chips acquire echo signals from the anterior and posterior bladder walls, and corresponding fitting algorithms are developed for different layouts. Results show that the nine-point fitting method achieves the highest accuracy, exceeding 95%, because it reconstructs bladder morphology with multiple fitting surfaces and reduces geometric simplification errors. This work supports the development of low-cost, miniaturized, and high-accuracy wearable bladder monitoring systems.

papers.title: A Wearable Ultrasound Patch for Diaphragmatic Monitoring
papers.abstract: This study developed a wearable ultrasound patch for monitoring diaphragmatic thickness during the respiratory cycle. The device incorporates a miniaturized transducer with a dual matching layer design and flexible circuit connections to improve acoustic performance and adaptability. The fabricated patch achieved a center frequency of 10.5 MHz and a −6 dB bandwidth of 72%. Preliminary in experiments showed that the system could track diaphragm thickness changes, with measurements of approximately 1.3 mm during exhalation and 1.8 mm during inhalation. These results indicate that the proposed device can provide continuous and relatively stable diaphragmatic monitoring, offering a potential alternative to conventional ultrasound probes.

papers.title: Capacitive Micromachined Ultrasound Transducer (CMUT)-Based Linear Array with Beam Steering for Low-Profile Wearable Doppler Ultrasound
papers.abstract: This study presents a CMUT (capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducer)-based linear array for simultaneous measurement of vessel diameter variation and blood flow. Vessel wall motion and diameter variation are key biomarkers reflecting vascular elasticity and are widely used in cardiovascular diagnosis. To address this, a compact CMUT-based linear array is proposed. The fabricated CMUT is a 44-channel linear array operating at 3.57 MHz (nominal 5 MHz), with a cell size of 52 μm, a channel pitch of 155 μm, and a die size of 8×8 mm. The system enables simultaneous measurement of vessel wall motion and Doppler-based flow using a single transducer under normal incidence and beam steering. The results show that vessel wall reflections are separated, enabling estimation of diameter variation and wall motion. The estimated displacement shows consistent trends compared with a fabricated single-channel flat piezoelectric transducer. Measurements on human arteries, including carotid and radial arteries, demonstrate feasibility. These findings suggest that CMUT-based linear arrays with beam steering enable simultaneous measurement of vascular dynamics in wearable ultrasound systems.

papers.title: A Flexible Wearable Ultrasound Patch for Measuring Abdominal Subcutaneous Adipose Tissue Thickness
papers.abstract: This study presents a flexible wearable A-mode ultrasound patch for accurate abdominal subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) thickness measurement. Conventional B-mode ultrasound is limited by manual operation and variable probe pressure, while A-mode systems often have difficulty separating skin thickness from SAT. The proposed 8-channel patch integrates 5 MHz three-layer transducer elements on a polyimide/copper flexible circuit substrate with Ecoflex encapsulation and a 5 mm-thick elevated structure. Eleven subjects across normal, overweight, and obese BMI levels were tested, with measurements validated against B-mode ultrasound imaging. The patch achieved relative errors of 6.00% for skin thickness and 3.29% for SAT thickness. Correlation and Bland-Altman analyses showed strong agreement with B-mode references, demonstrating its potential for standardized wearable SAT assessment.

sessions.title: ASM: Spurous Mode Suppression

papers.title: High-Power C-Band SAW Filter Employing a Multi‑Layered Substrate and a High Heat Dissipation Package
papers.abstract: The increasing deployment of Massive multiple-input multiple-output (mMIMO) base stations with a large number of antenna elements is driving stronger demand for compact and lightweight radio-frequency (RF) filters. Replacing conventional ceramic filters with surface acoustic wave (SAW) filters is an effective approach. However, the limited power handling capability of SAW filters has restricted their use in transmit filters for base stations. In this study, a high-power C band SAW filter was realized using a low loss guided mode SAW device combined with a high heat dissipation package for enhancing power handling performance. The filter operating in the C-band (3.6 - 3.7 GHz) was designed with a 48° Y X LiTaO₃ / intermediate layers / sapphire substrate with a series split configuration and a face up wafer level package. As a result, stable power linearity was confirmed up to an input power of 39.5 dBm and an output power of 38 dBm. These results demonstrate the feasibility of the SAW filter for the practical application of mMIMO type base station.

papers.title: Suppression of Transverse Mode Spurious and Quality-Factor Enhancement in SAW Resonators Using an Inner-Shifted Raised (ISR) Structure
papers.abstract: In Surface Acoustic Resonator (SAW) resonators, transverse mode spurious responses degrade resonator characteristics. This leads filter performance degradation, making their suppression important. Various approaches have been proposed, including apodization, piston-mode structures, and slowness-curve control. The conventional piston-mode structures, Q may degrade because of lateral energy leakage and scattering when the slow/raised region is placed directly at the IDT edges. In this study, an Inner-Shifted Raised (ISR) structure was investigated, in which the slow/raised region is shifted inward from the IDT edges. The ISR structure achieves improved Q-factor while maintaining suppression of transverse mode spurious. This improvement is attributed to reduced lateral energy leakage and scattering near the IDT edges by placing the slow/raised region at an appropriate distance from the edges. These results indicate that optimizing the position of the slow/raised region makes it possible to improve Q while preserving the transverse-mode suppression effect of the conventional piston-mode structure.

papers.title: Scandium-Content-Dependent Power Handling Characteristics in AlScN Thin-Film Bulk Acoustic Resonators
papers.abstract: In this work, we fabricate and evaluate Al1-xScxN FBARs with different Sc concentrations to assess their suitability for sub-7-GHz wideband RF applications. BAW resonators based on Al₀.₈Sc₀.₂N, Al₀.₇Sc₀.₃N, and Al₀.₆Sc₀.₄N were successfully fabricated with the corresponding parallel resonance frequencies (fp) of 5.473 GHz,5.721 GHz, and 6.436 GHz, respectively. The measured breakdown powers are 32.77 dBm, 20.38 dBm, and 23.59 dBm, corresponding to power densities of 9.46 × 10⁸ W/m², 0.68 × 108 W/m², and 1.91 × 10⁸ W/m², respectively. These results indicate that increasing the Sc concentration from 20% to 30% reduces the power density by 92.8%, while increasing from 20% to 40% leads to a reduction of 79.8%.This work provides an experimental basis for evaluating high-Sc-content AlScN resonators for wideband RF filters and highlights the need to balance enhanced coupling with material quality, acoustic loss, and thermal reliability in high-Sc AlScN devices.

papers.title: Suppression of Longitudinal Spurious Modes in Lithium Niobate-on-Insulator (LNOI) SH-SAW Resonators via Electrode-Width Modulation
papers.abstract: This work addresses longitudinal spurious modes (LMs) in thin-film LNOI SH-SAW resonators, which degrade RF filter performance by introducing passband ripples. While transverse modes have been widely studied, LM suppression remains less explored. Here, phase-velocity transition zones are introduced between the IDT active region and reflectors to disrupt longitudinal standing wave formation. Two design strategies are proposed: (1) edge perturbation, which creates an abrupt phase-velocity discontinuity by modifying outermost IDT finger widths, and (2) unilateral tapered electrode-width modulation, which introduces a gradual phase-velocity gradient. Devices were fabricated on X-cut LNOI with propagation at −10° from +Y to optimize SH-mode coupling. Experimental results show that both methods effectively suppress the dominant LM near 1.08 GHz, achieving reductions of 6.1 dB and 7.3 dB, respectively. Importantly, key performance metrics such as admittance ratio and Bode-Q remain nearly unchanged, demonstrating that LM suppression can be achieved without compromising the main resonance characteristics.

papers.title: SAW Transverse Mode Suppression on LiNbO3/Quartz Bonded Structures by Placing Voids Below the Electrode Edges
papers.abstract: In high-Q SAW resonators, spurious responses arising from transverse modes tend to be more pronounced. Because these spurious responses induce ripples in the filter passband, their suppression is required. In this study, we propose a method for suppressing transverse modes in LiNbO3 (LN) /quartz (Qz) bonded structures with high-Q leaky SAW (LSAW) properties by introducing voids on the surface of the quartz support substrate below the electrode edges. The LSAW resonance property of an Al-interdigital transducer /36°YX-LN/AT90°X-Qz structure with a wavelength λ of 10 μm was analyzed using the finite-element method. According to the analysis results, while distinct transverse mode spurious responses were observed between the resonance and anti-resonance frequencies in the absence of voids, they were significantly suppressed when voids were introduced. This suggests that voids modify the transverse particle displacement distribution to cancel the excitation of the transverse modes, thereby realizing a piston mode.

papers.title: Suppressing Spurious Modes in Laterally Excited Bulk Acoustic Wave Resonators Using Serrated Electrodes
papers.abstract: To meet 5G/6G communication demands for wide bandwidths, acoustic resonators with large electromechanical coupling coefficients (keff2) are urgently required. Laterally excited bulk acoustic wave resonators (XBARs) on suspended LiNbO3 thin film are considered promising candidates due to their excellent high-frequency performance and large keff2. However, previously reported XBARs are often plagued by severe spurious modes. Although enhancements in electrode configurations have been demonstrated, a trade-off exists between effective spurious suppression and the realizations of high keff2 and Q. This work demonstrates the elimination of spurious modes in A1-mode XBARs with a serrated IDT, which breaks strict electrode periodicity and disrupts standing-wave conditions via non-parallel boundaries. The serration parameter of the IDT is optimized by finite element method, and the simulated displacement field confirms the suppression of the A1-5 spurious mode, while the acoustic energy of A1 mode is well confined. The fabricated A1-mode XBAR on a 400 nm thick Z-cut LiNbO3 film operates at 4.45 GHz without unwanted spurious modes, achieving a high keff2 of 25.81% and a maximum Q of 302.
keywords: laterally excited bulk acoustic wave resonators (XBARs)

sessions.title: NPA: Photoacoustics

papers.title: * INVITED * Sensing in Oil-Gas industry and in Biomedical Applications
papers.abstract: Modern industrial and biomedical challenges increasingly demand multimodal sensing solutions that integrate acoustic, optical, and electromagnetic approaches. In complex environments—ranging from oil and gas pipelines to physiological monitoring, no single modality can capture the full spectrum of relevant information. Combining techniques such as ultrasonics, optics, and microwaves enables deeper insight into material, chemical, and biological systems. This presentation will highlight examples of cross-domain sensor development, showing how multimodal integration leads to enhanced data reliability, process efficiency, and diagnostic precision. The main emphasis will be on ultrasonic sensing.

papers.title: Ratiometric Photoacoustic Microscopy-OCT Monitoring of Transplanted hiPSC-RPE Using ROS-Responsive CGNP-IR775c Nanoprobes
papers.abstract: Monitoring transplanted cell viability in vivo remains a major challenge. Here, we present a non-invasive and quantitative approach using multi-wavelength photoacoustic microscopy with a reactive oxygen species (ROS)-responsive contrast agent. The contrast agent comprises colloidal chain-like gold nanoparticles clusters conjugated with IR775c (CGNP-IR775c), undergoes selective oxidative quenching under elevated ROS conditions associated with cellular apoptosis. Self-calibrated ratiometric measurements at 620 nm and 775 nm can distinguish between viable and apoptotic cells. In vitro studies confirmed biocompatibility and dose-dependent ROS sensitivity to physiologically relevant H2O2 levels. For in vivo validation, human induced pluripotent stem cell-derived retinal pigment epithelium (hiPSC-RPE) cells labeled with CGNP-IR775c were transplanted into the living rabbit eyes and monitored over two weeks. Laser-induced oxidative stress resulted in measurable changes in photoacoustic signals that were correlated with the viability of the transplanted cells. This platform enables non-invasive, longitudinal monitoring of transplanted cell viability in vivo.

papers.title: A Kirigami-Inspired Reconfigurable Photoacoustic Patch Toward Focused and Distributed Neuromodulation
papers.abstract: Photoacoustic patches (PAPs) provide a compact, optically driven approach for acoustic-wave generation, but most existing devices produce fixed acoustic fields after fabrication. Here, we propose a kirigami-inspired reconfigurable PAP that switches between focused and distributed acoustic fields through mechanical transformation, without electronic phased control. A spherical unfolding algorithm was used to convert a spherical cap into a planar petal layout while retaining a central connector for reversible switching between merged curved and unfolded planar states. The design used a 5 mm cap radius and 45° cutoff polar angle, giving a 7.07 mm merged aperture, 9.85 mm unfolded diameter, and 2 mm center connector. Three-dimensional k-Wave simulations showed that the merged state generated a focused field with a 5.50 mm focal depth, 2.27 mm lateral FWHM, and −8.22 dB sidelobe level. The unfolded state produced a distributed field with 9.96 mm coverage FWHM and 1.50 mm −6 dB penetration depth. Prototype images verified reversible mechanical reconfiguration, demonstrating a low-complexity PAP platform for switchable focused and distributed neuromodulation.

papers.title: On the Interplay Between Laser Pulse Width and Absorber Size in Laser diode-Based photoacoustics
papers.abstract: Low-cost optical sources such as laser diodes (LDs) and LEDs are enabling the translation of photoacoustic (PA) imaging to point-of-care settings, but their lower peak power requires longer pulses (>50 ns), reducing efficiency and shifting the acoustic spectrum to lower frequencies. Here, the PA wave equation is numerically analyzed by jointly considering pulse duration, shape, and absorber size, providing criteria to optimize excitation and detection. The model is validated with a custom LD-based PA microscope using absorbers of 50–150 µm and pulses of 20–150 ns. Results show that PA efficiency depends on the relation between pulse duration and the absorber’s acoustic transient time. Under constant-power conditions, shorter pulses do not necessarily increase pressure amplitude. Asymmetric pulses further reduce efficiency and shift the optimum duration. For small absorbers (<100 µm), pulses longer than ~75 ns are inefficient. Most energy is concentrated below 15 MHz, highlighting trade-offs between resolution, contrast, and penetration depth.

papers.title: Portable Photoacoustic Imaging with Pulsed Laser Diodes for Bedside Deep Tissue Oxygenation Assessment
papers.abstract: Photoacoustic (PA) imaging exploits optical absorption contrast to generate acoustic waves via the thermoelastic effect, enabling oxygenation mapping through spectral unmixing of oxyhemoglobin (HbO₂) and deoxyhemoglobin (Hb). Clinical translation is bottlenecked by bulky, high-cost Class-IV laser systems. We developed a portable prototype using miniaturized pulsed laser diodes (PLDs). A porcine tissue phantom with hemoglobin-filled tubing demonstrated >4cm imaging depth. In vivo capability was assessed in Sprague-Dawley rat kidneys (n=3) through layered porcine tissue overlays, demonstrating >3cm penetration. Oxygenation quantification was validated pre- and post-euthanasia at 905nm and 1060nm, with spectral unmixing confirming the expected difference in renal oxygenation. Human forearm vasculature was imaged transversely and longitudinally at both wavelengths, co-registered with B-mode ultrasound. These results establish that low-power PLDs are sufficient for deep-tissue PA imaging and in vivo oxygenation discrimination, representing a path toward portable, bedside PA systems. Future work will focus on device optimization and a full human pilot study.

sessions.title: MIS: Acquisition & Applications in Ultrafast Ultrasound

papers.title: * INVITED * Continuous emission echography: a new paradigm to break the temporal resolution in ultrasound imaging
papers.abstract: This talk introduces continuous emission echography as the convergence of sparse array design, compressed acquisitions, and computational methods for image reconstruction. We will outline its core principles, the methods designed to decode the received raw signals and beamform M- and B-mode images, and demonstrate its ability to reach unprecedented imaging speeds—exceeding 100,000 frames per second—through simulations and early experimental results.

papers.title: Ultrafast Ultrasound Navigation of a Neurosurgical microrobot Within a Vascular Network Mapped with 3D Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (3D ULM)
papers.abstract: Microrobots are now being designed for neurosurgery to improve access to deep brain regions through non-rigid trajectories. Real-time submillimetric tracking of these instruments is crucial, especially to preserve the integrity of the surrounding vascular system and avoid intracranial hemorrhage. Both navigation and microvascular imaging have been performed independently with multi-elements ultrasound system, often requiring further registration methods. This work shows an in-vitro proof of concept of a system that performs 3D ultrafast ultrasound imaging with a matrix array to jointly track microbubbles within vessels, to perform volumetric ULM, and the position and orientation of a neurosurgical tool in real-time.

papers.title: Sparse Deconvolution for Contrast-Free Microvascular Imaging in Ultrafast Power Doppler Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Ultrafast power-Doppler imaging combined with singular value decomposition (SVD) clutter filtering is the de facto standard for label-free microvascular ultrasound, since it enables visualization of small vessels without microbubble contrast agents. However, in the absence of contrast, SVD-filtered Doppler images are simultaneously limited by blurring induced by the imaging system point spread function (PSF). This study proposes a sparse-deconvolution framework that jointly recovers both contrast and resolution from SVD-filtered Doppler images. Compared with conventional SVD, sparse deconvolution improves vessel-to-background contrast by approximately 20 dB in deep imaging regions, and reduces vessel full-width-at-half-maximum by approximately 2× in both axial and lateral directions, enabling visualization of capillary-scale microvasculature that is unresolved in conventional SVD images. These results demonstrate that sparsity-based super-resolution principles, originally developed for live-cell fluorescence microscopy, transfer directly to label-free ultrafast Doppler ultrasound, providing a practical front-end for high-resolution microvascular imaging without contrast agents.

papers.title: GPU Baseband Beamforming and FP32-Robust Decimated Covariance SVD for Real-Time Ultrafast Doppler Imaging
papers.abstract: Ultrafast Doppler compounding enables kilohertz-rate microvascular imaging, but real-time use is limited by beamforming and clutter filtering. We present an RTX A5000 GPU pipeline integrating baseband beamforming and covariance-domain SVD. Baseband reduces arithmetic cost, but DC-demodulated tissue clutter can dominate covariance estimation, widen the dynamic range over weak flow, and cause FP32 precision loss. Decimated covariance SVD estimates the clutter subspace from decimated IQ data and projects it out from full-resolution IQ data, reducing SVD cost and recovering FP32 headroom without resolution loss. Beamforming uses periodic-mixer demodulation with FIR decimation and pixel-driven DAS with precomputed delays, F-number aperture, texture-cache IQ fetch, and register accumulation. Experiments used a Verasonics with a GE 9L-D 192-element linear array, 9 plane-wave angles, and 400-frame ensembles. With stride 4, the pipeline processed 400 frames in 297.04 ms versus 1,918.75 ms for un-decimated DAS (6.46x, ~0.74 ms/frame, ~1.35 kfps). Decimated SVD reduced clutter filtering from 156.90 to 55.04 ms (2.85x), improving SNR from 5.69 to 20.75 dB and CNR from -0.65 to 1.30 dB.

papers.title: Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing for Ultrafast Ultrasound Imaging in Tissue
papers.abstract: This work explores orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) as a multiplexing strategy for ultrafast ultrasound imaging. While conventional ultrasound imaging relies on sequential transmissions, limiting frame rate, ultrafast imaging employs multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) schemes with simultaneous transmissions. Code-division multiplexing (CDM) is commonly used for this purpose but suffers from reduced robustness in the presence of hardware imperfections and tissue-induced nonlinearities due to imperfect code orthogonality. In this study, OFDM is investigated as a frequency-domain alternative to CDM. Wire phantom and tissue imaging experiments demonstrate that OFDM preserves target detectability and peak signal-to-noise ratio (pSNR) relative to conventional time-division multiplexed (TDM) chirp-based imaging while enabling an eightfold increase in frame rate. Compared to CDM, OFDM shows improved robustness under non-ideal conditions, making it a promising approach for practical ultrafast ultrasound imaging in tissue.

sessions.title: MIM: Neuroimaging

papers.title: Data-Driven Extraction of Spatiotemporal Patterns for single-Trial Decoding in Functional Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) is a neuroimaging modality that enables high resolution, sensitivity, and depth of penetration. Current fUSI methods used for sensory mapping and functional connectivity rely on correlation-based approaches, use atlas-based brain parcellations that introduce inherent biases, and require multiple trials (5+) to extract functional information, which limits the temporal resolution. On the contrary, data-driven approaches can decode intrinsic spatiotemporal structures with fewer assumptions and fewer trials. Here, we investigate how preprocessing and number of trials affect the stability and interpretability of data-driven fUSI analyses.

papers.title: Deep learning-Based Compressive Functional Ultrasound Imaging for Functional Connectivity Analyses
papers.abstract: Functional ultrasound imaging (fUSI) enables high-resolution mapping of brain activity but requires long acquisitions and computationally intensive processing pipelines. Deep learning-based reconstruction methods can recover power Doppler signals from sparsely sampled data, but their ability to retain meaningful functional information has not been fully validated. Here, we determined whether a deep learning reconstruction framework (Deep-fUS) can preserve functional connectivity patterns under high data compression factors.

papers.title: Toward Operator-Independent Neonatal Brain Imaging with Transcranial Ultrasound Tomography
papers.abstract: Early and reliable detection of brain injury in premature neonates remains challenging because cranial ultrasound is operator dependent and limited by fontanelle access, while MRI is often impractical for unstable infants and CT involves ionizing radiation. This study evaluates transcranial ultrasound tomography (TcUST) as a safe, operator-independent approach for bedside structural and vascular neonatal brain imaging through the skull. Simulations showed that transmit frequencies below 3 MHz provide a favorable balance between skull penetration and structural contrast. Point-spread-function analysis demonstrated that skull-induced aberration primarily degraded tangential resolution, while radial resolution and overall anatomical visibility were largely preserved. Phantom experiments showed that TcUST could detect millimeter-scale hemorrhagic inclusions, recover major anatomical features in an ex vivo sheep-brain phantom, and reconstruct vascular flow through a skull mimic. These results support the feasibility of TcUST for transcranial whole-brain neonatal imaging and motivate further development toward bedside longitudinal neuromonitoring.

papers.title: Transcranial Ultrasound Tomography of Cadaveric Human Hemorrhage Models
papers.abstract: Rapid detection of intracranial hemorrhage (ICH) and traumatic brain injury (TBI) is critical for timely treatment, yet CT and MRI are impractical at the point of injury. Conventional ultrasound (US) is portable but limited by poor skull penetration and narrow field of view. This study investigates ultrasound tomography (UST) to overcome these challenges for whole-head imaging in cadaveric models. Using a 256-element ring array and a Verasonics NXT system, tomographic data were collected and reconstructed via full-waveform inversion. A hemorrhage-mimicking water inclusion was implanted in a cadaveric brain and imaged with and without the skull. Results showed clear differentiation between skull, healthy brain tissue, and the inclusion, with consistent sound speed measurements and high signal-to-noise ratios. Radiologists successfully identified the inclusion in all cases. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of UST for transcranial imaging and its potential as a portable, point-of-injury diagnostic tool for TBI and stroke, with ongoing work to improve signal quality in practical systems.

papers.title: Synthetic Aperture Diverging Wave Imaging with Complete Complementary Code for Enhanced Transcranial Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Synthetic aperture ultrasound imaging is often limited by low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), particularly in transcranial applications where skull attenuation further degrades image quality. Coded excitation is a well-established strategy for SNR improvement, but different coding schemes involve tradeoffs in artifact level and near-field behavior. In this work, Synthetic Aperture Diverging Wave Imaging with Complete Complementary Code (SADWI-CCC) is proposed, combining diverging-wave transmissions with virtual sources and CCC excitation to enhance the SNR and contrast. Eight virtual sources were encoded across 8 transmissions using CCC sequences, with each transmission consisting of 8 cycles at 2.841 MHz and sequence-specific polarity encoding. The received RF data were decoded by exploiting the perfect autocorrelation and zero cross-correlation properties of CCC, enabling independent recovery of each virtual source's contribution. The results demonstrate that SADWI-CCC provides a favorable balance between resolution, CNR, and artifact suppression. The transcranial B-mode results support its potential for through-skull imaging applications.

papers.title: Intracranial Pressure Estimation with Ultrasound and a Microfluidic Sensor
papers.abstract: Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is a life-threatening condition affecting over 1.3 million patients annually, yet current diagnostic methods are invasive or inaccurate. This work utilizes a microfluidic sensor placed in a burr hole cover, featuring a serpentine fluid channel that translates pressure to fluid levels. Manually sweeping an ultrasound transducer across the sensor generates C-scan images from which ICP is estimated. Two estimation pipelines were developed and compared: a feature-informed image processing algorithm and a convolutional neural network (CNN). The CNN slightly outperformed the feature-based method, achieving an MAE of 1.78 mmHg and R² = 0.76 compared to the feature-based method with an MAE of 3.05 ± 2.46 mmHg, RMSE = 4.04 and R² = 0.74 in ex vivo pig head trials. A confidence scoring system further reduced error by ~24% through image quality thresholding. Both methods demonstrated clinically relevant accuracy within physiological pressure ranges, with the feature-based approach offering greater interpretability. Overall, these approaches present a promising solution for reliable, quantitative ICP monitoring in post-surgical neurological patients.

sessions.title: MSR: Microcorticality

papers.title: Linking Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (ULM) Metrics to Physical and Neurophysiological Parameters
papers.abstract: Microvascular alterations are central to cerebral small vessel disease. Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (ULM) enables super-resolution imaging by tracking microbubbles (MB) and provides quantitative parameters such as MB count and velocity. However, the physical and physiological meaning of MB count remains unclear. We investigate how ULM-derived parameters relate to cerebral blood flow (CBF), cerebral blood volume (CBV), and local velocity. We develop a framework linking voxel-wise MB flux to MB count and define MB density as flux normalized by velocity. The model is validated in a flow-controlled tube, tested in vivo 3D ULM for flux conservation at vascular bifurcations, and assessed during whisker stimulation using 2D fULM. MB flux increases linearly with flow rate (slope = 1.01, R² = 0.99) and varies with depth, while density remains constant (slope = −0.002, p = 0.13). In vivo, parent and branch fluxes are conserved (p = 0.16). During stimulation, flux increases like CBF whereas density remains stable, consistent with CBV. Overall, ULM-derived flux and density provide a physiologically grounded description of microvascular perfusion.

papers.title: Physiologically Annotated Single Capillary Reporters Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Maps
papers.abstract: Recent ULM advances (long-ensemble (LE) SVD1 and spatiotemporal tracking2) enable continuous single capillary reporter MB tracking across thousands of frames , including capillary quantification1. Here, we propose a novel approach to further classify long MB tracks to identify arterial, precapillary arterial, capillary, postcapillary venous and venous categories, distinguishing for the first time in ULM sub-categories of arterial and venous flow. Since vessel types serve distinct physiological roles — precapillary arteries control flow resistance3; postcapillary veins mediate leukocyte extravasation4 — their discrimination enables brain-wide vessel-type-specific microvascular function mapping mapping, opening new avenues for studying microcirculatory regulation and dysfunction at the organ scale. Classification is achieved by fitting a GMM to hemodynamic features of single tracks.

papers.title: Awake Longitudinal fUS, ULM, and fULM Imaging Reveal Sequential Vascular and Functional Alterations in 5xFAD Mice
papers.abstract: This study uses awake longitudinal functional ultrasound (fUS), ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM), and functional ultrasound localization microscopy (fULM) to define the temporal progression of neurovascular alterations in 5xFAD mice. Monthly imaging over 7 months was performed in 5xFAD-positive mice and non-transgenic controls, with behavioral testing and histological assessment of amyloid beta (Aβ) deposition and plaque–vessel association. ULM detected reduced microvascular flow velocity as early as 4 months, before changes in microvascular density. Later abnormalities included impaired flow organization, reduced hippocampal resting-state functional connectivity at 6 months, attenuated microvascular stimulus-evoked flow responses at 7 months, and reduced mesoscale cerebral blood volume responses at 8 months. These abnormalities preceded or accompanied associative memory impairment and were associated with Aβ accumulation and plaque–vessel proximity. These findings show that awake longitudinal fUS, ULM, and fULM provide complementary structural, flow, resting-state, and stimulus-evoked readouts for tracking staged neurovascular decline in Alzheimer’s disease models.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Ultrasound Localization Microscopy for Evaluating Cerebrovascular Responses After focused-Ultrasound blood-Brain Barrier Opening
papers.abstract: We used three-dimensional ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) to assess acute cerebrovascular structural and hemodynamic responses following focused ultrasound (FUS)-mediated blood-brain barrier (BBB) opening in the mouse brain. Each animal underwent baseline 3D ULM, MRI, FUS BBB opening, post-FUS MRI, and post-BBB 3D ULM. MRI and 3D B-mode ultrasound volumes were rigidly registered to localize the gadolinium-enhancing opening region for targeted ULM analysis. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted MRI confirmed focal BBB opening, while the tested exposure conditions produced no overt edema. Regional ULM comparison within the segmented opening zone showed similar vascular structure and velocity maps before and after BBB opening, with no significant paired change in mean ULM velocity across animals. These findings suggest that edema-free BBB opening does not induce substantial acute disruption of cerebrovascular structure or flow.

papers.title: 3D Whole-Brain Functional Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Reveals Neurovascular Activation in Awake Mice
papers.abstract: Functional ultrasound localization microscopy (fULM) has demonstrated strong potential for mapping brain-wide neurovascular activity at microscopic resolution. While 2D fULM has been extended to awake animals with improved functional sensitivity, it cannot capture whole-brain functional interactions among distributed regions. Extending fULM to 3D would address this limitation, but volumetric imaging suffers from increased data burden, sparse microbubble distributions, and reduced imaging quality, leading to decreased functional sensitivity. Existing 3D fULM has consequently been limited in performance and confined to anesthetized animals, where neurovascular responses are suppressed. Here, we present high-sensitivity 3D fULM in awake mice using a row-column-addressed array and a track-based analysis to mitigate signal sparsity in volumetric fULM. Compared with anesthetized imaging and conventional pixel-based methods, this approach reveals stronger, more spatially extensive, and more continuous activation patterns, enabling mapping of brain-wide neurovascular dynamics under natural physiological conditions.

papers.title: Longitudinal 3D Transcranial Ultrasound Localization Microscopy for Monitoring Cerebral Vasospasm
papers.abstract: Cerebral vasospasm is a severe complication of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), causing delayed cerebral ischemia and long-term neurological disability. Conventional imaging tools such as CT angiography and MRI are impractical due to limited portability and the need for patient transport, highlighting the need for bedside, non-invasive alternatives. This study evaluates 3D Transcranial Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (ULM) as a tool to detect, differentiate, and longitudinally monitor vasospasm in two preclinical murine models: focal vasoconstriction induced by intra-striatal endothelin-1 injection, and diffuse vasospasm mimicking SAH via cisterna magna blood injection. Using a 32×32 matrix array at 8 MHz, microbubble tracking was performed at baseline, 5 minutes, 1 hour, and 24 hours post-intervention. Vascular proximity served as a marker of local tissue oxygenation. 3D ULM distinguished focal unilateral hemodynamic reduction from bilateral diffuse disruption at 1 hour, verified by MRI at 24 hours. These results demonstrate ULM's sensitivity for quantitative cerebrovascular monitoring, supporting its potential for non-invasive vasospasm surveillance in neurocritical care.

sessions.title: MBF: Advanced Blood Flow Imaging Methods

papers.title: High-Volume Rate 3D Vector Flow in Multiplexed 2D Array Imaging Using Motion-Compensated Beamforming
papers.abstract: 3D vector flow imaging using ultrasound can be realized using matrix arrays, but the increased element count typically incurs exorbitant hardware costs. Time-domain channel multiplexing can be used to ameliorate but this workaround decimates the effective pulse repetition frequency for full volume reconstruction and induces motion artifacts. In this study, we devise a novel 3D vector flow framework based on motion-compensated beamforming and speckle tracking to realize robust velocimetry imaging using multiplexed matrix arrays. We devised a beamformer that estimates the motion of targets between receives for adaptive delay-and-sum focusing, enabled by a unique multiplexing configuration. Our framework was realized on a 32x32 matrix array and speckle tracking was used for time-resolved 3D velocimetry. Validation was performed using in vitro phantoms including a straight tube and 3D helical toroid, as well as an in vivo carotid. The proposed solution achieved improved flow registration and lower RMSE on all tested scenarios. In all, the presented framework may significantly bring down the hardware costs of 3D vector flow imaging.

papers.title: 3D Vascular Vector Flow Mapping from Single-Acquisition Matrix Array Color Doppler: Simulations and Experiments
papers.abstract: We present 3D vascular vector flow mapping (3D-vVFM), a physics-constrained optimization method designed to recover all three velocity components from a single volumetric color Doppler dataset. The 3D velocity field was estimated by minimizing a regularized least-squares cost function that combined a data fidelity term enforcing agreement between the projection of velocity onto the steered beam vector and the measured Doppler velocities, a Tikhonov regularization term to ensure spatial smoothness, and a soft parallel-flow prior to regularize under-determined transverse velocity components. Mass conservation and no-slip wall boundary conditions were enforced as hard constraints. The proposed method was validated with synthetic test cases and CFD based simulations. Experimental feasibility was demonstrated on a commercial vascular flow phantom using a 1024-channel programmable OpenSonics Discovery research system with two transmit steering configurations. The results suggests that 3D-vVFM enables volumetric vascular vector flow estimation from a single color Doppler volume using clinical matrix arrays, offering potential for non-invasive transtenotic pressure estimation.

papers.title: Directional Ridge Estimation and Mapping (DREAM) for contrast-Free Small Vessel detection: a Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: High-frame-rate ultrasound combined with contrast agents enables visualization of blood microcirculation in organs such as brain and kidney, but requires long acquisitions (several minutes) and contrast injection. Recently, methods like SURE have been proposed to enhance small vessel detection by compressing envelope images at their local maxima. Since reducing the envelope to discrete points may discard critical information, we developed DREAM, which compresses the blood signal envelope by shrinking it to a minimally connected ridge. We tested rat datasets at 15.6 MHz and rabbit kidney datasets at 8 MHz acquired on a Vantage 256. IQ images were beamformed using delay-and-sum, clutter removed via SVD filtering, and envelopes compressed to minimally connected ridges in each frame. The final image accumulates these ridges over time, applied separately to positive and negative Doppler components to distinguish flow directions, and repeated with different SVD filters to increase ridge detections. DREAM images from 4-second acquisitions show clearer vessel delineation than Power Doppler, with vascular architecture consistent with Ultrasound Localization Microscopy reports.

papers.title: Ultrahigh-Resolution and High Contrast Ultrafast Power Doppler with Two-Way Hyperbeam Plane Wave Compounding Imaging
papers.abstract: To improve the spatial resolution of ultrafast power Doppler (PD) imaging, we explored two-way hyper-Beamforming (two-way HBF) as an alternative to conventional delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming. HBF is a nonlinear technique that manipulates two subarrays through addition and subtraction operations, using the characteristic null in the difference beam pattern to enhance image resolution. In this study, we further improved this method by implementing the HBF technique on both the transmit (TX) and receive (RX) ends. By combining two-way HBF with plane-wave compounding, we leverage the nonlinear nulling effect at both the TX and RX ends to generate ultrahigh-resolution, high-contrast PD images. The in vivo experimental results suggest that the two-way HBF method effectively enhances the spatial resolution of PD images while providing superior image contrast.

papers.title: Synthetic Aperture Universal Sequence and Transverse Oscillation for in Vivo Wall Shear Imaging
papers.abstract: Wall shear stress (WSS) is a hemodynamic driver of plaque formation and rupture, yet noninvasive quantification remains challenging; MRI lacks precision and conventional ultrasound is limited by angle dependency. While vector flow imaging improves accuracy, it often compromises B-mode image quality. We propose an interleaved sequence combining SA with transverse oscillation for WSS imaging (WASHI) that maintains high-quality B-mode imaging without sacrificing flow estimation accuracy. Our framework utilizes singular value decomposition for clutter filtering and directional transverse oscillation for 2D velocity estimation. Tracked vessel wall positions are used to regularize the velocity field, and WSS is extracted from spatial gradients using a 2D Sobel filter. The obtained median WSS values were within the physiological range (1–3 Pa). The median coefficient of variation across 19 CCAs was 10.2%, indicating high precision and no significant differences in intrasubject variability were observed across participants (p = 0.45), supporting reproducible performance. These results demonstrate that WASHI enables precise and reproducible WSS estimation.

papers.title: Real-Time Alias-Free Ultrasound High-Frame-Rate Vector Flow Imaging Using Staggered Pulse Repetition Frequency
papers.abstract: High frame rate (HFR) vector flow imaging (VFI) enables angle-independent estimation of 2-D blood velocity fields but is limited by pulse repetition frequency (PRF) constraints, leading to aliasing in high-speed flows. This work presents a real-time HFR-VFI implementation based on staggered PRF (S-PRF) transmission for alias-free imaging. The approach was implemented on a heterogeneous platform including FPGAs, DSPs, and an embedded GPU. An FPGA beamformer reconstructed two RF images from separate apertures associated with opposite receive angles. Signals were demodulated, filtered, and streamed to the GPU, where clutter filtering, autocorrelation phase estimation, persistence filtering, and spatial smoothing were performed. Dual-PRF de-aliasing was applied using a lookup-table-based unwrapping method. Experimental validation on a rotating-disk phantom demonstrated effective aliasing suppression and accurate velocity estimation, with RMSE below 0.04 m/s and extended Nyquist limit.

sessions.title: MCA: Therapeutic cavitation and bio-effects

papers.title: Microbubble Cavitation for Augmentation of Immunotherapy in Head and Neck Cancer: Preclinical and Clinical Results
papers.abstract: We aimed to use stable microbubble cavitation to improve immunotherapy response rates in head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Mechanistic studies are provided from syngeneic preclincial tumor models and recent clinical data from a pilot clinical trial is also discussed.

papers.title: Ultrasound Mediated Microbubble Drug Delivery Inhibits Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma in a Mouse Model
papers.abstract: Two potential anti-tumor drugs targeting HNSCC, BAY-876 and STF-118804, were successfully encapsulated into the shell wall of a surfactant stabilized ultrasound contrast microbubble, SE61, without altering the microbubble properties. Administration of these microbubbles utilizing ultrasound mediated delivery in a mouse model over a three-week period significantly reduced tumor growth and improved survivor times compared to an unloaded SE61 control. This indicates that the delivery of these drugs utilizing microbubbles to the tumor via ultrasound are feasible, and that both drugs have potential to treat HNSCC and should be further evaluated.

papers.title: In Vitro Cavitation Platform with Lens-Enhanced Focal Coverage for Biofilm Disruption
papers.abstract: Chronic wound biofilms hinder antibiotic penetration and contribute to treatment failure. Ultrasound‑mediated cavitation enhanced by phase‑change contrast agents (PCCAs) offers a noninvasive disruption strategy, but progress has been limited by variable in‑vivo results, inadequate in‑vitro models, and restricted transducer coverage. To address these gaps, a 10% PVA multi‑well phantom was fabricated to mimic wound geometry using freeze-thaw crosslinking. A focused ultrasound transducer (~1 mm focal spot) was confocally aligned with a broadband transducer for passive cavitation detection, and a holographic acoustic lens designed via time‑reversal simulations and 3D‑printed expanded the focal spot to 6 mm without loss of sensitivity. Methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus biofilms on 6‑mm paper disks were treated at 1.1 MHz, 9.09% duty cycle, and 750 or 1400 kPa for 5 minutes. Cavitation dose was quantified from harmonic and broadband emissions. Pressure‑dependent PCCA activation produced distinct cavitation regimes, and variability at fixed pressures supported dose‑based over pressure‑based analysis. Treatment at 750 kPa yielded ~2‑log CFU reduction.

papers.title: Low Frequency Ultrasound-Enhanced Microdroplet Cavitation for Dynamic Scaffold Modulation and Localized Antibiotic Release
papers.abstract: Tissue engineering scaffolds face a trade-off between porosity and mechanical integrity, while post-implantation infection limits regeneration. We present an ultrasound (US)-driven strategy to modulate collagen scaffolds using embedded antibiotic-loaded phase-shift microdroplets (MDs). Lipid-shelled MDs containing perfluorohexane and ciprofloxacin were fabricated via microfluidics and incorporated into hydrogels. Upon activation by a rotating US transducer followed by 200 kHz insonation, MDs vaporize and cavitate, generating microporosity and enabling localized drug release. This produced scaffolds with increased porosity (~56%) and uniform micropores (~39 µm), alongside enhanced mechanical properties. Controlled antibiotic release yielded effective antibacterial activity against Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria. Fibroblast studies showed improved proliferation in treated scaffolds. Overall, this acoustic programming approach enables real-time, spatial control of scaffold architecture and therapeutic delivery, offering a promising platform for improved tissue regeneration.

papers.title: Sonoporation Disrupts Membrane Lipid Order: Direct Observations in Organelle-Free Giant Unilamellar Vesicles
papers.abstract: Sonoporation is a promising drug delivery paradigm, but the corresponding membrane biophysics is still poorly understood.
