The next phase will implement and validate the method on a programmable Verasonics Vantage NXT scanner with in vivo scans.

papers.title: Quick Flow-Informed SVD Thresholding for Densely Scanned Volumetric Power Doppler Micro-Angiography of Adult Zebrafish
papers.abstract: Densely scanned micro-Power Doppler Imaging (µPDI) using ultrafast, high-frequency ultrasound (>30 MHz) has revolutionized 3D micro-angiography of adult zebrafish without contrast agents. However, a Nyquist dense scans often produce hundreds of slices with large frame ensembles which make quick and reliable SVD threshold selection challenging. We propose a flow-informed SVD thresholding method that maps singular components to flow speed. Using the method, we can infer the thresholds adaptively based on the flow speed of the zebrafish. We found that our approach retained variety of vessel at multiple speeds in one frame. The final volume result showed the consistency of the dense volume at uniform half-lambda volume spacing of the adult zebrafish. Importantly, the proposed method operates in constant time, O(1), significantly outperforming conventional approaches such as STA-SSM (O(n²)). This efficiency makes it particularly well-suited for large-scale volumetric µPDI, where both computational speed and robustness are essential.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Normalization Preprocessing of Pulsed-Wave Doppler Images for Robust Deep Learning Clinical Tasks
papers.abstract: We propose a physics-informed, task-aware preprocessing pipeline for Pulsed Wave Doppler (PWD) ultrasound to improve deep learning robustness across heterogeneous clinical data tasks. Unlike conventional image normalization, our approach leverages the physical meaning of PWD signal axes to reduce variability introduced by differing acquisition settings. The pipeline includes three components: (1) temporal normalization, standardizing the horizontal axis to two cardiac cycles using autocorrelation; (2) baseline alignment with aliasing-robust padding, positioning zero velocity axis consistently; and (3) velocity normalization, fixing the vertical axis to a clinically relevant range. We validate the method on coronary flow classification using a diverse multi-vendor dataset. Results show improved out-of-fold accuracy (from 0.916 to 0.924) and substantial gains in generalization to unseen vendors and operators and acquisition setups (from accuracy 0.806 to 0.976). PCA analysis further indicates enhanced class separability. Overall, physics-informed normalization provides a simple, effective strategy for improving generalizable deep learning performance in clinical ultrasound.

papers.title: Comparing Power Doppler and Ultrasound contrast-Agent Imaging Methods on Ex Vivo Kidney Stones
papers.abstract: The color Doppler twinkling artifact is used to aid in detecting urinary stones. However, it appears on some urinary stones and not others. Here we compare nonlinear imaging methods to Doppler imaging of urinary stones in ex vivo porcine kidneys. Using an L7-4 on a Verasonics machine, we acquired beamformed IQ data from: B-mode, 5 versions of amplitude modulation (AM), pulse inversion (PI), amplitude-modulated pulse inversion(AMPI), power Doppler, and pulse-inverted power Doppler (PI Doppler). To compare the methods, we drew a region of interest (ROI) around the urinary stone and an ROI around tissue to calculate signal-to-tissue ratios (STRs) in dB. Compared to B-mode as a reference, the median STRs across the 20 stones were 11.7 (IQR: 10.2) dB for AM, 3.3 (4.4) dB for PI, 8.1 (7.4) dB for AMPI, -0.6 (9.2) dB for power Doppler, and 0.6 (6.6) dB for PI Doppler (Fig. 1B). AM (p = 0.004), PI (p = 0.041), and AMPI (0.004) had a significantly higher STR than B-Mode. The median STR of AM was significantly different than all other methods. These results suggest that contrast imaging methods, especially AM, may improve kidney stone detection by ultrasound and should be further explored.

papers.title: Non-Invasive Multiparametric Hemodynamic Profiling of Pulmonary Arterial Hypertension Using Multimodal Ultrasound Learning
papers.abstract: Hemodynamic profiling is fundamental to pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH), where mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP), pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), and cardiac output (CO) characterize disease severity and treatment response. However, reliable hemodynamic quantification still depends on invasive right heart catheterization (RHC). We developed MU-PAH, a multimodal ultrasound learning framework that jointly analyzes multi-view B-mode videos, Doppler images, and echocardiographic measurements for non-invasive multiparametric hemodynamic profiling. A total of 400 PAH patients from three medical centers were enrolled, with ultrasound imaging paired with RHC within 24 hours. In an independent external test, MU-PAH demonstrated improved accuracy in mPAP prediction over clinical assessments, achieving an MAE of 8.359 mmHg, reducing the MAE by 13.5% relative to cardiologists. Crucially, it also estimated PVR and CO with MAEs of 2.592 WU and 0.764 L/min. These findings demonstrate that MU-PAH enables routine ultrasound to accurately estimate invasive hemodynamics, serving as a competitive tool for non-invasive therapeutic evaluation and longitudinal monitoring of PAH.

sessions.title: MCA: Multimodal Methods and Advanced Acoustic Mapping

papers.title: Monitoring Intracranial Hypertension with subharmonic-Aided Pressure Estimation
papers.abstract: This pilot study assessed the utility of SHAPE for noninvasive intracranial pressure (ICP) estimation in patients scheduled to undergo lumbar puncture (LP). A total of 20 patients were enrolled. A significant negative correlation was observed between the SHAPE gradient and the reduction in ICP following drainage (r = –0.61, p = 0.01). ROC analysis showed that the SHAPE gradient identified elevated ICP with an AUC = 0.75, which increased to 0.89 when all the parameters were combined. In conclusion, SHAPE may have potential for noninvasive monitoring of ICP trends.

papers.title: Screening for Esophageal Varices in Patients with Advanced Compensated Chronic Liver Disease Using subharmonic-Aided Pressure Estimation (SHAPE)
papers.abstract: The objective of this study was to determine subharmonic-aided pressure estimation’s ability to identify patients with compensated chronic advanced liver disease who should receive endoscopic screening for esophageal varices, compared to the clinical reference standards.

papers.title: Multimodal Ultrasound and MRI Tracking of Engineered Macrophages in Brain Tumor Models
papers.abstract: Brain tumor immunotherapy depends on effective immune cell homing, yet no imaging tool tracks this process noninvasively in real time. We engineered a multimodal cellular probe by internalizing lipid microbubbles into macrophages, producing concurrent nonlinear ultrasound and susceptibility-based MRI contrast on clinically compatible hardware. Bubble size dominated acoustic output, and macrophage internalization raised the inertial cavitation threshold across formulations, indicating cellular shielding of the gas core. In a 4T1 breast-to-brain metastasis cohort imaged across 11 timepoints, treated mice showed tumor-localized ultrasound contrast peaking at 4 h and MRI hypointensity peaking at 8 h, both resolving by 24 h, while controls showed neither. Flow cytometry confirmed time-localized tumor accumulation followed by reticuloendothelial clearance, a profile consistent with active homing on a same-day diagnostic timescale. The platform extends to other engineered immune cell therapies for monitoring CNS cellular immunotherapy.

papers.title: Dual-Locked Nanosensors As activatable Imaging Biomarkers for Predictive Photoacoustic Imaging of Immunotherapy Responses
papers.abstract: Dual-locked nanosensors were developed as activatable imaging biomarkers to noninvasively assess functional T cell activity during adoptive T cell therapy (ACT). These nanosensors incorporate granzyme B (GzmB, released by activated cytotoxic T cells) and matrix metalloproteinase (MMP, upregulated in the tumor microenvironment)-responsive peptide substrates on gold nanospheres, enabling Boolean logic-gated activation only when both proteases are present. Dual activation induces nanosensor aggregation, enhancing near-infrared absorption and generating amplified photoacoustic (PA) signals via plasmon coupling. In vivo ultrasound-guided PA imaging in MC38 and antigen-specific MC38-OVA tumor models showed that, following ACT, PA signals increased selectively in MC38-OVA tumors, reflecting antigen-specific cytotoxic T cell activity. PA signal differences emerged early after therapy, and receiver operating characteristic analysis demonstrated high sensitivity and specificity for distinguishing responders from nonresponders. This platform enables longitudinal, noninvasive monitoring of immune function and early prediction of immunotherapy response.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Control of Microbubble Cavitation Activity with 3D Passive Acoustic Mapping Using Row-Column Arrays
papers.abstract: In microbubble (MB) cavitation based focused ultrasound therapies, real-time control of MB cavitation activity is essential for safe and effective treatments. For that, closed-loop controllers based on passive cavitation detection or 2D passive acoustic mapping (PAM) have been proposed. In this study, we demonstrate that using a recently proposed method for 3D PAM with row-column arrays, the level of MB cavitation activity can be more robustly controlled compared to the controller based on 2D PAM. A controller adjusts the output pressure to maintain the cavitation level within ±3% of the target. For comparison, in 2D PAM closed‑loop experiments, the controller reaches the target only when the focus lies inside the imaging plane; when it lies outside, inaccurate detection prevents target achievement. In contrast, 3D PAM consistently achieves the target regardless of focus position, with a rise time of 5 s and stable control over 60 s. These results demonstrate that 3D PAM overcomes the spatial limitations of 2D PAM, enabling sensitive and robust closed‑loop control of MB cavitation activity in 3D.

papers.title: Angular Spectrum Reconstruction of Passive Acoustic Mapping with Spatial Coherence from Sub-Aperture Multiply-and-Sum (SA-MAS)
papers.abstract: Passive acoustic mapping (PAM) is vital for monitoring cavitation during HIFU. While the angular spectrum (AS) method is computationally efficient, it suffers from limited axial resolution and high sidelobes. This study proposes a nonlinear AS framework using sub-aperture multiply-and-sum (SA-MAS). The receiving array is partitioned into non-overlapping sub-apertures for independent frequency-domain back-propagation. Their spatial coherence is estimated via the MAS algorithm to suppress incoherent noise and artifacts. The final PAM is synthesized by nonlinearly compounding sub-aperture spectra across a selected frequency range, leveraging inter-group coherence to narrow the point spread function. Simulation results show that SA-MAS significantly enhances image quality. Quantitative analysis reveals that the Image Signal-to-Noise Ratio (ISNR) improves by up to 9 dB and 8 dB for single and dual sources. A partition of 8 sub-apertures provides an optimal balance between complexity and quality, addressing the intrinsic resolution limits of conventional AS methods.

sessions.title: PAT: Acoustic Tweezers & Particle Manipulation

papers.title: Thermal Diffusion in Laser-Programmed Polymer Acoustic Holograms: Effects and Compensation
papers.abstract: Conventional acoustic metasurfaces generally have fixed phase profiles, limiting their adaptability. Reconfigurable polymers offer a promising alternative, but their performance depends on both acoustic properties and thermal pattern transfer. The sound-speed contrast between material states determines the film thickness required for phase modulation, whereas film thickness and laser-heating conditions govern writing precision. Here, we examine phase switching in polymers, calculate the thickness required for binary phase modulation, and generate binary holograms using the iterative angular spectrum approach. We then analyze how thermal diffusion expands the molten region and degrades pattern fidelity, and use the measured expansion to precompensate the binary hologram. Experiments show that the compensated pattern more closely reproduces the designed phase distribution and improves the fidelity of the reconstructed acoustic field. These results provide practical guidance for precise and reconfigurable polymer-based acoustic holography.

papers.title: Single-Element Three-Dimensional Ultrasound Imaging Through an Aberrating Layer Using a Chaotic Cavity
papers.abstract: 3D ultrasound imaging usually requires matrix arrays with many elements and channels. Chaotic cavities offer an alternative: a single transducer coupled to a reverberant cavity encodes spatial information and can behave as a virtual array after calibration. In this work, we test whether this approach can retain 3D imaging capability when propagation is distorted by an aberrating layer. A 2 MHz single-element transducer attached to a chaotic cavity was used as the imaging device. The transmitted field was measured with a hydrophone. The signal was cross-correlated with the measured impulse responses to estimate the virtual aperture wavefield, and delay-and-sum beamforming was used to obtain a 3D image. Without the aberrator, the hydrophone was localized at its expected position. With the aberrating layer, the reconstruction failed to localize the hydrophone correctly. After including the known layer properties in the time-of-flight calculation, the hydrophone image was recovered at its expected position. These results show that a single-element chaotic cavity can retain 3D imaging capability through an aberrating layer when an appropriate time-of-flight correction is used.

papers.title: Acoustic-Optical Observation of Inertial Cavitation and Coalescence Dynamics in Shell-Less Nanobubbles
papers.abstract: Traditional microbubbles (MBs) are restricted by their micrometer size, preventing extravasation into deep tissues. Shell-less nanobubbles (NBs, ~100 nm diameter) overcome this barrier for targeted delivery but endure a massive ~28.4 atm internal Laplace pressure, complicating rupture threshold prediction. We developed a confocal acoustic-optical system (HIFU, passive cavitation detection, high-speed camera) to quantify threshold discrepancies and dynamics. Our results show MBs cavitate at merely 4.87 MPa. Conversely, NBs remain acoustically silent until reaching 15-20 MPa, bursting at 25.17 MPa. This >5-fold difference confirms the extreme Laplace pressure barrier. We also observed an acoustic-optical threshold lag, suggesting NBs undergo nanoscale micro-rupture first, followed by gas coalescence to form visible clouds. Particle size distribution integration and freeze-thaw tests proved this mechanism. Ultimately, 100-nm NBs resolve MB size limitations for deep-tissue penetration, and we proved they can be effectively triggered by localized high-pressure HIFU, positioning them as highly reliable agents for targeted drug delivery.

papers.title: 3D-Printable Passive Acoustic Field Synthesizer at 40 Khz
papers.abstract: This work presents a 3D-printable cross-pillar gradient-index (GRIN) structure as a prototype passive acoustic field synthesizer for 40-kHz airborne ultrasound. Unlike active phased arrays, which require many driven channels, phase synchronization, calibration, and bulky electronics, the proposed passive structure encodes the target acoustic response into a discrete effective-index map. By controlling the local cross-pillar geometry of each subwavelength unit cell, the device imposes spatial phase delays and redistributes acoustic energy to shape both wavefront and pressure amplitude. A 21 × 21 × 5 cross-pillar lattice with a 2.14-mm pitch and an effective index range of approximately 1.00–1.66 was designed and evaluated by frequency-domain finite-element simulation. As a first demonstration, the prototype synthesizes two symmetric focal spots at 40 kHz, located at approximately x = ±9.36 mm and z = 3.48 mm, with a pressure enhancement of approximately 26.4 dB over the no-lens reference. The results suggest a manufacturable passive route toward arbitrary three-dimensional acoustic field synthesis.

papers.title: The Interactions of Elastic Waves with Two-Dimensional Crystals from Molecular Dynamics Simulations
papers.abstract: This work investigates the interaction of elastic waves with the interfaces of two-dimensional and bulk crystals from molecular dynamics simulations. It finds that under normal physical and chemical conditions, there is negligible transmission of kinetic energy from an elastic wavefront. The origin of this negligible transmission is determined by independently varying the physical coupling and acoustic mismatch of the interface. It is found that the nonbonded (weak van der Waals) interaction is the primary contributor, and transmission can be broadly tuned by increasing the adhesion energy to values closer to that of a bonded interaction (8× increase). This work is valuable for isolating elastic waves with atomic layers that are orders of magnitude less voluminous than traditional acoustic isolation.

papers.title: Experimental Realization of a Triple-Negative Complementary Metamaterial for Ultrasonic Pulse Transmission Through Elastic Barriers
papers.abstract: We present a triple-negative complementary metamaterial that enables ultrasonic transmission through an elastic barrier. The metamaterial exhibits negative effective mass density and elastic moduli, effectively canceling the barrier. Its monolithic aluminum unit cell incorporates symmetrically arranged local resonators, where inertial masses are connected to the host matrix via thin flexural beams. This design induces monopolar, dipolar, and quadrupolar resonances corresponding to negative bulk modulus, mass density, and shear modulus. Based on boundary effective medium theory, the unit cell is designed to achieve these properties near 50 kHz. Transient simulations using a 10-cycle Gaussian pulse predict enhanced transmission when attached to one side of the barrier. Fabricated via wire electrical discharge machining, the metamaterial demonstrates a fourfold increase in transmitted intensity in water-tank experiments, with a 14.2% bandwidth. The enhancement is reciprocal, yielding an echo intensity that is over 16 times higher. Applications include transcranial therapy, neuroimaging, nondestructive evaluation, and underwater communication.

sessions.title: MBB: Advanced Beamforming and Coded Excitation

papers.title: Physically Plausible Beamformer Augmentations for Ultrasound Image Enhancement
papers.abstract: Most ultrasound augmentations act in the image domain and cannot fully reproduce degradations originating in the beamforming chain, or resort to simulations where domain shifts are challenging. We introduce five physically plausible beamformer degradations applied to in vivo cardiac channel data from a 2D matrix array, including reducing the receive-aperture, beamforming using an incorrect speed-of-sound, simulating an aberatting screen, shifting the receive filter, and applying inverse coherence weighting. We use the degradations to create paired degraded/reference beamspace B-mode images and train a U-Net to undo the degradations. We show that combining beamformer degradations with in vivo channel data allowed controlled shaping of the image-quality distribution and enabled an image enhancement task where overall image quality was improved both qualitatively and with the Arqee image-quality estimator.

papers.title: Improving SNR in 3D Coherent Multi-Transducer Ultrasound Imaging Using Time-Space Encoding
papers.abstract: Coherent multi-transducer ultrasound (CoMTUS) synthesizes large apertures for improved 3D image quality, but sparse matrix arrays and the current standard of sequential narrowband transmission limit SNR. We introduce a time-space encoding framework in which arrays transmit frequency-modulated chirps simultaneously, increasing transmit efficiency while preserving separability using Hadamard encoding. RF data are decoded to recover the four multistatic datasets, then matched-filter compressed and beamformed for coherent reconstruction. The method was evaluated using Field II simulations and validated experimentally with two synchronized ULA-OP 256 systems and two 256-element sparse matrix arrays. Compared with sequential transmission, Hadamard-chirp encoding enhanced noise suppression, improved target and cyst detectability, and increased gCNR by up to 0.56 across noise levels. In phantom experiments, the method enabled detection of a deep ovoid target not visible with sequential imaging and improved cyst gCNR from 0.48 to 0.65. These results show that time-space encoding improves SNR, detectability, and contrast in 3D CoMTUS, with gains expected to increase as more arrays are added.

papers.title: ReFOCUS-Based Spatial-Frequency Apodization for Grating Lobe Suppression in Coherent Multi-Transducer Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Coherent multi-transducer ultrasound (CoMTUS) synthesizes a large aperture by combining data from multiple arrays, improving resolution, SNR, and field of view. However, aperture discontinuities introduce grating lobes that degrade image quality. Element-level apodization can suppress these artifacts, but requires the full multistatic Tx/Rx dataset. We introduce spatial-frequency apodization for CoMTUS REFoCUS imaging. REFoCUS recovers an element-resolved Tx/Rx representation from ultrafast transmissions, enabling pair-wise weighting of Tx/Rx contributions. Three angled arrays formed a sparse hyper-array with gaps in the effective aperture. Weights were derived by comparing support with an idealized gap-free aperture, enhancing underrepresented spatial frequencies. The method was evaluated in Field II simulations and validated with wire targets and a CIRS phantom against unapodized DAS. It reduced the simulated grating lobe by 8.5 dB, reduced experimental grating lobes by 6.6 dB on average, and improved cyst gCNR from 0.62 to 0.66. The results show that REFoCUS-based spatial-frequency apodization suppresses discontinuous-aperture grating lobes and improves CoMTUS image quality.

papers.title: Robust Minimum Variance Beamforming by Quantitatively Guided Local Sound Speed Correction
papers.abstract: Minimum Variance (MV) beamforming has superior resolution. Unfortunately, in heterogeneous tissues, phase aberrations induced by sound speed mismatches cause MV beamforming to lose its resolution advantage. In this paper, we propose a joint framework of local sound speed correction with MV beamforming (LSSC-MV). First, we quantify the MV degradation trend under sound speed errors and introduce the relative degradation coefficient (RDC). On this basis, the optimal search step size is analytically derived based on the RDC. Second, shifting the correction range from global to local region of interest (ROI), LSSC-MV mitigate phase errors caused by tissue heterogeneity, and forces MV to consistently operate at its theoretically optimal high-resolution state. Furthermore, this local strategy enables a hybrid imaging framework. Preliminary results from in vivo human liver scans demonstrate that LSSC-MV effectively prevents MV collapse in complex acoustic environments. The proposed framework achieves real-time ROI imaging at 17 fps, which provides an achievable pathway to break the resolution limits of clinical ultrasound.

papers.title: High-SNR Harmonic Ultrasound with Multipulse Coded Excitation
papers.abstract: Ultrasound image quality is constrained by tradeoffs among resolution, frame rate, and signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), especially for deep or attenuating targets where transmit energy is limited by safety and hardware. While coded excitation improves SNR, existing methods suffer from motion sensitivity, harmonic incompatibility, or hardware complexity. We propose a spatiotemporal multipulse coded excitation framework that improves SNR while being compatible with conventional systems and supporting both fundamental and harmonic imaging. Each transmit event includes repeated pulses separated by short delays, with two strategies: spatiotemporal codes with varying delays across pulses and transmissions, and temporal codes with fixed delays. Spatiotemporal coding enables flexible designs, while temporal coding simplifies decoding and improves motion robustness. Using REFoCUS-based frequency-domain decoding, the method preserves frame rate. Simulations and phantom experiments show a 12.02 dB SNR gain with 16-bit spatiotemporal coding and up to 3.6 dB with 3-bit temporal coding, preserving resolution and enabling extension to longer codes within safety limits for deep-tissue imaging.

papers.title: Simultaneous Transmission of Coded Diverging Waves for Ultrafast echocardiography: a Comparative Simulation Study of Different Coding Schemes
papers.abstract: Ultrafast echocardiography enables imaging of rapid cardiac motion, but achievable framerates are fundamentally limited by pulse repetition frequency. Simultaneous transmission of multiple coded diverging waves is a promising solution, allowing several images to be reconstructed from a single transmit event. The success of this approach, however, depends strongly on the correlation properties of the applied coding schemes and their impact on crosstalk and image quality. This study presents a systematic simulation-based comparison of seven coding families for simultaneous diverging wave transmission using a phased-array cardiac probe. Image quality was evaluated against conventional sequential transmission using resolution and contrast metrics on synthetic phantoms. Overall, the results show that chirp coding consistently provides the best trade-off between framerate gain and image quality, achieving strong crosstalk suppression and high contrast, albeit with reduced axial resolution.

sessions.title: MTC: Simulations, Phantoms & Advanced Image Analysis

papers.title: Microstructural Tissue Phantoms for Realistic Ultrasound Simulations
papers.abstract: This study presents a novel approach for constructing 2D numerical tissue phantoms by explicitly modelling tissue microarchitecture. Using spatial statistical models, tissue-specific microstructures for tendon, artery, and cartilage were generated based on the geometry and arrangement of collagen fibres and cells. The resulting cells and fibers were low pass filtered, resampled onto the simulation grid, and assigned tissue specific acoustic properties to generate spatial maps of density and sound speed. Ultrasound simulations performed with k Wave showed close agreement with ex vivo B mode measurements, as quantified by Jensen–Shannon divergence.

papers.title: In vivo-Style Anatomical Phantom Generation for Multitask Quantitative Ultrasound Learning
papers.abstract: Deep learning based quantitative ultrasound (QUS) relies on simulated data with paired ground truth, yet conventional phantoms lack anatomical realism, limiting generalization to in vivo data. We propose an in vivo-style phantom generation framework based on Gaussian random fields (GRFs) with distance-transform–based blurring, enabling controllable and diverse anatomical structures. The framework further supports multitask learning of speed of sound (SoS) and attenuation coefficient (AC).

papers.title: Paired Ground Truth Learning with Simulated Focused Ultrasound for Deep Learning-Driven QUS: a Transmit Focus Study
papers.abstract: Deep learning-based quantitative ultrasound (QUS) estimation has been predominantly developed using plane wave (PW) transmissions. However, line-by-line (LBL) transmission—the dominant mode in commercial scanners—involves diverse transmit (Tx) parameters whose effects on QUS estimation remain unexplored. This is the first study to systematically isolate and quantify the effect of Tx focus on deep learning-based QUS under a paired ground-truth framework. Specifically, we analyze the impact of Tx focal depth on speed-of-sound (SoS) estimation and in vivo lesion differentiation, and propose a training strategy robust to Tx focus variations.

papers.title: Measurement-Informed Acoustic Modeling for Lipid Sensitivity Assessment in Ultrasound Thermal Strain Imaging
papers.abstract: Ultrasound thermal strain imaging (US-TSI) estimates tissue composition from temperature-dependent speed of sound (SoS) changes that induce thermal strain. However, the quantitative relationship among temperature rise, composition, and strain remains unclear. This study establishes such a framework using phantom experiments and simulation. Oil–gelatin phantoms (0–40% oil) were fabricated, and SoS of oil and gelatin (24–40 °C) was measured and incorporated into a Wood’s equation model. Experiments used a customized probe (dual 32-element heating arrays + 192-element imaging array) with thermocouple monitoring. Thermal strain was estimated from axial displacement gradients. Matching Field II simulations applied the same model and methods. Results showed consistent trends: higher temperature increased strain magnitude, while higher oil reduced negative strain toward zero. Thermal strain varied linearly with both temperature and oil fraction (R² > 0.85), with close simulation–experiment agreement, supporting a physics-based explanation of US-TSI sensitivity.

papers.title: Robust Data-Driven Parameter Estimation for Quantitative Acoustic Microscopy
papers.abstract: Quantitative acoustic microscopy (QAM) enables high-resolution characterization of biological tissues using high-frequency ultrasound, but conventional model-based parameter estimation methods (e.g., autoregressive method) suffer from degraded performance under challenging conditions such as low SNR or thin sample thickness, leading to frequent outliers. To address this, we propose a robust data-driven framework for QAM parameter estimation. The approach leverages a large-scale simulated dataset to learn signal-to-parameter mappings and employs domain-adversarial training to bridge the gap between simulated and experimental data. A lightweight alignment network further calibrates predictions using a small set of reliable model-based estimates. Experimental validation on human lymph node and guinea pig eye tissues demonstrates that the proposed method significantly reduces outliers (<1%) while maintaining comparable accuracy to AR on inlier regions and improving robustness on challenging regions. These results highlight the method’s effectiveness and practical potential for real-world biomedical QAM applications.

papers.title: Texture-Based Ultrasound Foundation Model for Vitreous Hemorrhage Detection in Ocular Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Vitreous hemorrhage (VH), a vision-threatening condition, is often diagnosed with ultrasound, but automated detection is constrained by data scarcity. Foundation models are often used to ease the data requirement of such applications, but most foundation models commonly used today are based on frameworks designed for natural images. We develop a self-supervised texture-based framework for training ultrasound foundation models that forces foundation models to recognize common textures from various organs across the body. Thus, our texture model is able to adapt to unseen organs like the eye, detecting vitreous hemorrhage and outperforming other recent foundation models in latent-space detection. Our findings indicate that prioritizing ultrasound-specific features may offer significant advantages for downstream ultrasound applications like the detection of vitreous hemorrhage.

sessions.title: TMU: Piezoelectric Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducers: Novel Materials and Structures

papers.title: Spectrum Fusion in Dual-Frequency PMUTs via Excitation-Vibration Phase Shift
papers.abstract: This work presents an out-of-phase excitation strategy to achieve continuous broadband performance in dual-frequency piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) without increasing fabrication complexity. It is revealed that the spectral dip conventionally observed in dual-frequency PMUTs originates from the inherent phase shift between electrical excitation and mechanical vibration, which is determined by the membrane structure. To address this issue, a dual-frequency PMUT was designed and fabricated using a 30% scandium-doped aluminum nitride thin film, featuring circular membranes with two distinct radii and independent electrode pads. Finite element method and modal analysis confirm that the spectral dip stems from vibration phase divergence between units in the mid-frequency region. Experimental results in deionized water demonstrate that the proposed out-of-phase excitation completely eliminates the spectral dip, increasing the -3 dB fractional bandwidth from 18% to approximately 62%—a threefold improvement. This approach offers dual-mode operation for harmonic and broadband imaging using a single transducer.

papers.title: Crosstalk Suppression in Air-Coupled pMUT Arrays Using DC Bias Control
papers.abstract: Crosstalk inevitably emerges in transducer arrays when pitch size approaches operational wavelength, creating unpredictable effects on imaging quality and pressure field distribution. This phenomenon has remained critical throughout the evolution from lead zirconate titanate (PZT) bulk arrays to capacitive (CMUTs) and piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (pMUTs). Researchers have extensively explored complex structural modifications to control acoustic, mechanical, and electrical coupling in pMUT arrays, but these approaches also introduce fabrication complexities, higher costs, and performance compromises. This paper presents a novel approach using DC bias modulation of adjacent elements. Our comprehensive investigation demonstrates a cost-effective, simple, and efficient method for crosstalk management and acoustic coupling analysis in air-coupled pMUT designs. With bias control on surrounding, the driven cell's displacement increased to 6082 nm while adjacent cells decreased to 223 nm (3.7%), achieving 20-fold crosstalk reduction while enhancing the driving element's mechanical vibration.

papers.title: A High-Performance Sc₀.₃Al₀.₇N Piezoelectric-Capacitive Hybrid Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer (C+P MUT) Based on a Single-Sided Sacrificial Layer Process
papers.abstract: This work details the design, simulation, and characterization of a high-performance Sc₀.₃Al₀.₇N-based piezoelectric-capacitive hybrid micromachined ultrasonic transducer (C+P MUT). Finite element method (FEM) simulation and equivalent circuit modeling results show that the proposed C+P MUT achieves a center-point resonant displacement sensitivity of 383.67 nm/V at 815.57 kHz, an effective electromechanical coupling coefficient of 2.10%, and a peak transmitted sound pressure of 27.02 Pa/V at a 1 mm distance under 100 V DC bias and 1 V AC drive. Compared with an identical-size PMUT, the C+P MUT exhibits a 27% improvement in resonant displacement and a 23.8% enhancement in transmitted sound pressure, providing a high-performance, easy-to-fabricate solution for air-coupled ultrasonic ranging systems.

papers.title: Multimodal Analysis and Design of a Tessellated PMUT Array with Irregular Cell Geometry
papers.abstract: Bandwidth is a key performance metric for PMUT arrays in water-coupled applications such as medical imaging. A common approach to increase bandwidth consists in varying the dimensions of the cells within the array element so that different damped resonances are combined. However, this approach leads to spatially non-uniform response across the transducer surface, which can degrade beam coherence, limit elevational focusing, and increase sidelobe level. In this work, bandwidth extension is pursued by exploiting multiple vibration modes within each PMUT cell, combined with a controlled variation of cell geometries across the array, resulting in a tessellated layout composed of irregularly shaped membranes enabling a more spatially consistent broadband response. To evaluate this approach, a hybrid modeling framework is developed and experimentally validated. Based on this framework, a tessellated PMUT array with irregular cell geometry is designed, fabricated, and characterized.

papers.title: Influence of Dual DC Biasing on Bandwidth and Sensitivity of a Dual-Electrode PMUT for Air-Coupled Applications
papers.abstract: Air-coupled piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) are often limited by low sensitivity and narrow bandwidth. While single DC biasing has been used to improve performance, the potential of independently biasing multiple electrodes remains underexplored. This work investigates dual DC biasing in a dual-electrode PZT PMUT to actively control membrane stress and enhance performance. The device, fabricated on SOI with a 1 µm PZT layer, operates near 308 kHz. Finite-element simulations and experimental characterization, including impedance analysis, laser Doppler vibrometry, and acoustic measurements, are used to evaluate performance under different bias conditions. Applying opposite-polarity DC biases significantly improves performance, extending the −3 dB bandwidth by about 52% and increasing displacement sensitivity by more than twofold. Acoustic measurements show an 80% increase in transmission sensitivity (≈10.7 dB). These results demonstrate that dual DC biasing is an effective approach for improving bandwidth and sensitivity in air-coupled PMUTs.

papers.title: Enhanced Ultrasonic Transmission for Multi-Frequency Sensing Enabled by Co-Sputtered 42% Sc-Doped Aluminum Nitride PMUT Arrays
papers.abstract: This work demonstrates a co-sputtered 42% Sc-doped AlN (ScAlN) PMUT array for broadband multi-frequency underwater ultrasonic sensing. High-quality ScAlN films were deposited by optimized co-sputtering and integrated into PMUT arrays through MEMS microfabrication. Material and device characterizations were conducted, including wafer-level piezoelectric coefficient extraction and nonlinear vibration analysis. Compared with 30% ScAlN, the 42% ScAlN film showed enhanced electromechanical performance, with e31,f of −1.95 C/m² and coupling coefficient of 8.3%. Benefiting from the improved piezoelectric response, the 263 kHz PMUT achieved a displacement amplitude of 845 nm/V and a maximum underwater transmitting pressure of 1.82 kPa/V. The PMUT array integrates elements with different resonance frequencies, enabling broadband acoustic transmission. Under mixed-frequency excitation, the array showed a more uniform spectral response than a conventional ultrasonic probe, with a reduced peak-amplitude coefficient of variation of 0.446. These results highlight the potential of high-Sc-content ScAlN PMUT arrays for compact underwater multi-frequency ultrasonic monitoring.

sessions.title: AIL: Improving Loss and Power Handling

papers.title: Balancing Electrical and Acoustic Losses in High-Frequency BAW Resonators via Geometry Engineering
papers.abstract: This work investigates active-region geometry engineering to balance electrical and acoustic losses in high-frequency BAW resonators. As frequency increases, thinner piezoelectric stacks and electrodes raise electrode resistance, degrading Zs and Qs. Increasing the length-to-width aspect ratio can reduce current-path resistance and improve series-side performance, but excessive elongation may weaken acoustic confinement and increase acoustic loss. To clarify this trade-off, Al0.8Sc0.2N BAW resonators with the same active area of 1500μm2 and aspect ratios of 2:1, 3:1, 4:1, and 5:1 were designed, fabricated, and characterized. Simulations and de-embedded measurements show that the 2:1 devices exhibit higher Zp and a higher Qp of about 330, compared with about 206 for the 5:1 devices, indicating stronger acoustic confinement and lower acoustic loss. Wafer-level statistics further reveal that larger aspect ratios reduce electrical loss but increase acoustic loss. These results demonstrate that aspect-ratio optimization provides an effective guideline for loss-balanced high-frequency BAW resonators for wideband RF filters.

papers.title: Evaluation of Intrinsic Qm of Bulk Crystal Plate and Comparing with Thin Films
papers.abstract: The intrinsic mechanical quality factor Qm of resonator materials critically affects the Q factor of BAW filters. In the last conference, a new method for evaluating Qm of the bulk crystal plate using an input impedance modulated GHz pulse-echo technique without using a water coupler was proposed. In this method, the thin film ScAlN film ultrasonic transducer is grown directly on the bulk crystal specimen. However, the film quality of ScAlN transducer sometimes depends on the variety of the underlying bulk crystal specimen. In this study, Qm of the bulk crystal specimens were evaluated using a Au bonding technique. The bulk crystal specimens were bonded to the delay line substrate with thin film ultrasonic transducer (HBAR). Although this method requires an additional bonding process, it allows the Qm evaluation of any kind of bulk crystal specimen. Our motivation is to compare Qm of the bulk crystal plates with that of the thin films. Qm of thin films tend to be lower than that of bulk materials. On the other hand, the significant degradation of Qm was not found between thin film and bulk plate for the amorphous silica glass.
keywords: The intrinsic mechanical quality factor Qm

papers.title: Ultra-Low Loss LLSAW Resonator Using X-123°Y Lithium Niobate
papers.abstract: We propose a new crystalline orientation, X-123°Y LiNbO3 (LN), to excite LLSAW with a much smaller leakage. Unlike conventional X-46°Y LN that shows significant loss and special configurations like acoustic mirrors or high velocity substrate (e.g., SiC) are required to confine energy, the proposed resonator exhibits a decreased energy leakage even using bulk LN. The measured Z-ratio using X-123°Y LN is 51 dB and shows 15 dB improvements compared to those employing X-46°Y LN. Furthermore, when employing a layered structure like LN/Si and LN/SiC, the performance can be further enhanced using X-123°Y LN, but significant Q degradations or spurious modes can still be observed using X-46°Y LN. The proposed resonator exhibits an ultra-low loss and a spurious-free response and shows great potential for filtering applications above 3.4 GHz.

papers.title: 11 GHz ScAlN FBAR Resonator Structure with Low Resistance Electrodes
papers.abstract: A novel FBAR resonator structure providing a combination of very low electrode resistance and high coupling at high frequency is designed. The structure consists of ScAlN piezoelectric layer sandwiched between thin Q layers providimg the high frequency and coupling, further sandwiched between thick layers of Al and W providing low resistance but not reducing the frequency. Fabrication process was optimised for the complex multilayer stack of metals and ScAlN to yield a combination of low sheet resistance and good crystalline ScAlN texture for high K2. Resonators at 11 GHz yield sheet resistance of 0.2 Ohm/square, series resistance < 1 Ohm per resonator, K2 of 13.6 % and Q up to 200 and over.
keywords: FBAR BAW 6G FR3 ScAlN AlScN multilayer electrode resistance

papers.title: Investigation on the Improvement of Qm and TCV in sputter-Deposited SiO2 Films
papers.abstract: With their positive TCV, SiO2 films are crucial for achieving zero-TCF RF filters. Although a positive correlation between intrinsic Qm and TCV in sputtered SiO2 films was reported, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. This study combines a GHz pulse-echo technique with FT-IR and XRD to elucidate them. TCV and Qm were evaluated using ScAlN transducers and SiO2 films on opposite substrate sides. Longitudinal wave velocity from echo time delays enabled TCV estimation during heating. Propagation loss from insertion loss differences yielded Qm via quadratic fitting. XRD and FT-IR evaluated the intermediate-range order and Si-O-Si bond angles, respectively. Results confirm a strong positive Qm-TCV correlation. Structural analysis linked these improvements to increased intermediate-range order, Si-O-Si bond angles, and the longitudinal optical mode. Compared to bulk silica glass, sputtered films exhibit a denser network and smaller bond angles. This suggests Qm and TCV improvements are driven by relaxing structural frustration toward lower density. The presentation will discuss negative ion bombardment during sputtering as the probable cause.

papers.title: Superior Performance of Al0.8Sc0.2N FBAR Resonator Enabled by Improved Crystallinity of Piezoelectric Film
papers.abstract: This work systematically evaluates the impact of Al₀.₈Sc₀.₂N film crystallinity on FBAR performance. Two resonators with identical structures but different XRD (002) rocking curve FWHM values (0.44° and 1.54°) were compared. The high-crystallinity device achieved a significantly higher Q (~1573 vs. ~374) and improved kₑff² (13.3% vs. 11.7%). MBVD analysis shows that improved crystallinity reduces dielectric loss resistance R₀ (0.28 Ω to 0.04 Ω) and motional resistance Rₘ (0.32 Ω to 0.14 Ω), indicating suppressed dielectric and acoustic dissipation. The broader FWHM film suffers from grain misalignment and defect-related losses, while the narrow FWHM film preserves well-oriented c-axis structure and stronger piezoelectric response. These results establish a clear link between AlScN crystallinity and FBAR loss mechanisms, highlighting the importance of film quality optimization for achieving high-Q, low-loss BAW devices.

sessions.title: NDE: General NDE Methods, Process Control, Industrial Ultrasound and Structural Health Monitoring

papers.title: In-Situ Ultrasonic Monitoring of Zn-Ion Batteries for Non-Destructive State Tracking
papers.abstract: Aqueous zinc-ion batteries (ZIBs) are promising for medical devices due to their intrinsic safety, yet their state-of-charge (SOC) is difficult to assess non-destructively. Electrical methods are indirect, and existing ultrasonic techniques and industrial probes are not well adapted to ZIB structures.Here, a 3.25 MHz dual-matching-layer ultrasonic transducer (75% bandwidth) is developed for efficient acoustic coupling and in-situ SOC monitoring. A pulse–echo method extracts time-of-flight (TOF) and signal amplitude (SA), combined with X-CT and EIS for cross-scale analysis.Unlike lithium-ion batteries, ZIBs show increasing TOF and SA with SOC during charging. This trend is linked to phase-transition-induced mechanical evolution (α-MnO₂ to ZnxMnO₂/MnOOH). TOF agrees well with EIS, indicating coupled interfacial and acoustic dynamics.These results demonstrate a structure-adapted ultrasonic method for quantitative, non-destructive SOC evaluation of ZIBs.

papers.title: Off-Resonant Electromechanical Response for Rapid Defect Screening of Multilayer Ceramic Capacitors
papers.abstract: mlccs are prone to internal cracks during manufacturing, yet conventional non-destructive methods are too slow for 100% inline screening. while electromechanical transient response has been proposed as a rapid alternative, methods relying on fundamental resonant frequencies lack sufficient sensitivity. a dataset of 264 mlccs was evaluated using sequential toneburst excitations (1–10 mhz) superimposed on a 15 v dc bias. eleven time- and frequency-domain features were extracted, with a mahalanobis distance (md) criterion identifying the most defect-discriminative driving frequencies, validated using a random forest classifier. md analysis confirmed that off-resonant frequencies are significantly more discriminative than the primary resonance. using only six md-selected frequencies, the model achieved an roc-auc of 0.9529 and accuracy of 0.8901. shap analysis further revealed that time-domain features — particularly crest factor and skewness — were more decisive than frequency-domain metrics. the framework reduces per-unit inspection time to the millisecond scale, confirming viability for 100% inline screening.

papers.title: Pose-Adaptive Wavenumber-Domain Plane Wave Imaging for Automated Online Rail Inspection on Curved Tracks
papers.abstract: Automated ultrasonic inspection of rails using plane wave imaging (PWI) suffers from image distortion and blind zones on curved tracks, where superelevation tilts the probe and invalidates the precalculated focal delays of conventional Delay-and-Sum beamforming. Real-time delay recalculation is computationally prohibitive and degrades the frame rate. This work proposes a pose-adaptive wavenumber-domain plane wave full-focusing imaging method for online rail inspection. Laser sensors and cascaded neural networks measure the probe pose in real time and generate steered emission delays, producing planar wavefronts through the curved couplant-rail interface. A dynamic wavenumber-domain pipeline then reconstructs the image via wavefield rotation migration, non-stationary phase-shift migration, and Lu's frequency-wavenumber migration. The method reduces computational complexity by orders of magnitude over conventional PWI-DAS, achieving up to 1493 fps on a commercial platform with an emission delay error below 51.2 ns. Experiments on a rail sample with manufactured cracks and a side-drilled hole confirm high sensitivity and accuracy on both straight and curved tracks.

papers.title: Residual Torque Prediction for Bolted Joints Using a Physics-Prior Fusion Network with Guided-Wave Nonlinearity
papers.abstract: This study proposes a physics-prior fusion network for residual torque prediction in bolted joints using square-wave-excited ultrasonic guided waves. To reduce the influence of inherent harmonics in square-wave excitation, the indicator Re, defined as the band energy ratio between the third harmonic and the fundamental component, is introduced as a physics prior. The network combines multi-path waveform features extracted by learnable Sinc filters and a Transformer with path-wise Re features for torque regression. Experimental results on a bolted lap-joint aluminum plate show accurate prediction over 0–30 N·m, with the learned attention distribution reflecting path-dependent contributions, demonstrating improved accuracy and interpretability for bolted-joint state evaluation.

papers.title: Portable Real-Time 3-D Air-Coupled Ultrasound Imaging Using Sparse Array and Synthetic Aperture Beamforming
papers.abstract: A portable real-time 3-D air-coupled ultrasound (ACU) imaging system is presented using a sparse array and synthetic transmit aperture (STA) beamforming. The system operates at 41 kHz and employs a 64-channel sunflower sparse receive array with an 11.8-cm aperture. Five transmit elements arranged in a center-plus-cardinal configuration are sequentially fired to realize 5-Tx STA. High-voltage burst excitation is used for transmission, and multi-channel echoes are acquired by MEMS microphones with analog amplification. To enable real-time embedded operation, a ROI-based multi-C-scan reconstruction framework is adopted to restrict beamforming to valid depth regions, significantly reducing computational load. Beamforming is implemented on an FPGA-based platform with parallel processing, combining delay-and-sum, coherence factor weighting, and STA compounding. Experimental results show that the proposed STA system achieves 1.97-cm resolution and –56.6 dB peak sidelobe level at 50 cm depth, outperforming single-transmit imaging. Volumetric experiments further demonstrate clear separation of targets at different depths, confirming effective 3-D spatial discrimination.

papers.title: A Low-Voltage-Driven, Broadband PMUT Array with Anisotropic Plane-Wave Compounding for Structural Health Monitoring of CFRP Composites
papers.abstract: Carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites are widely utilized in aerospace engineering, making their continuous structural health monitoring (SHM) critically important. Compact, low-power piezoelectric micromachined ultrasonic transducers (PMUTs) are ideal for this. However, conventional PMUTs suffer from narrow bandwidths causing "ringing" effects that degrade axial resolution. Furthermore, the multi-layered anisotropy of CFRPs introduces severe acoustic attenuation and wavefront distortion. To overcome these challenges, this work proposes a broadband 1×32 PMUT array integrated with an Anisotropic Plane-Wave Compounding (APWC) algorithm, which achieves an exceptional fractional bandwidth (FBW) of 80% consistent with EQC results, improves the Contrast-to-Noise Ratio (CNR) by 63% and the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) by 9 dB compared with standard isotropic algorithms.

sessions.title: MEL: Pulse Wave Imaging and Arterial Nonlinearity

papers.title: Time-Aligned Plane Wave Compounding for Pulse Wave Imaging
papers.abstract: Pulse Wave Imaging (PWI) requires high imaging frame rates (FR) usually achieved using PWC. There is a tradeoff in PWC between the number of compounded angles and the FR vs. PRF. Time-aligned PWC (TAPWC) has been proposed to increase FR using IQ interpolation but has not yet been applied to PWI. We compare PWC and TAPWC for PWI. We also point out that TA IQ interpolation can be performed at rates above the PRF which we call time-aligned upsampled (τ) PWC. Pulsatile flow was induced in two vascular phantoms. Imaging was performed using angled plane waves at several PRFs. PWI was performed on a healthy volunteer. In vivo data were subsampled to simulate reduced PRFs. Data were compounded using PWC, TAPWC, and τPWC. Phantom PWC-estimated PWVs are highly variable at PRFs below 1000 Hz. TAPWC PWVs were stable as low as 500 Hz PRF, and τPWC PWVs as low as 250 Hz. For in vivo acquisitions, PWV IQRs estimated using time alignment are reduced or nearly identical to those obtained with PWC, except for the 468 Hz RCCA PWVs. Pulse wave upstroke markers are more readily discriminated using the time-aligned techniques. Results suggest time alignment reduces the necessary PRF for robust PWI.

papers.title: In Vivo Detection of Guided Waves in the Carotid Wall Using a skin-Mounted Piezoelectric Patch and Ultrafast Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Arterial wall stiffness is an established predictor of cardiovascular events. Pulse Wave Imaging tracks the natural pressure wave to estimate regional pulse wave velocity but provides a single frequency point per cardiac cycle. Shear wave elastography based on acoustic radiation force suffers from operator dependency and limited reproducibility. Time-Harmonic Elastography uses inversion schemes assuming bulk shear waves not adapted to guided waves in thin arterial walls. Here we propose a skin-mounted piezoelectric patch generating continuous harmonic excitation at 250 Hz to detect guided waves in the carotid wall in vivo. A 35 mm patch driven at 250 Hz / 60 Vpp was applied on the neck of three healthy subjects. Imaging used a Ula-OP system with an 8 MHz linear probe at 5000 fps. The complex field at 250 Hz was extracted from IQ data by Fourier transform, and phase velocity computed from the spatial gradient of the unwrapped phase. Across the three subjects, a clear guided wave was tracked along the wall with a wavelength of ~15 mm and a phase velocity of 3.75 m/s, consistent with the literature. Future work will use multi-frequency excitation to recover the dispersion curve

papers.title: A Feasibility Study of 4-D Pulse Wave Imaging Using a Row-Column-Addressed Array: in Phantom and in Vivo
papers.abstract: Pulse wave imaging (PWI) is a high-frame-rate ultrasound elastography technique for characterizing arterial mechanics, but conventional implementations rely on 1-D transducers that capture only a single 2-D spatial plane. This study shows the feasibility of 4-D PWI using a row-column-addressed (RCA) array in phantom and in vivo. Coherently compounded plane wave acquisitions (7 angles per orientation, PRF = 7000 Hz) were performed on a polyvinyl alcohol carotid-mimicking phantom and on the common carotid artery of a healthy human subject. Axial wall velocity was reconstructed via 1-D normalized cross-correlation, and pulse wave velocity (PWV) was computed by planar linear regression at peak acceleration during end-diastole. In the phantom, RCA-derived PWV (8.08 ± 0.62 m/s) closely matched the nanoindentation reference based on the modified Moens–Korteweg equation (8.23 ± 0.87 m/s). In vivo, RCA-derived PWV (4.57 ± 1.15 m/s) agreed with an L7-4 linear-array reference (4.71 ± 0.68 m/s). Ongoing work will validate the framework in a larger in vivo cohort and assess its sensitivity in resolving 3-D modulus anisotropy and mapping stiffness across distinct plaque constituents.

papers.title: Disentangling pulse-Wave Velocity from Blood pressure: Ultrafast Ultrasound Reveals Nonlinear Arterial Stiffness Dynamics in Humans
papers.abstract: Hypertension, the leading preventable cause of stroke, is linked to arterial stiffness (AS), but its relationship with blood pressure (BP) remains poorly understood. Current AS assessments using pulse wave velocity (PWV) overlook non-linearity between AS and BP, introducing bias. We developed a custom ultrasound-cuff device to modulate pressure conditions, enabling noninvasive characterization of arterial walls' nonlinear biomechanics while overcoming BP confounding. Our prototype coupled a water-filled cuff to an 8MHz ultrafast ultrasound scanner to image pulse wave propagation in brachial artery walls under varying cuff pressure. PWV was measured via cross-correlation of wall acceleration, corrected by √(radius/wall thickness). Data from 2 volunteers (23 and 35 yo) revealed a non-linear PWV–cuff pressure relationship (β = -0.10 ± 0.02 and -0.04 ± 0.01 mmHg⁻¹). PWV decreased with increasing cuff pressure due to reduced arterial stress. Overcoming BP confounding, we observed significant PWV differences above diastolic pressure (p < 0.001), but not below it (p = 0.15). This work paves the way for identifying a reliable AS biomarker for hypertension.

papers.title: Estimating Arterial Nonlinearity and Anisotropy Using Shear Wave Elastography
papers.abstract: In this work, we present a shear wave elastography (SWE) framework for estimating arterial nonlinearity and anisotropy. Longitudinal wave velocity (group velocity) measured across the cardiac cycle is used to characterize nonlinear behavior, whereas circumferential wave velocity captures anisotropic contributions. Experimentally measured wave velocities were matched with semi-analytical finite element simulations for hyperelastic inversion. The framework was first validated in a PVA hydrogel vascular phantom under 21 biaxial loading states spanning different axial and circumferential stretches. A representative Gent hyperelastic model was used to fit both longitudinal and circumferential wave velocities. The inversion showed low reconstruction error and a clear minimum in the Gent parameter space, supporting the robustness of the framework. The validated framework was then applied in vivo to the human carotid artery using a simplified Holzapfel-Gasser-Ogden model, where the simulated results captured the nonlinear and anisotropic trends of wave velocities across the cardiac cycle.

papers.title: Evaluation of Common Carotid Artery Mechanical Properties and Their Relationships with Brain Magnetic Resonance Imaging Features
papers.abstract: Ultrasound-based assessments of common carotid artery (CCA) mechanical properties could serve as an important predictor of target-organ damage in the brain. Arterial Dispersion Ultrasound Vibrometry (ADUV) was used to evaluate the relationship between brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and CCA mechanical properties. Twenty-four subjects with at least two cardiovascular risk factors underwent arterial health measurements including ADUV measurements. Measurements were ECG-gated such that 10 equally spaced cardiac stage (CS) timepoints were evaluated for each subject over the cardiac cycle. The median phase velocity dispersion curve was measured and an inversion to determine the CCA shear modulus, G, at each CS was performed. The subjects also had brain MRI examinations and brain region volumes were segmented and quantified. Spearman correlations were calculated for relationships of G with WMH, ARTS, and carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (cfPWV). Preliminary findings indicate that shear modulus CCA measurements may be related to brain MRI vascular features and systemic arterial stiffness.

sessions.title: MIS: Biomedical Monitoring & Tissue Dynamics

papers.title: Studying the Dynamics of Pleural Line for Vibration Excitation in 29 Lung Disease Patients
papers.abstract: Vibroelastography uses continuous low-frequency excitation to enhance pleural line detection in lung ultrasound, but vibration-derived features (RMS, spectral, autocorrelation) are rarely benchmarked against proper negative controls. We analyzed 29 lung disease patients (CPFE, emphysema, ILD) scanned at 0 Hz (control), 100, 150, and 200 Hz with a 6.5-MHz probe. Eight vibration features were computed above vs below the auto-detected pleural and quantified by per-patient AUC. The 0 Hz negative control matched or exceeded all vibration-on conditions (median AUC up to 0.85), with Bandpass-RMS showing reversed dose-response (0.85 at 0 Hz vs 0.66–0.70 at 100/150/200 Hz). Pleural depth correlated negatively with AUC (Spearman r = −0.62 to −0.67, p<0.01), while BMI showed no significant correlation. The apparent vibration signal is dominated by depth-dependent acoustic impedance, not biomechanics. We recommend benchmarking against B-mode-only controls and focusing future work on surface wave speed quantification

papers.title: Spatially Resolved Pulse Waveform Measurement Using Ultrasound Strain Imaging
papers.abstract: Ultrasound strain imaging may enable noninvasive, spatially resolved measurement of local arterial pulse waveforms beyond conventional surface methods. In this pilot study, a Vevo F2 system acquired RF data from three fingertips of a healthy volunteer under resting, post-exercise, and postprandial conditions. Pulse-driven tissue deformation was quantified using accumulated axial strain, and arterial-region strain waveforms were used as surrogates of local pulse waveforms. The extracted waveforms consistently demonstrated key features including the systolic peak, notch, and reflected peak. Normalized waveform analysis revealed physiologically meaningful changes across conditions, including variations in reflected peak amplitude and systolic-to-notch timing following exercise, recovery, and food intake. These results support the feasibility of ultrasound strain imaging for localized pulse waveform assessment and suggest potential applications in cardiovascular and hemodynamic monitoring.

papers.title: Feasibility Study of SVD-Based Needle Tracking at Steep Insertion Angles
papers.abstract: Ultrasound guidance often fails to provide reliable needle visualization during deep interventions, such as sciatic nerve or lumbar plexus blocks, where needle insertion angles commonly exceed 30°. At these steep angles, specular reflection redirects the ultrasound beam away from the transducer, rendering the needle invisible in conventional B-mode imaging and increasing the risk of nerve or vascular injury. In this study, we investigated the feasibility of using a Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)-based algorithm to track needles at steep insertion angles by extracting spatio-temporal features from ultrasound data. The proposed framework was validated through both Field II simulations and water tank experiments. Results demonstrated that the SVD-based method successfully tracked needles at insertion angles up to 65°, where conventional B-mode imaging failed to visualize the needle. These findings suggest that SVD offers a robust solution for high-precision needle tracking at steep insertion angles, with the potential to enhance procedural accuracy and improve patient safety.

papers.title: Ultrasound Texture Features As a Biomarker of Decompression Stress in bycaught Sea Turtles
papers.abstract: Decompression sickness can occur in humans after a decrease in ambient pressure and is likely caused by gas emboli formation in bubbles and tissues. Diving animals can also get gas emboli, specifically, sea turtles develop this pathophysiology when their diving behaviors are interrupted via bycatch events. In this study, ultrasound images were taken of the hearts, livers, and kidneys of bycaught sea turtles, scanned either on shore or on fishing boats. These data were graded on an ordinal scale from 0 – 5, separated by scanning location (shore or boat), and time courses of grades per organ were elucidated. Additionally, image processing metrics including region of interest pixel brightness and texture were calculated. A difference in gas evolution per organ was found. Brightness was found to increase with increasing gas grade, before decreasing at the highest grades, consistent with acoustic shadowing. Texture features were found to trend with gas grade, and logistic regression showed texture features ability to predict scan group (shore or boat) as a grade and time delay proxy. These results suggest future use of these metrics in human diving ultrasound scans.

papers.title: Critical Structure Detection Using Temporally Enhanced Ultrasound (TeUS)
papers.abstract: Unintended vascular injury during image-guided surgery can lead to severe complications. While arteries, veins, nerves, and surrounding tissue often share similar static echogenicity in conventional ultrasound imaging, they differ in pulsatility, biomechanical response, and subtle micro-motion. We introduce Temporally Enhanced Ultrasound (TeUS) as a label-free approach for detecting critical neurovascular structures using in-vivo ultrasound consecutive sequences acquired from neurovascular bundles in eight piglet hind-limb models. Artery, vein, nerve, and surrounding tissue regions were segmented from obtained sequences, and their mean temporal traces were analyzed using power spectral density. TeUS revealed structure-specific temporal fingerprints: arteries showed strong pulsatile fluctuations with spectral power approximately 2–3 orders of magnitude greater than veins, veins had lower spectral magnitude with low-frequency variation, and nerves showed intermediate dynamic behavior. These results demonstrate that TeUS converts visually ambiguous ultrasound data into physiologically meaningful temporal contrast for automated intraoperative critical-structure detection.

papers.title: Estimation of Finger Joint Angles and Index Finger Contact Force from B-Mode Ultrasound Using Deep Learning: a Preliminary Study
papers.abstract: Ultrasound-based hand motion interpretation is promising for rehabilitation and assistive interfaces. While surface electromyography is widely used, it can be degraded by electrode displacement, limited deep-muscle selectivity, and crosstalk. This study proposes a proof-of-concept framework for jointly estimating finger joint angles and index finger contact force from a single B-mode ultrasound frame. Ultrasound images were acquired at the wrist and forearm using a Verasonics Vantage 128 with an L12-5 probe. Ground-truth angles were recorded using Quantum Metagloves, and contact force was measured using a force-sensitive resistor with microcontroller-based calibration. A pretrained ResNet-18 encoder was adapted into a multi-output regression network to simultaneously estimate 15 finger joint angles and force. Data were collected from one participant performing grasp and pinch tasks at three force levels, with four repetitions per condition. Using 4-fold cross-validation, the wrist placement achieved lower angle and force RMSEs than the forearm placement, suggesting that wrist-level B-mode ultrasound may provide informative features for simultaneous hand posture and force decoding.

sessions.title: MBE: Brain, Neurons, Microbubbles, Cells I

papers.title: Vortex ultrasound–induced Shear Stress Regulates Neuronal Ciliary Bending
papers.abstract: Cilia are hair-like organelles found on most cells, where they transduce extracellular cues into intracellular signals critical for brain development and function. Their motility is modulated by shear stress from cerebrospinal fluid flow, and disturbances can disrupt ciliary bending and lead to neurological dysfunction. Current methods to induce ciliary motility (microfluidics, optical tweezers, magnetic, genetic, or optogenetic approaches) lack precision and are poorly suited for in vivo applications. Here, we present that a vortex ultrasound (VUS) strategy generates shear stress via helical acoustic streaming, enabling modulation of neuronal cilia bending and activity.

papers.title: Acoustofluidic Real-Time Mechanophenotyping and Sorting of Oocytes
papers.abstract: Oocyte mechanics determine embryonic developmental potential, yet current assessment methods are invasive and low-throughput. Surface acoustic wave (SAW) tweezers enable non-contact manipulation by acoustic radiation forces (ARFs) and streaming but lack functionality for mechanical interrogation. Here we develop an Automated Acoustic Deformation-Based Cell Sorting (ADCS) platform for translation, deformation-based mechanophenotyping and sorting of oocytes. Holographic interdigital transducers generate localized acoustic fields that induce streaming. Streaming-driven forces enable precise capture and immobilization, followed by deformation under tunable micro-Newton-scale ARFs. Deformation is quantified by image-based contour analysis, enabling threshold-based classification and on-demand acoustic manipulation for sorting. ADCS achieves real-time mechanophenotyping and sorting with up to 92% accuracy at ~20 cells/min. Mechanical phenotype correlates with developmental outcomes: compliant oocytes exhibit 88.68 ± 2.21% fertilization, whereas stiff oocytes show developmental arrest. ADCS establishes a direct, quantitative link between oocyte mechanics and developmental potential.

papers.title: Cumulative Permeability Enhancement and Altered Junctional Integrity in Tumor Vessels After Repeated microbubble Cavitation
papers.abstract: Ultrasound-stimulated microbubble (USMB) cavitation enhances vascular permeability for drug delivery, but its cumulative effects under repeated treatments remain unclear. Therefore, we used a murine pancreatic tumor (Panc02) model to evaluate vascular density, permeability, and endothelial junction integrity after single and repeated USMB. H&E staining showed no observable vascular damage. CD31 analysis showed no significant difference among groups, suggesting preserved vessel density. In contrast, VE-cadherin became more discontinuous, with reduced coverage after repeated USMB, accompanied by increased permeability. These findings indicate that repeated USMB enhances vascular permeability without altering vessel density, but may compromise endothelial junction integrity, raising potential concerns regarding vascular function. Future work will further evaluate long-term vascular effects and inflammatory responses in tumor and surrounding normal vessels, combined with chemotherapy, to assess vascular safety and functional outcomes relevant to prognosis.

papers.title: Focused Ultrasound Stimulation of the preoptic Hypothalamus Evokes a torpor-Like State in non-Torpid Mammals
papers.abstract: Torpor exemplifies the brain’s ability to drive systemic metabolic suppression through coordinated neural control of energy balance and thermoregulation. However, inducing synthetic torpor in non-torpid species requires genetic manipulation or intracerebroventricular drugs, limiting clinical translation. Here we show that focused ultrasound (FUS), a noninvasive neuromodulation technique, can induce synthetic torpor in non-torpid rats by targeting the preoptic area (POA). FUS significantly reduced oxygen consumption (−28.53 ± 1.46 %), core body temperature (−1.04 ± 0.23 °C) compared with sham controls. RNAscope revealed increased neuronal activity in POA glutamatergic neurons during FUS. Fiber photometry showed activation of POA neurons and neural circuits by FUS. No tissue damage or inflammation was observed. Together, these findings establish FUS as a safe, noninvasive method for inducing synthetic torpor in non-torpid mammals, supporting the potential translation of ultrasound-based metabolic modulation to humans.

papers.title: When Pressure Becomes Signal: Region-Dependent Neurostimulation and Injury Thresholds in FUS-Induced BBB Opening
papers.abstract: In this study, we evaluated the neurostimulative effects and safety of focused ultrasound (FUS) with microbubbles during blood–brain barrier (BBB) opening under high mechanical index conditions (MI > 0.5). We show that in microbubble-mediated BBB opening protocols, combined mechanical stimulation from acoustic waves and bubble oscillations induces a pressure- and region-dependent neurobiological response. At high pressures, neurostimulation remains largely non-damaging in regions lacking mechanosensitive channels. In contrast, the hippocampus exhibits strong c-Fos activation within 2 hours, indicating intense neuronal activity. This response is associated with early neuronal damage, including apoptosis, suggesting that excessive stimulation may lead to neurotoxicity. These effects also correlate with markers of neuroinflammation, pointing to early and potentially persistent inflammatory processes. Overall, FUS-induced neurostimulation is not uniformly safe and depends critically on brain region and acoustic parameters, highlighting the need to optimize conditions to balance BBB opening, safety, and neuromodulation control.

papers.title: Spatially Divergent Immune Remodeling Across the Skull–Meninges–Brain Axis via Focused Ultrasound-Induced Blood-Brain Barrier Opening
papers.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS), when paired with intravenously injected microbubbles, can transiently open the blood–brain barrier (BBB), offering a promising immunotherapy approach for neurodegenerative disorders. However, how this process reshapes the brain’s immune environment and communicates with the peripheral immune system through complex anatomical routes—particularly at the skull and meninges, where ultrasound waves enter—remains underexplored. To address this, we separately harvested tissue from the sham group and from the ipsilateral (treated) and contralateral (untreated) halves of the brain, meninges, and skull after FUS-BBBO. Immune cells from these tissues were processed for single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), with validation by flow cytometry and qPCR. Our results reveal spatially divergent immune regulation after FUS: a localized, pro-inflammatory, proliferative microglial response in the treated hemisphere, alongside transient bilateral activation of immune cells and transcriptomic programs in the skull and meninges. These findings highlight coordinated remodeling across the skull–meninges–brain axis, with potential implications for immunotherapy.

sessions.title: PGP: General Physical Acoustics

papers.title: Coupled microbubble array-Induced Virtual acoustofluidic Potential Well Enables Selective Particle Manipulation
papers.abstract: Acoustic tweezers enable label-free manipulation of bioparticles through acoustic radiation forces and streaming-induced drag forces. Oscillating microbubbles act as efficient secondary acoustic sources generating strong pressure gradients and microstreaming. While extensive research has focused on single-microbubble dynamics, the collective behavior of acoustically coupled microbubbles remains elusive. Here, we developed the coupled microbubble array to achieve selective particle manipulation and revealed the underlying physical mechanisms of the coupled microbubble array. By arranging a hexagonal microbubble configuration, a virtual acoustofluidic potential well was established. Unlike traditional potential wells induced by acoustic pressure gradients, this virtual acoustofluidic potential well is dominated by microstreaming-induced drag forces, which are three orders of magnitude larger than those of acoustic radiation forces. Exploiting this size dependence, we achieved the separation of 1-μm and 10-μm microparticles within the virtual potential well. This demonstrates a size-selective particle separation method entirely driven by coupled microbubble array.

papers.title: Acoustic Streaming with a Single Cell Gigahertz Ultrasound AlN BAW Pixel
papers.abstract: This work presents a chip-scale, CMOS-compatible acoustic streaming platform utilizing a 50 × 50 µm² Aluminum Nitride (AlN) Bulk Acoustic Wave (BAW) pixel to address the limitations of bulky, high-voltage systems in microfluidic applications. The device successfully demonstrates the manipulation of 1 µm polystyrene particles in a confined water column using low drive voltage of 1 V RMS. The concept was first validated via COMSOL Multiphysics 2D FEM simulations, which predicted symmetric streaming vortex pairs with tunable velocities based on applied acceleration. Experimental validation confirmed these models; the monolithically integrated transducer, with resonances near 1 GHz and 1.85 GHz, induced particle transport under continuous-wave frequency sweeps with particle velocities 50 - 200 um/s and also at pulsed excitations with 1.85 GHz drive voltage. The results showed that streaming strength is tied directly to these resonant frequencies and increases with longer pulse durations. Ultimately, this work establishes the AlN BAW pixel as a compact, power-efficient RF acoustic source, paving the way for scalable, addressable acoustic-fluidic arrays in lab-on-a-chip technologies.

papers.title: A Transparent Planar Ultrasonic Transducer for Bulk-Acoustic-Wave Cell Stimulation and Manipulation
papers.abstract: We present a transparent planar ultrasonic transducer with acoustic gratings for complex bulk acoustic wave generation, maintaining an unobstructed coaxial optical path. This design overcomes bulky microscopy setups, enabling direct cell stimulation. The device integrates a transparent transducer stack with a quartz grating. A polished LiNbO3 piezoelectric layer (15x15 mm2 aperture) is paired with transparent matching and backing layers. Operating at a 22.5 MHz center frequency, the total thickness is under 3 mm. For wavefront control, 1-mm-thick quartz glass was patterned via femtosecond laser to form a Fresnel zone plate (FZP) for focusing and a spiral phase grating for vortex generation. Experiments show the FZP produces a symmetric focus, while the spiral grating creates a stable acoustic vortex for microparticle trapping. In cell stimulation, FZP-mediated ultrasound induced clear fluorescence flickering, indicating ion-channel modulation. This demonstrates the device's potential for microscopy-compatible cell modulation.

papers.title: Multibody Modelling of Particle Clustering in Acoustic Levitation
papers.abstract: Acoustic levitation enables contactless manipulation of particles for applications such as laboratory automation, volumetric display, and contactless fabrication. When multiple particles are levitated, they accumulate at pressure nodes and form clusters.
