DAS provides the baseline beamformed image, while eigenspace MVDR serves as an adaptive refinement step to suppress incoherent noise and enhance coherent signal components. The proposed method is evaluated using the PICMUS dataset, with multi-angle coherent compounding used as the reference. The hybrid approach improves image contrast and target detectability, leading to clearer visualization of target regions. Although structural similarity may be lower than that of the reference the proposed method provides enhanced contrast performance and improved target visibility.

sessions.title: MCA: Targeted ultrasound contrast agents and specialized (pre)clinical imaging

papers.title: A Computational Model for Magnetomotive Ultrasound Magnet Design with Applications
papers.abstract: Magnetomotive Ultrasound (MMUS) is a contrast-enhanced imaging technique that uses magnetic nanoparticle (MNP) contrast agents. MNP-labeled tissues are subjected to a temporally modulated magnetic force, inducing submicron-scale displacements. This motion is subsequently detected using phase-resolved ultrasound imaging, allowing for visualization of tissues that may otherwise be invisible under conventional B-mode imaging. Implementing appropriate magnetic force delivery remains a significant engineering challenge. “Traditional” MMUS systems locate the transducer and a single solenoid on opposite sides of the tissue, limiting imaging area, while “open-air” systems locate a transducer and two solenoids on the same side of the tissue, limiting the applied force. In this work, a finite element model was validated and used to predict new magnet geometries toward the goal of maximizing contrast and minimizing coil inductance without encroaching upon the imaging region.

papers.title: Screening Ultrasound Imaging Test for Portal Hypertension Using the Hepatic Vein Contrast-Enhanced Subharmonic Signal
papers.abstract: Portal hypertension (PH) is the underlying cause of most complications associated with cirrhosis, which is currently optimally diagnosed by the hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) which can also be used to evaluate disease progression. Subharmonic imaging (SHI) is a contrast-specific ultrasound (US) imaging technique receiving at half the transmit frequency resulting in better tissue suppression. The aim of the study was to. determine if the presence of SHI signals inside the hepatic vein can be used as a qualitative screening sign of PH. SHI findings were compared to findings on HVPG measurement (i.e., the clinical reference standard). The overall accuracy of presence of SHI signals in the hepatic veins for the diagnosis of any degree of portal hypertension was 93% (155/167) with a sensitivity of 100% (87/87) and specificity of 85% (68/80). The presence of optimized SHI signals inside the hepatic vein can be used as a qualitative screening test for PH. SHI of the hepatic vein is a noninvasive and safe method that could be used as a new initial, qualitative sign of PH minimizing the need for invasive procedures.

papers.title: Characterizing Rupture, Elasticity, and Buckling Transitions of Monodisperse Microbubbles During Dissolution Evolution
papers.abstract: To design state-of-art bubbles for ultrasound applications, it is crucial to identify bubble states during nature dissolution. This study use monodisperse microbubbles (MDMBs) to characterize bubble states via pressure-dependent resonance frequency (PRF) curve. MDMBs with lipid shell and C₃F₈ core were fabricated by microfluidics. Under varying ambient pressures, radial changes and attenuation spectra were measured. Pressure dependent shell elasticity was derived by fitting a linear oscillation model to the measured attenuation spectra. 1) Slope changes in the pressure-dependent radius curves reveal distinct regimes: rupture, elastic, and buckling. Notable slope changes in the PRF curve subdivide the elastic regime into elastic–rupture transition, elastic, and elastic–buckling transition regimes.2) The measured surface-area-dependent resonance-frequency (SRF) curve is consistent with the calculated one under dissolution, showing regulating radius by ambient pressure can simulate natural dissolution. The resonance frequencies during dissolution transitioned along SRF curve, showing bubble states during dissolution closely approximate those from varying ambient pressure.

papers.title: Bridging Intra- and Extravascular Tumor Signal Enhancement with Mid-Sized Bubbles
papers.abstract: Microbubbles (MB) and nanobubbles (NB) are widely used as ultrasound (US) contrast agents with distinct intravascular and extravascular behaviors within tumor morphology. NB can accumulate in tissue after exiting permeable endothelium, while MB remain restricted to vascular space. Acoustically, their responses are size-dependent. We formulated a polydisperse mid-sized bubble (MsB) solution to test whether the behaviors of a heterogeneous bubble population can combine NB and MB properties. The acoustic response and tumor contrast abilities of this MsB solution were evaluated both in vitro and in vivo. At matching gas volumes in vitro, MsB had intermediate signal intensity. In vivo tumor imaging showed peak normalized signal increases of 17x for NB, 12x for MsB, and 5x for MB relative to baseline. NB were most persistent, MB had quick washout, and MsB had intermediate peak intensity. These results indicate the potential utility of MsB as contrast agents able to endure in intra- and extravascular spaces for extended times.

papers.title: Macrophage membrane-functionalized Biomimetic Microbubbles for Inflammation-Targeted Imaging of Acute Kidney Injury
papers.abstract: Ultrasound molecular imaging is widely used for inflammation-targeted imaging due to its noninvasiveness, absence of ionizing radiation, and high sensitivity. Biomimetic microbubbles coated with macrophage membranes have attracted attention for their inflammatory tropism and immune evasion. Here, an acute kidney injury (AKI) model was used to evaluate the effects of macrophage polarization on targeting performance. Conventional microbubbles (MB), undifferentiated macrophage membrane-coated microbubbles (MB@M0), and M1 macrophage membrane-coated microbubbles (MB@M1) were fabricated via membrane emulsification–mechanical oscillation, with membrane protein integrity preserved. In vivo imaging showed that biomimetic microbubbles significantly enhanced renal vascular signals after injection. Although their circulation time was shorter than MB, signal intensity was markedly higher, indicating a “responsive–disruptive” capability at the cost of reduced stability. These findings reveal a trade-off between stability and responsiveness, providing a basis for optimizing biomimetic microbubbles with both prolonged circulation and sensitive targeted imaging.
keywords: ultrasound molecular imaging、macrophage 、Biomimetic Microbubbles、acute kidney injury

papers.title: Shape-Dependent Magnetomotive Forces: a Framework for Optimizing Particle Geometry in Magnetomotive Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Magnetomotive ultrasound imaging (MMUS) is an emerging modality using magnetic nanoparticles as a contrast agent. Tissue-embedded magnetic nanoparticles are set in motion by a rotating external magnetic field, enabling ultrasound detection. However, the reach of the magnetic field limits magnetic nanoparticle motion and thereby imaging depth and sensitivity. The aim of this study is to investigate whether tailoring particle geometry in MMUS increases the field induced forces acting on the magnetic nanoparticles. We derived an extended expression for the magnetomotive force that incorporates particle shape dependency, providing a general framework for comparing geometries. This formulation was implemented in a simulation model and applied to ellipsoidal particles. Our model predicted up to a 110% increase in magnetically induced displacement for an ellipsoid of aspect ratio 8 compared to a sphere with the same volume. These results suggest the existence of an optimal ellipsoid aspect ratio range for MMUS contrast agents that maximizes magnetic forces, providing design guidelines for next generation MNPs aimed at improving MMUS imaging depth and sensitivity.

papers.title: Gas Vesicle Tumor Targeted Ultrasound Imaging Using site-Specific Antibody Conjugates
papers.abstract: Ultrasound for tumor imaging is greatly improved with the use of acoustic contrast agents such as the conjugate-ready gas vesicle (GV) nanoprotein. GVs naturally increase vessel resolution, and we hypothesized that with assistance from a targeting agent, such as monoclonal antibodies (mAb), would also provide accumulated tumor morphology and cellular expression information. Here we propose a stable immune evading mAb-GV click chemistry conjugation for ultrasound imaging to target tumor cell surface markers and provide helpful tumor monitoring data to increase treatment plan efficiency.

sessions.title: NWP: Wave Propagation and Flow Measurement

papers.title: Surface Acoustic Wave Propagation Measurements for Monitoring Acne Development with in Vivo Optical Coherence Elastography in Human Facial Skin
papers.abstract: This study explores the use of surface acoustic wave (SAW) propagation to monitor acne development in human facial skin. Acne alters skin biomechanics, and SAWs provide a sensitive way to detect stiffness changes associated with inflammation. Using a phase-velocity-based optical coherence elastography approach, acne datasets were non-invasively acquired through depth-resolved wave propagation and converted into quantitative elasticity maps. Fifteen datasets from three participants were collected over a 15-day period. A piezoelectric actuator generated SAWs across a frequency range of 0.1–7 kHz. Elasticity was derived from phase velocity, enabling visualization of lesion stiffness and depth. Results showed that inflamed regions had significantly higher stiffness (406.52 kPa) than surrounding tissue (281.27 kPa). Over time, both lesion stiffness and size decreased by 69.99% and 66.96%, respectively, indicating healing progression. In conclusion, this method enables high-resolution, non-invasive monitoring of acne biomechanics and shows potential for improving the diagnosis and evaluation of dermatological conditions involving altered skin mechanics, such as skin cancer.

papers.title: Defect-Structure Effects in Ultrasonic Guided Waves Coupling to Local Resonances
papers.abstract: Local defect resonance (LDR), a phenomenon arising from the interaction of guided waves with defects, enhances defect response, providing improved sensitivity in NDE. Yet its potential is not leveraged, since its origin and implementation have not been fully understood. This work studies the coupling of ultrasonic guided waves with local resonances in plates with horizontal defects, with the goal of identifying relationships between incident waves and standing modes and their dependence on waveguide and defect properties. Different defect and plate systems are investigated from a theoretical, numerical and experimental perspective. Analytical methods are used to extract the resonance frequencies of the defect and are compared to scattering spectra obtained from the semi-analytical model over a broad frequency domain. Commercial solvers are then used to visualize the phenomenon. Finally, an experimental setup is tested. Dependencies of the resonance patterns on defect size and location are shown from parametric studies of different waveguide-defect configurations. Proper boundary conditions of coupling are needed to describe the phenomenon accurately and improve NDE applications.
keywords: Ultrasonic guided waves. Local Defect Resonance

papers.title: Dual-Transducer-Based Focal Volume Reduction for Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound (LIFU) enables non-invasive neuromodulation with high spatial resolution. However, due to inherent geometrical limitation, at sub-MHz frequency, acoustic energy spreads to larger volume. To generate a more compact focus for more precise targeting, this study evaluates a dual-transducer focal volume reduction method and validates consistency between simulated and experimental results. A dual-transducer configuration at 660kHz was used to achieve focal volume reduction by controlling superposition of acoustic fields at the target region, enhancing energy concentration. Simulation and experimental results show similar patterns in pressure enhancement and focal volume reduction, confirming such transducer arrangement could increase energy concentration, in the meantime, significantly reduce focal volume. This agreement also validates the reliability of simulation for predicting focal characteristics before experiments. The proposed method provides a simpler and effective strategy for focal control and prediction in LIFU applications.

papers.title: Numerical Simulation of Ultrasonic Wave Propagation for Cancellous Bone Assessment in the Human Proximal Femur
papers.abstract: Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DEXA), the standard for diagnosing osteoporosis via bone mineral density, uses ionizing radiation and cannot assess bone elasticity. Ultrasound reflects both bone mass and elasticity; Radiofrequency Echographic Multi Spectrometry (REMS) targets cortical bone in the femoral neck. As a first step toward ultrasonic assessment of internal cancellous bone, we built two 2-D elastic models of the anterior proximal femur from CT images of a 73-year-old female: Model A (cortical and cancellous bone) and Model B (cortical only). Using the Finite-Difference Time-Domain (FDTD) method, each of nine transducers on a convex probe emitted a single-cycle 1-MHz sinusoid received by all sensors. Strong cortical-surface echoes appeared just after the wavefront; subtracting them revealed cancellous-bone scattering after about 11 μs. Spectrograms at transducers 2, 5, and 8 (femoral head, neck, trochanter) showed a clear signal at the head (−13 dB at 1 MHz) and weaker ones at the neck (−18 dB) and trochanter (−16 dB), consistent with bone volume fractions (BV/TV) of 8.1%, 5.7%, and 6.7% and suggesting the potential to evaluate cancellous-bone BV/TV distribution.

papers.title: Measuring Acoustic Streaming in Air Using a Low-Cost Experimental Setup
papers.abstract: In this study, we measure acoustic streaming velocities in air by visually observing the movement of smoke using a simple, low-cost experimental setup. The experimental setup consists of a cardboard box, the smoke from an incense stick, an LED strip and a camera. Tracker video analysis and modeling tool was used to estimate the airflow velocity from these recordings by manual tracking of identifiable smoke features such as streaks or regions of varying intensity, frame by frame. The setup was tested on a phased array of 40 kHz ultrasonic transducers. The measured streaming velocities were in the range of a few centimeters per second up to 14 cm/s. The streaming velocity appears to scale linearly with the applied voltage, implying a square-root dependence on the total acoustic power, which is consistent with the existing literature for high streaming Reynolds numbers.

sessions.title: MTH: Physical Mechanisms of Ultrasound-Induced Tissue Modification and Immune Response

papers.title: Comparing Monodisperse and Polydisperse Microbubbles in Cavitation-Mediated Blood-Brain Barrier Opening
papers.abstract: Compared to polydisperse microbubbles (PDMBs), monodisperse microbubbles (MDMBs) with uniform size generate stable, high intensity cavitation, enhancing BBBO efficiency. This study compares PDMB and MDMB effects on BBBO at equal bubble concentration and total cavitation dose (TCD) PDMBs and MDMBs were generated via mechanical agitation and a microfluidic chip, respectively. Mice received tail vein injections of either microbubble type and Texas Red labeled 3 kDa dextran, followed by RaSP ultrasound exposure of the right hippocampus. BBBO efficiency and delivery uniformity were assessed via normalized optical density (NOD) and the coefficient of variation (COV) of dextran. Under the same MB concentration, achieving the same TCD required a shorter time for MDMBs (~160 s) than for PDMBs (~300 s). The instantaneous cavitation intensity generated by each pulse was significantly higher for MDMBs than for PDMBs. Compared to PDMBs, MDMBs produced a significantly higher NOD, showing enhanced BBBO efficacy, while achieving a comparable COV. These indicate that MDMBs improve BBBO through both high cavitation efficiency and size matching with capillaries.

papers.title: Deciphering Histotripsy Induced-Stresses in a Viscoelastic Material with Mechanophore
papers.abstract: Histotripsy is a focused ultrasound therapy that relies on cavitation to disrupt soft tissues mechanically. Visualization and quantification of the cavitation-induced stress responsible for treatment outcomes is challenging due to its transient and nonlinear nature. Here, we present a mechanophore-embedded tissue-mimicking hydrogel to assess histotripsy. A rhodamine-based mechanophore was covalently linked into a polyacrylamide network. Upon mechanical perturbation, the gel transited from a colorless, spiro-lactam form to a red, open form. Minimal color change is observed at histotripsy pulse peak negative pressures of 15 MPa, which were largely insufficient to generate cavitation. In contrast, pronounced mechanophore activation was observed in gels under conditions associated with robust bubble activity (i.e., peak negative pressures ~ 35 MPa). Importantly, the energy associated with bubble activity via passive detection of acoustic emissions was found to correlate with the mechanical stress derived from mechanophore activation. Overall, this platform provides an optical readout to visualize and quantify cavitation-induced stress fields.

papers.title: Modulation of Pancreatic Tumor Fibrosis via Oxygen microbubble Therapy
papers.abstract: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is characterized by dense fibrotic stroma and excessive collagen deposition, which compress blood vessels, induce hypoxia, sustain solid stress, and limit therapeutic efficacy. Although oxygen microbubble therapy (OMBT) has been applied to reduce tumor hypoxia and normalize tumor vessels, its effect on extracellular matrix organization and tumor fibrosis remains unclear. This study investigates whether OMBT attenuates pancreatic tumor fibrosis at different stages of tumor progression. Self-prepared OMBs showed dissolved oxygen increased by 1.01 mg/L after destruction, confirming oxygen loading. PSR staining showed extensive collagen fiber deposition in the control group, while both early and late OMBT groups showed reduced fibrosis. These results suggest that OMBT may inhibit pancreatic tumor fibrosis progression across different treatment time points. Future work will investigate repeated OMBT-induced extracellular matrix remodeling and evaluate hyaluronan distribution and lymphatic drainage in relation to solid stress and interstitial fluid pressure.

papers.title: High-Speed Video-Microscopy Elucidates Mechanical Effects of Cavitation Agents on Blood Clots
papers.abstract: This study aims to better understand the mechanical effects of cavitation agents on clot deformation using high frame rate microscopy imaging. Single ultrasound pulses were transmitted with peak negative pressures of 3, 5.5, or 7 MPa. Experimental conditions of ultrasound only, microbubbles, nanodroplets, and a combination of microbubbles and nanodroplets were tested. At 5.5 and 7 MPa, nanodroplets with ultrasound caused the greatest clot interface displacement. Moreover, a pressure dependence was observed within the experimental conditions tested.

papers.title: Rapid Short Pulse Ultrasound Achieves for blood-Brain Barrier Disruption in Rats Using a Low Center Frequency (300 kHz)
papers.abstract: This study investigates whether rapid short pulse (RaSP) ultrasound can safely and effectively open the blood-brain barrier (BBB) at a low center frequency of 300 kHz — a clinically relevant frequency capable of traversing the skull with minimal attenuation, unlike the 1 MHz frequencies used in prior work. Twenty-one Sprague Dawley rats received hippocampal sonication at three mechanical index levels (MI: 0.4, 0.5, 0.6) alongside microbubbles and a fluorescent drug tracer, with contralateral hemispheres serving as controls. Significant drug delivery was achieved at MI=0.5 and MI=0.6, while MI=0.4 produced no significant delivery. Crucially, no tissue damage or vascular extravasation was detected at MI=0.4 or 0.5. Minor extravasation was observed at MI=0.6. These results confirm that RaSP ultrasound remains both effective and safe at 300 kHz, achieving meaningful BBB opening at pressures as low as 0.27 MPa without detectable tissue injury. This advances the translational potential of RaSP for clinical drug delivery to the brain.

papers.title: Identification of Sonication Timelines for Maximal Immune Cell Infiltration in Brain
papers.abstract: For peripheral immune cells to be effective against brain tumors, multiple coordinated steps are required, including trafficking, followed by survival, proliferation, and persistence, all while remaining functional. In brain tumors, trafficking is especially hindered due to the blood-brain barrier (BBB). Focused ultrasound combined with microbubbles (FUS-MB) can open the BBB and upregulate key integrins on blood vessels for immune cell extravasation. However, optimal timing and conditions of sonication with respect to cell transfer for maximal infiltration is yet to be fully understood. To address that, we intravenously delivered bone marrow derived macrophages (BMDMs) before, during, or after FUS with the goal of understanding the best sonication timing for maximal cell infiltration into the brain. We found that after opening of BBB (Figure A), there was a significant increase in infiltrating BMDMs 24 hours post adoptive transfer, especially for BMDMs delivered after FUS compared to control group.

papers.title: Mechanical Evaluation of Focused Ultrasound and Dry Needling Treatments in Ex Vivo tendinopathy Models
papers.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS) is being developed as a noninvasive alternative to dry needling (DN) for tendinopathy treatment. This study evaluated FUS and DN in ex vivo bovine superficial digital flexor tendons using two laboratory tendinopathy models: localized collagenase injury and cyclic mechanical overload. Tendons received sham, DN, or FUS treatment. FUS exposures used 2.45 MHz dual-amplitude bursts and were monitored with a passive cavitation detector. After treatment, tendons were assessed by H&E histology or mechanical testing to failure. In the collagenase model, DN showed significantly greater Young’s modulus and ultimate tensile stress than sham, while DN-FUS differences were not significant after correction. In the mechanical overload model, no significant differences were detected across groups. Histology showed fiber fraying in DN- and FUS-treated tendons relative to sham. These results suggest that immediate treatment response depends on injury model and that FUS can produce mechanical effects comparable to DN under the tested conditions.

papers.title: An Innovative FePt Nano-Sonosensitizer for Ferroptosis-Driven Sonodynamic Therapy: Cell Study
papers.abstract: This study explores a synergistic cancer treatment strategy by combining sonodynamic therapy (SDT) with ferroptosis using FePt nanoparticles (NPs) as novel sonosensitizers. Upon ultrasound (US) stimulation, FePt NPs release iron ions, triggering excessive reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, glutathione (GSH) depletion, and glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) downregulation—key events that induce ferroptosis. In vitro experiments using A549 cells demonstrated that FePt NPs combined with US significantly enhanced cell death compared to NPs alone. While ROS levels showed an increasing trend, lipid peroxidation was markedly elevated and could be suppressed by the ferroptosis inhibitor Ferrostatin-1, confirming ferroptosis involvement. Additionally, intracellular GSH and GPX4 levels were significantly reduced following treatment. These findings indicate that FePt NP-mediated SDT effectively induces ferroptosis and apoptosis through oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation. This work highlights a promising nanomaterial-assisted therapeutic approach for improving the efficacy of cancer treatment, particularly for deep-seated tumors.

papers.title: Histotripsy Dose Impact Comparison in Highly Immunogenic MC38 and Poorly Immunogenic mT4 Subcutaneous Murine Models
papers.abstract: Histotripsy utilizes high-pressure microsecond pulses to generate cavitation and mechanically ablate tissue in a noninvasive, non-ionizing, and non-thermal way. Currently, the Histotripsy Edison system has been FDA-approved for liver treatments. The treatments are done with a single, universal dose. However, previous results show that different tumors require different histotripsy doses for complete treatment, and the induced immune response also varies with histotripsy dose (which is defined as pulses delivered per volume in this study). In this study, we investigate the impact of histotripsy dose on the survival benefit and immune response in in vivo murine MC38 colorectal (highly immunogenic) and mT4 pancreatic (poorly immunogenic) murine tumors. We demonstrated that complete or close to complete tumor disruption generated by histotripsy resulted in the best survival and immuen stimulation in both models. Whereas, treated too low of a dose (generating partial damage) or too high of a dose (generating overtreatment) resulted in reduced survival benefit and immune stimulation.

sessions.title: MTN: Theranostic treatment monitoring

papers.title: A Novel Ultrasound-Based Strategy to Enhance Follicular Delivery of Surgical Skin Cleansers for Infection Prevention
papers.abstract: Post-operative infections (~3% of surgeries) are largely caused by skin flora (70–95%), such as S. aureus and E. coli, which are displaced from hair follicles during incision, and current antiseptic methods are insufficient to prevent this transfer. This study evaluated whether combining different hair removal strategies with ultrasound can enhance follicular antimicrobial delivery in ex vivo porcine skin using a chlorhexidine–methylene blue tracer. Samples were prepared with waxing, depilatory cream, clipping, or no hair removal and exposed to ultrasound at 4–33 MHz for 2–5 minutes. Waxing provided the highest baseline penetration (62.3 ± 28.3%), while ultrasound significantly increased follicular delivery across all conditions (p ≤ 0.001), reaching up to 80.3 ± 18.2%. In clinically relevant clipped skin, 18 MHz was optimal (64.0 ± 24.4%), and extending exposure to 5 minutes further improved penetration to 73.8 ± 26%. Overall, the results show that ultrasound markedly enhances follicular antimicrobial penetration regardless of hair removal method, offering a promising non-invasive strategy to improve preoperative skin antisepsis and reduce infection risk.

papers.title: Bubble-dissolution-Guided Feedback Controller for histotripsy
papers.abstract: Histotripsy is a non-thermal, non-invasive focused ultrasound therapy that disrupts tissue via controlled bubble cloud activity. However, persistence of bubbles between successive pulses leads to re-excitation, reducing treatment efficacy and efficiency and causing non-uniform ablation. In this study, a feedback controller was developed to adapt the pulsing rate based on ultrafast imaging of residual bubble clouds, aiming to maintain uniform cavitation activity and improve treatment outcomes. Histotripsy pulses (1 MHz, 10 µs, 30 MPa) were applied to agarose gel, while bubble dynamics were monitored at 1 kHz over a 5–10 ms window using plane wave imaging. Time-dependent signals were analyzed using a nonlinear controller to achieve target degrees of dissolution (DoD: 25%, 50%, 75%) by adjusting pulsing rate. Compared to fixed conditions (2 Hz for maximum efficiency, 200 Hz for maximum efficacy), the controller achieved steady-state pulsing rates of 199 ± 2, 175 ± 5, and 25 ± 3 Hz for 25%, 50%, and 75% DoD, respectively. Ablation areas at 25% and 50% DoD were comparable to 200 Hz, while efficiency improved by 2 and 4 times for 50% and 75% DoD.

papers.title: A Spatial Histotripsy Damage Monitoring Framework
papers.abstract: A framework for using acoustic cavitation emission signals to spatially monitor histotripsy damage during treatment.

papers.title: 3-Dimensional Ultrasound Imaging During Needle Tip Histotripsy Enables Characterization of Cavitation Damage of This Novel Ablative Mechanism
papers.abstract: We investigate the cavitation bubble cloud associated with a novel histotripsy ablative mechanism: needle tip histotripsy (NTH). NTH liquefies tissues at the tip of a fine hypodermic needle by laterally vibrating the needle using a cam-based actuation mechanism. Rapid 3D ultrasound imaging of NTH operation in ex-vivo chicken breast enabled the characterization of the associated cavitation bubble clouds that were generated around the needle tip. The full breadth of the induced cavitation was observed to expand in all 3 dimensions, despite the needle motions falling largely in a single plane. This study shows both the capacity for potential real-time volume rendering of cavitation damage during histotripsy operations, as well as demonstrating the interventional surgical potential of the NTH device.

papers.title: Frequency of Mechanical Stress Events Governs Ultrasound-Assisted Drug Delivery: a Modified Rayleigh-Plesset Modeling Approach
papers.abstract: This study establishes a physics-based framework to optimize ultrasound-mediated drug delivery for retinoblastoma. We modeled microbubble dynamics using a modified Rayleigh-Plesset equation (Marmottant/Zhou) to capture shell-buckling and damping effects. By defining a 10GPa stress threshold for nanoparticles, we predicted intracellular drug concentrations as a function of stress-event frequency. Results demonstrate that drug internalization is governed by the frequency of discrete stress events rather than average intensity. At maximum intensity, microbubbles expanded 3.7-fold (74 micrometer), and while stress frequency increased 1.58-fold, the intracellular AUC rose 10.37-fold. These findings were validated by FACS analysis, showing 95% delivery coverage and MFI > 600 a.u.—a 100-fold increase over nanoparticle-only groups. This frequency-driven framework provides a precise, quantitative guideline for optimizing safe and effective targeted ultrasound therapies.

papers.title: Explainable machine-Learning Framework for real-Time Breast Cancer Ablation Monitoring and Tissue Viscoelasticity Evaluation Using HMI-Guided FUS
papers.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS) ablation offers a non-surgical treatment option for breast cancer. The noninvasiveness of FUS allows for fewer complications and immune activation. During ablation, the high intensity exposure induces necrosis within seconds; however, tissue condition changes during treatment remain unknown due to the lack of monitoring methods. This study presents an automated, interpretable machine-learning (ML) framework to analyze tissue mechanical property changes during ablation using Harmonic Motion Imaging (HMI). To the authors’ knowledge, this is the first-ever framework to map the HMI-monitored FUS-lesion formation in the physical feature space and to understand the evolution of tissue viscoelasticity during successful ablation.

papers.title: Multi-Modal Imaging of sonoporation-Induced Vascular and Stiffness Responses in triple-Negative Breast Tumors
papers.abstract: Breast cancer is the most common female malignancy, with neoadjuvant chemotherapy as standard of care for locally advanced disease. Microbubble-assisted focused ultrasound (FUS) sonoporation can enhance drug delivery, but contrast-enhanced power-Doppler-guided targeting (CEPDgSNPR) uses perfusion alone, without mechanical or vascular response feedback. We pair harmonic motion imaging (HMI) with ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) to characterize 4T1 triple-negative tumors at sonoporation-target resolution. Across 32 targets in 2 mice, baseline HMI and microvascular density (MVD) percentiles were positively correlated (ρ = 0.44, p = 0.012), with off-diagonal cases showing that stiffness adds information beyond perfusion alone. Acute imaging revealed a focal, target-localized vascular response (target/non-target ΔMVD ratio 2.28 at +0 min decaying to 1.07 at +30 min), with velocity changes that did not always track MVD, consistent with sonoporation-induced changes in vessel tone. Paired HMI-ULM identifies three target-level biomarkers (baseline stiffness/perfusion coupling, acute MVD response, MVD/velocity decoupling) as candidate predictors of sonoporation response.

sessions.title: TMU: Capacitive Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducers

papers.title: Comparison of Conventional and Temperature-Ramp Anodic Bonding for the Fabrication of CMUT Arrays
papers.abstract: This work compares conventional anodic bonding with a temperature-ramp anodic bonding method for fabricating row-column addressed CMUT arrays. Large CMUT arrays benefit from anodic bonding with low-resistivity metal electrodes, but high bonding voltages can cause vertical short circuits, while lower voltages may reduce extracted charge and bond integrity. The temperature-ramp method applies the voltage before increasing the temperature, aiming to improve charge transfer during bonding. CMUT arrays with λ/2 pitch at 15 MHz were fabricated using the same process flow, differing only in bonding method, with bonding voltages from 150 V to 500 V. More than 11,000 elements per method were characterised using Z-f and I-V measurements, with selected C-V measurements. The temperature-ramp method doubled the extracted charge at 150 V and remained 25% higher at 500 V, indicating improved bond strength. Both methods showed similar electrical behaviour, confirming that the temperature-ramp method improves bond integrity while maintaining CMUT performance.

papers.title: CMUT with a Force Plate: Design, Fabrication, and Experimental Results
papers.abstract: We present a new CMUT structure (CMUT-FP) with a higher pressure and wider bandwidth. It has a second thinner plate beneath the CMUT plate operating in collapse mode, while the CMUT plate delivers the pressure. We use time-domain finite element simulations to optimize the parameters. The simulations show that the new structure can produce more pressure than the collapsed mode CMUT. The new structure can be also designed to have a much larger sensitivity in a narrow band with a bias controlled center frequency. Measurements of the fabricated CMUT-FP support the findings.

papers.title: Characterization of Gold Thermocompression Bonded CMUT Arrays
papers.abstract: Gold thermocompression bonding (TCB) is a lower-temperature alternative to fusion and anodic bonding for CMUT fabrication and is attractive for centimeter-scale high-frequency arrays due to its compatibility with microfabrication and low electrode resistance. This work presents initial characterization of 15-MHz linear CMUT arrays fabricated using gold TCB. 384-element arrays with λ/2 pitch, 42 µm cell diameter, and 4 µm plate thickness were fabricated alongside 16-element test arrays. Wafer-level C-V, impedance, and bias-stability measurements showed expected parabolic CMUT behavior with C₀ = 6.69 pF, , a bias-dependent resonance peak exhibiting spring softening from 0 to −150 VDC, 19% electromechanical coupling, and stable operation up to −150 VDC. These results validate gold TCB for scalable high-frequency CMUT arrays.

papers.title: Near-Field HIFU Ablation in Ex Vivo Tissue Using an FPGA-Pulser System Based on Capacitive Micromachined Ultrasound Transducer (CMUT)
papers.abstract: Emerging near-field applications like ophthalmic treatments and neuromodulation demand miniaturized high-pressure devices, unlike conventional piezoelectric HIFU. CMUT fabricated via MEMS offers miniaturization, array integration, and versatile channel design. We present a 16×16 mm, 23-channel annular CMUT array (5 MHz center frequency) driven by an FPGA pulser for localized near-field HIFU lesion formation. Hydrophone measurements show a 5-14 kPa/V surface sensitivity at 3.57 MHz. The FPGA pulser controls time delays to synthesize a focused field at 12 mm depth, operating four grouped channels with 90-degree phase delays for stable high output. Thermal ablation potential is evaluated using CEM43, considering biological acoustic attenuation. Focal pressure reaches 6.87 MPa (1.57 kW/cm² spatial-peak pulse intensity). In an ex vivo porcine liver model, the thermal dose exceeds the 250 CEM43 threshold for exposures over 165 ms. Furthermore, TX sensitivity variations based on channel/cell layout and device self-heating under high AC voltages are analyzed to establish safe limits. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of CMUTs with FPGA beamforming for near-field HIFU ablation.

papers.title: Design Considerations for Frontend Transmit Drivers for a Dual-Frequency Duplex CMUT Array
papers.abstract: Acoustic angiography (AA) uses low-frequency excitation of microbubbles to generate high-frequency harmonics for imaging. A duplex CMUT structure with stacked low-frequency transmitters and high-frequency receivers enables efficient AA, but generating clean MHz-range excitation signals is challenging due to limitations in high-voltage DAC/amplifier solutions. Conventional square pulses introduce strong harmonic distortion that contaminates the receive band. This work proposes a system-level approach using multi-level pulsers (e.g., 5-level and 7-level) to approximate sinusoidal excitation, reducing unwanted harmonics. Experimental hydrophone measurements show that multi-level excitation significantly suppresses spectral leakage into the high-frequency band (10–15 MHz). The distortion level improves from −35.6 dB (square pulse) to about −45 dB (multi-level), approaching the performance of a pure sine wave (−46.28 dB). Overall, multi-level pulse shaping provides a practical and scalable alternative to high-voltage analog excitation, improving signal quality and reducing noise in duplex CMUT-based acoustic angiography systems

papers.title: A High-Gain Broadband Capacitive Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer with Integrated Electronics for Passive Acoustic Imaging
papers.abstract: Passive Acoustic Imaging is a technique for real-time monitoring blood-brain barrier opening protocols, based on ultrasound-mediated sonoporation with microbubbles. Transcranial propagation constrains working around 500 kHz. Achieving sufficient spatial resolution requires collecting the generated harmonic waves by microbubbles, in the MHz range. The development of transducers capable of receiving over a very wide frequency range, from 200 kHz to 2 MHz, while maintaining the lowest possible pressure detection threshold, remains challenging. In this work, we propose a solution combining Capacitive Micromachined Ultrasonic Transducer technology with dedicated integrated electronics.
keywords: Ultrasonic transducers - matrix array - Blood-Brain-Barrier - sonoporation

papers.title: Design and Fabrication of 128+128 Element Row-Column Addressed CMUT Arrays Optimized for High Frame Rate Imaging Applications
papers.abstract: Capacitive micromachined ultrasound transducers (CMUT) technology offers broader bandwidth, higher sensitivity and easier integration with electronics compared to existing piezoelectric transducers. Row-column addressed (RC) arrays require fewer connections than individually addressed 2D arrays for system integration and require fewer data acquisitions per frame, making them ideal for high frame rate imaging applications. In literature, RC CMUT arrays with broad bandwidth have been presented and utilized for high frame rate imaging applications. Higher transmit pressure and receive sensitivity improve the image contrast while higher frequency and broad bandwidth are important for high image resolution. In this work, we designed and fabricated a 128+128 element RC addressed CMUT array with optimizations to increase transmit pressure and SNR while keeping the frequency comparable to the highest values reported previously and preserving the wide bandwidth.

papers.title: Characterisation of polyCMUT Devices with Different Geometries at Low Bias Voltage
papers.abstract: Capacitive micromachined ultrasound transducers with polymer membranes (polyCMUTs) are popular in conformal imaging and pressure sensing due to their flexibility. Key properties like resonant frequency, bandwidth and transmit sensitivity are determined by finite element analysis, but these methods often neglect fabrication induced variations which significantly change device behaviour. Also, low bias operation is critical for wearable devices. We fabricated polyCMUT arrays with membrane radii of 20–60 µm, cavities of 350 nm,550 nm and different flexural rigidities, and characterised them at 40 V DC bias using impedance analysis and laser Doppler vibrometry. Although theory says smaller membranes have high transmission sensitivity, centre displacement at resonance increased with membrane radius. Resonant frequencies decreased with radius. Bandwidths in air decreased with radius. Water immersion increased bandwidth whilst reducing resonant frequency. We conclude large membrane devices offer better transmission performance at low bias conditions.

sessions.title: PGP: General Physical Acoustics III

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Viscoelasticity Estimation for Tissue-Engineered Corneal Stromal Models Using Optical Coherence Elastography
papers.abstract: This study presents a deep learning-based approach (VENet) for rapid estimation of viscoelastic properties in tissue-engineered corneal stromal models using optical coherence elastography. By directly predicting elastic and viscous parameters from phase images, VENet eliminates the need for computationally intensive dispersion curve fitting. Trained on collagen-based hydrogels with varying concentrations and cellular compositions, the model achieves higher accuracy than conventional architectures while dramatically reducing processing time. These results highlight VENet’s potential for real-time, non-invasive biomechanical assessment, with promising applications in ophthalmology for early disease detection and quantitative tissue evaluation.

papers.title: Ultrasound-Based Skull Porosity Estimation Using a Three-Phase Poroelastic Model
papers.abstract: We present a three-phase poroelastic–scattering framework to quantify skull porosity from ultrasound measurements. The model treats the skull as a composite of mineralized matrix, trabecular solid, and pore fluid, incorporating frequency-dependent attenuation via Biot–JKD viscous coupling and scattering loss. Numerical simulations computed attenuation spectra across porosity and frequency ranges, guiding inversion of local porosity from through-transmission measurements on phantoms and ex vivo skulls. The model accurately reproduced observed attenuation trends, and reconstructed porosity maps for monkey skulls (30–40%) closely matched CT-derived values. These results demonstrate a physically interpretable method for quantifying skull microstructure and support improved skull-aware transcranial ultrasound modeling and correction.

papers.title: Enhanced Physics-Informed Machine Learning for Real-Time Torque Estimation in Ultrasonic Motors
papers.abstract: Closed-loop torque control of ultrasonic motors (USMs) requires fast, low-cost torque feedback that remains robust to temperature-dependent changes in stator contact, dielectric behavior, and friction. This work proposes a hybrid real-time output-torque estimator that combines a physics-informed torque model with a data-driven residual correction branch. Electrical and vibration measurements are used as primary inputs, while additional motor-state features are extracted from drive admittance and a weak high-frequency voltage probe. Lock-in measurements of the probe current provide capacitance- and loss-related descriptors that capture temperature-sensitive electromechanical changes. Experiments on independent PID torque-control trials show that the proposed estimator substantially improves torque-estimation accuracy over the physical model alone and captures key torque-transition stages, including non-contact behavior, contact-induced torque drop, and post-contact plateau. These results demonstrate that weak high-frequency probing can enhance real-time torque estimation without modifying the physical model branch, supporting compact implementation on MCU-based systems.

papers.title: Particle Manipulation with Acoustic Radiation Force Using Langevin Transducer and ELIPS
papers.abstract: In this study, we propose a non-contact acoustic trapping method combining a low-frequency Langevin transducer and ELIPS, a high-frequency transducer, and demonstrate its ability to manipulate particle structures. The Langevin transducer generates a wide-area standing wave at 110 kHz for standing wave trapping, while ELIPS produces a focused acoustic field at 1.7 MHz to apply localized acoustic radiation forces. Glass particles were used, and their motion was analyzed using high-speed imaging and particle image velocimetry (PIV), along with finite element simulations of acoustic fields. When ELIPS was activated, the trapped particles formed a torus shape with a central hole of about 1 mm. PIV results showed outward particle motion near the tip of ELIPS, consistent with simulated force distributions. These results demonstrate that combining low and high frequency acoustic fields enables precise, non-contact control of particle assemblies into complex geometries, suggesting potential applications in bioengineering and cell manipulation.

papers.title: Period ArrDesign of a Titanium-Integrated SAW Phononic Crystal on YX-15 O LiNbO₃/Silicon Substrateay SiO2 and Air Nano-Slots Wafer Fabricated and Application
papers.abstract: In conventional SAW devices, metallic reflecting gratings are placed on both sides of the IDT propagation path to act as reflectors. These gratings produce Bragg reflection, which has a sufficiently low reflection efficiency. This paper investigates a titanium-based phononic crystal reflector for use in surface acoustic wave resonators. The proposed phononic crystal exhibits a wide band gap spanning 1120 MHz to 1930 MHz, enabling it to reflect leaked acoustic energy back into the resonator body 。

papers.title: Resonance Control for High-Throughput Ultrasound Particle Separation
papers.abstract: We demonstrate high-throughput ultrasound-enhanced particle separation by implementing a standing wave control, ensuring precise resonance excitation and consistent particle separations outside the domain of microfluidics and laminar flow. In the case of greater throughput and flow rate, we must contend with turbulence in the fluid, resulting in fluctuations in the resonance of the flow cell. By continuously monitoring the impedance of the system and utilizing control software to rapidly update the excitation frequency, we are able to achieve high levels of particle separation efficiency. This tracking method has been shown to be effective both in COMSOL simulations as well as experimentally.

papers.title: Domain Wall Condition Controlled by DC Bias Application and its Effect on the Mechanical Q Factor of the Epitaxial KNN Film
papers.abstract: Thin film materials for BAW filters need to possess both high intrinsic mechanical Qm and high kt2. Such as ScAlN and LiNbO3, therefore, have been used. We recently found that the epitaxial (K, Na)NbO3 (KNN) exhibits both a high Qm of 660 at 2 GHz and a high kt2 of 17.2%. The Qm of 660 is comparable to that of ZnO or ScAlN films, suggesting that the epitaxial KNN film shows some potential for BAW filter applications. The KNN film contains ferroelectric domain walls. Consequently, acoustic energy dissipation caused by a domain wall vibration may be significant in the GHz range. In this study, we considered that the DC bias application suppresses the domain wall vibration, as shown in Fig. (a), and thus further improves Qm of KNN thin film. Qm of KNN layer were evaluated using a pulse-echo technique, with varying DC voltage. It is not entirely clear whether the applied DC bias voltage significantly enhanced Qm or not. However, when an electric field was applied from 0 kV/cm to -330 kV/cm, Qm and kt2 increased from 180 and 11.8% at 0 kV/cm to 310 and 17.9% at -330 kV/cm. This indicates that the DC bias application tends to increase Qm by suppressing domain wall vibrations.
keywords: The intrinsic mechanical quality factor Qm

papers.title: Toward Physics-Grounded Ai for Holographic Transcranial Focused Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Accurate wavefield manipulation is essential for transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS), where skull-induced aberrations degrade therapeutic performance. Acoustic holography enables aberration compensation and volumetric control, but its inverse formulation requires iterative, computationally demanding simulations and often relies on case-specific tuning or data-driven models with limited generalization and physical consistency. This work introduces a physics-grounded, AI-driven framework for holographic tFUS treatment planning, enabling computationally efficient and physically consistent patient-specific solutions. The approach integrates patient-specific modeling, hybrid forward–inverse wavefield prediction, and multi-objective design for holographic tFUS treatment planning. Performance is evaluated using targeting efficiency, inside–outside sonication ratios, peak pressure, and safety metrics across patients and neuromodulation targets, with validation against experimentally validated benchmarks.

papers.title: Epitaxial K0.35Na0.65Nb free-Standing Resonator Fabricated Using MgO Sacrificial Substrate
papers.abstract: PbTiO3 or PZT are known for their excellent piezoelectric properties. However, Q values of PbTiO3 was 70 at 2 GHz even in the epitaxial films. In contrast, last year, we found that K(Na, Nb)O3 epitaxial films possess both a high k2 value of 21.9% and a relatively high Q value of 660 at 2 GHz which is comparable values of 3600 for ScAlN and 800 for ZnO. In this study, a free-standing resonator (FBAR) based on K0.35N0.65N epitaxial film was fabricated using MgO sacrifice substrate. The electromechanical coupling properties under DC bias were investigated. KNN was epitaxially grown on the (100) SrRuO3/(100) Pt/(100) MgO substrate using RF magnetron sputtering. the kt2 was estimated to be 3.5%, by comparing with the theoretical curve simulated by Mason’s model. Using a resonance-anti-resonance method, kt2 of KNN free-standing resonator was calculated to be 11.3% in the as-grown state and 14.5% under the DC bias of -30 V. a dramatic decrease of kt2 indicating polarization inversion of KNN was observed under a DC bias.

papers.title: Targeted Single-Cell Focused Acoustic Modulation Platform for Tumor Cell Stimulation and Rupture
papers.abstract: Focused ultrasound can induce bioeffects from reversible cellular stimulation to localized rupture, but existing microscale tumor-modulation methods often face tradeoffs in device size, focal precision, thermal collateral damage, and microscopy compatibility. This study presents a compact on-chip acoustic modulation platform based on a focused acoustic interdigital transducer to generate a microscale acoustic vortex field for targeted single glioma cell stimulation and rupture. Analytical modeling was used to estimate the pressure distribution and focal acoustic beam size, followed by experimental validation under real-time 40× microscopic observation. To characterize the generated mechanical rupture within the targeted region, live/dead assays were used. Furthermore, fluorescence staining and Ca²⁺ imaging verified the cell stimulation ability of this platform. These results demonstrate that the focused acoustic modulation platform can switch between stimulation and disruption regimes with microscale spatial selectivity, providing a potential tool for tumor-cell mechanobiology studies and precision on-chip acoustic manipulation.

papers.title: Dielectrics-Mediated Barrier Shaping: Dynamic Control of Quantum Tunneling via Ultrasonic Waves
papers.abstract: Quantum tunneling has motivated significant advances in theoretical physics, proliferation of quantum devices, and progress of information technologies. Nevertheless, the dependence of electron tunneling behavior on dielectric medium within the tunneling region remains controversial. To this end, a theoretical model for the tuning of quantum tunneling barrier height via dielectric dependence was firstly established, which comprises the effects of interface dipole, image potential and external stimuli. Notably, a negatively exponential dependence between the barrier height and dielectric constant was explicitly revealed. This finding was further experimentally evidenced by using Au atomic quantum tunneling probe featuring a sub-3 nm gap across different dielectric media. Furthermore, dynamic control of barrier height was showcased by ultrasound-induced dielectric modulation within the tunneling region, paving the feasible avenues in developing broadband acoustic quantum devices and atomic-scale imaging inside the opaque and/or biological materials.

sessions.title: PMI: Modelling & Inversion

papers.title: Theory of Photoacoustics of Nanodroplets
papers.abstract: Nanodroplets subjected to laser-pulse irradiation enable extravascular molecular imaging with a high image contrast-to-noise ratio. The optimal design of nanodroplets and laser parameters requires characterization of the laser-induced vaporization, which is currently unavailable. To address this, we use a theoretical approach to investigate the underlying physics of laser-triggered nanodroplet vaporization and the resultant pressure wave. We consider nanodroplets containing laser-absorbing dyes undergoing nanosecond laser-pulse irradiation. The rapid heating raises temperatures close to the critical point. Such states are unstable and lead to the formation of vapor nuclei, which, with a slight increase in irradiation, will grow explosively, generating a strong pressure wave. We model explosive vaporization using the van der Waals’ capillarity theory and solve the resultant Euler-Lagrange equation to reveal the vaporization characteristics. Our analysis of photoacoustic signals from nonodroplets reveals that, compared to plasmonic nanoparticles, a thousand-fold higher pressure wave may be achieved with only a ten-fold higher laser fluence.

papers.title: Focused-Ultrasound-Induced Cavitation As Acoustic Dynamic Masks for High-Resolution Fluorescence Microscopy
papers.abstract: The spatial resolution of traditional optical microscopy is fundamentally restricted by Abbe’s diffraction limit, hindering the visualization of critical subcellular dynamics. Among various strategies, Fluorescence Emission Difference microscopy stands out as a cost-effective, low-intensity. However, the practical application of this technique is severely bottlenecked by the slow switching speed of conventional modulation hardware. Current tools, exhibit a physical latency. This temporal lag is unacceptable for capturing rapid physiological events, as it induces irreversible motion artifacts and increases phototoxicity due to prolonged laser exposure. To address this necessity, we engineered an "Acoustic Dynamic Mask" utilizing focused ultrasound-induced transient cavitation. This system enables microsecond-level beam switching, aiming to provide an artifact-free imaging platform for dynamic biological environments.

papers.title: Non-Invasive Ultrasound Sculpting of Light to Improve Fluorescence Depth of View
papers.abstract: Fluorescence imaging is a powerful tool to guide cancer surgery and visualize target cell types, like cancer or nerve, improving surgical outcomes and efficiency. However, the depth of view is limited to ~5 mm due to tissue scattering and absorption. We aim to develop a non-invasive approach to increase depth of view using an out-of-plane ultrasound source, which may be integrated into fluorescence-guided surgery workflows. In this work, we demonstrate increased light penetration through a 1 cm scattering medium using a custom focused ultrasound transducer.

sessions.title: NPC: Process Control and Industrial Ultrasound

papers.title: Quality-Aware Closed-Loop Ultrasonic Acquisition for Robust Inspection Under Variable Conditions
papers.abstract: Ultrasonic inspection in industrial environments is often affected by coupling variability, operator-dependent factors, and material inconsistencies, leading to localized degradation in A-scan signals and ambiguous interpretation. This work presents a quality-aware closed-loop framework for improving inspection robustness by identifying and addressing low-quality signals within each acquisition cycle. The method operates on element-wise A-scan data from a 15 MHz matrix probe with 52 active elements and employs signal quality assessment using statistical and structural indicators to detect degraded signals. A closed-loop strategy selectively refines low-quality signals through targeted processing while preserving high-quality data. Experimental evaluation on industrial platforms shows that conventional processing yields 7–10 ambiguous A-scans per acquisition, which is reduced to approximately 2 using the proposed framework, significantly improving inspection reliability under practical conditions.

papers.title: Toward a Network of Distributed Low-Power Wireless Ultrasound Systems Through Mesh Communication
papers.abstract: This work presents a distributed low-power wireless ultrasound system for scalable monitoring networks. Compact ultrasound units communicate through direct BLE and BLE mesh, allowing nodes to relay data beyond single-node range and support fault-resilient setups. The system includes firmware for multi-node acquisition, mesh networking, gateway operation, and a web-based interface for remote control. It was evaluated in the lab and validated during a vacuum-assisted resin infusion process using two battery-powered boards with eight micromachined ultrasound transducers. Direct BLE achieved a stable 19.9 Hz update rate with 400-sample A-scans, while BLE mesh operated at 0.2 Hz but successfully extended connectivity through relay nodes. In the VARI experiment, amplitude changes enabled real-time resin flow-front detection, agreement with optical reference observations, and flow-front speed estimation. Overall, the work demonstrates an open-source foundation for automated, scalable wireless ultrasound monitoring.

papers.title: Design of a System Architecture for External Fouling Control in Docked Ship Hulls Using Ultrasound Waves
papers.abstract: The article presents the design and validation of a resonance-tuned ultrasonic system for controlling external biofouling on docked ship hulls. Marine biofouling, caused by organisms such as barnacles and invasive corals, increases fuel consumption and maintenance costs while conventional methods rely on toxic coatings or hazardous cleaning operations. The proposed architecture uses ultrasonic transducer arrays (24–28 kHz, 100 W) mounted near hull surfaces and driven by a microcontroller-based generator with adaptive frequency tuning to maximize acoustic cavitation efficiency. Field validation over two years across multiple vessels showed significant fouling reduction, with 70–80% decrease in barnacle density and 50–60% reduction in coral coverage compared to untreated areas. The system operates without chemical contaminants or structural damage and reduces maintenance costs and cleaning frequency.

sessions.title: MIM: Contrast-enhanced & Molecular Ultrasound Imaging

papers.title: Microbubble Size Controls out-of-Plane Detection in Nonlinear sound-Sheet Imaging
papers.abstract: Nonlinear sound-sheet imaging (NSSI) enables high-resolution volumetric ultrasound by confining nonlinear microbubble signals to a thin transmit plane. At clinical frequencies, microbubble size determines resonance and thus the amplitude and spatial extent of nonlinear echoes. Using a physics-realistic ultrasound simulator, NSSI was modeled at 6 MHz in a vascular tree with microbubbles below, near, and above resonance. Power Doppler images show that below-resonant microbubbles produce weaker but spatially confined signals, selectively revealing in-plane vasculature. In contrast, near- and above-resonant microbubbles generate stronger signals but substantial out-of-plane detections, leading to projection of vessels across a larger volume. These results highlight the role of microbubble size in controlling spatial confinement in NSSI.

papers.title: Estimating the Statistical Correspondence Between Bubble Counting and Eftedal-Brubakk Grading of post-Dive Echocardiograms
papers.abstract: Venous Gas Emboli (VGE) detected post-dive using echocardiography can be quantified using the Eftedal-Brubakk (EB) ordinal scale and bubble counting methods. Increasing EB grades are related to increasing VGE quantity, but the two scales have not been related. Additionally, while bubble counting can be computer automated, only the EB scale has been related to decompression sickness (DCS) risk. Relating bubble counts and EB grades would harmonize VGE studies graded under different scales and could enable automated DCS risk approximation. 252 videos with EB grades and bubble counts were analyzed. 73 of these videos were counted on 10 and 30 frames to assess the impact of total reviewed frames on bubble counts was investigated. There was a strong, positive relationship between bubble counts and EB grades, and a strong correlation between 10-frame and 30-frame bubble counts. Potential bubble count ranges for each EB grade were determined. Results may inform future automation of DCS risk from VGE detection and a posteriori harmonization of historic data.

papers.title: Spatiotemporal Detection of Bound Microbubbles for Real-Time Nondestructive Ultrasound Molecular Imaging
papers.abstract: Ultrasound molecular imaging (UMI) is a promising approach to detect cancer through targeted microbubbles (MBs). We introduce Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)-based nondestructive UMI that balances a lightweight architecture compared to transformers and the capability to retain spatiotemporal information of MBs from previous frames. Our encoder consists of two hierarchical layers, with each layer incorporating iterations of a convolutional LSTM unit applied to 16 consecutive temporal frames. Our decoder predicts the MB probability. We evaluated our model performance using an in vivo animal model of breast cancer, comparing it with prior CNN and microbubble transformer (MBFormer). Our LSTM model achieved a significantly improved inference time of 4.6 ms (207 frame per second, FPS) compared to 59.8 ms for MBFormer (16.7 FPS), which is suitable to facilitate real-time applications. The LSTM model achieved performance comparable to or slightly lower than MBFormer in the detection of bound MBs. Notably, the higher CC and lower difference compared to CNN indicates improved bound MB detection with effective suppression of free floating MBs.

papers.title: Ultrasound Microvasculature Imaging for Monitoring Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy Response in Breast Cancer Patients
papers.abstract: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) can alter the intratumoral angiogenic activity in breast cancer. Monitoring microvascular variations using ultrasound as an accessible tool for early assessment of treatment response can guide clinicians in selecting appropriate treatment plans. In this study, we use a contrast-free ultrasound quantitative microvasculature imaging framework to assess morphological changes of tumor microvessel networks and predict patient response to NAC.

papers.title: Acousto-Optic Bubble Stacking for Multi-Depth Optical Microscopy
papers.abstract: US-OCM (Nature Photonics, 2022) enables deep microscopy via bubble generation at ultrasound standing-wave peaks, but suffers from low spatial precision. Optrasound improves precision but limits bubbles to the first peak, restricting depth. Multi-depth imaging requires transducer exchange to reconfigure the acoustic focus. To overcome this, we propose sequential optrasound- and US-induced bubble generation at different depths. A donut-shaped 3 MHz focused transducer (OD: 14.5 mm, focal length: 14.5 mm) was fabricated with FPGA-based timing control. Low-intensity ultrasound (~5.61 MPa) with a pulsed Nd:YAG laser (~0.65 mJ, 532 nm) generated optrasound bubbles, followed by high-intensity ultrasound (~7.39 MPa) for US-induced bubbles. Performance was evaluated using 1 µm fluorescent beads in a 1% Intralipid TMM phantom at ~50, ~165, and ~350 µm depths. Experimental bubble sizes (~150 µm and ~309 µm) agreed with FEM predictions (~130 µm and ~256 µm). Without bubbles, FWHMs were 2.14 µm and 6.35 µm at 165 and 350 µm depths; sequential generation recovered resolution to 1.44 and 1.55 µm, confirming resolution-preserved multi-depth imaging without transducer exchange.

papers.title: Null Subtraction Imaging for Enhanced Ultrasound Sensitivity of Gas Vesicles
papers.abstract: As endogenous acoustic reporters, gas vesicles (GVs) hold significant potential for biomolecular ultrasound, yet achieving highly sensitive detection and precise localization of GVs remains challenging within the complex background scattering of biological tissues. This study introduces Null Subtraction Imaging (NSI), a beamforming technique that utilizes three sets of specific apodizations to synthesize a null in the beam pattern, to enhance the detection sensitivity and lateral resolution of GV-expressing cells. Experimental results show that compared to DAS, NSI provides superior boundary definition and enables the precise localization of individual cells even at low intracellular GV concentrations. These findings validate NSI as a powerful tool for improving GV signal detection at the single-cell level, offering a promising technical framework for future in vivo molecular imaging applications.

papers.title: Ultrasonic Detection of Venous Gas Emboli and Tissue Gas in Rodents for Decompression Sickness Mitigation
papers.abstract: Decompression sickness (DCS) is the primary limitation in diving operations, likely caused by bubble formation in vessels and tissues. Venous gas emboli (VGE) are regularly detected in human divers and have been correlated with DCS; however, this only reflects the vascular system. Rodents are widely used for DCS endpoint monitoring, but no connection between imaging and DCS has been established in this model. In this study, rats were subjected to one of two dive profiles, with distinct model-predicted risk of DCS, and all underwent post-dive ultrasound monitoring. Images of the heart and kidney were collected every ten minutes to assess VGE presence and image brightness, respectively. Results show greater VGE presence after dives with higher probability of DCS. Additionally, kidney images tended to be darker at time points with concurrent high VGE load, possibly due to acoustic shadowing from high gas burden in tissues. This demonstrates feasibility of multi-organ monitoring in an animal model as a possible surrogate for DCS risk. Methods will be expanded to connect proximal tissue bubble formation to circulating VGE, towards physiologically relevant decompression models.

papers.title: Molecular Ultrasound Imaging Using 3D-Bioprinted Liver and Point-of-Care Ultrasound (POCUS)
papers.abstract: Liver transplantation is the only treatment for end-stage liver disease, yet donor demand exceeds supply and many livers fail quality standards. Bioengineered liver constructs are a promising solution but require non-invasive assessment of physiological relevance. We hypothesize that VEGFR2-targeted microbubbles (MBs) will show selective, prolonged adhesion within EC-lined channels of a 3D-bioprinted liver construct versus non-targeted MBs, assessed via molecular ultrasound imaging (MUS) with point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS). A 3D-bioprinted liver phantom with a perfusable EC-lined channel was imaged using Clarius (handheld POCUS) with three MB types: normal, scrambled, and VEGFR2-targeted. VEGFR2 MBs showed prolonged adhesion versus scrambled MBs, consistent with mouse liver findings. Time-intensity curves confirmed rapid washout for scrambled (-0.53 a.u./s) versus slower washout for VEGFR2 MBs (-0.06 a.u./s), validating selective EC targeting. Next steps include validating additional biomarkers (CD31, PD-L1) and longitudinal EC maturation imaging. MUS with POCUS is a scalable, translational tool for evaluating 3D-bioprinted organ quality for clinical transplantation.

sessions.title: MEL: Harmonic and Reverberant Shear Wave Elastography

papers.title: Frame-Interval-Induced Phase Wrapping Effects in Autocorrelation-Based Shear Wave Motion Estimation Using Harmonic External Vibrations
papers.abstract: In vibrator-based SWE, harmonic excitation enables frequency-controlled analysis; however, accurate elasticity reconstruction depends on reliable motion estimation. Autocorrelation-based methods are widely used but sensitive to temporal sampling. This study investigates the effect of frame interval on motion estimation and phase velocity reconstruction, focusing on phase wrapping. A 600 Hz shear wave was generated and tracked at 3 kHz. Particle velocity was estimated using 1D autocorrelation, with phase wrapping expected at k=5n. Under non-wrapping conditions, particle velocity maps show clear wave propagation and preserved spectral content. In contrast, wrapping produces distorted wave and frequency components, indicating phase-ambiguous motion. LPVI confirms that non-wrapping intervals yield stable velocity maps and accurate inclusion delineation, whereas wrapping leads to reduced contrast and unreliable results. Quantitative analysis shows amplitude minima consistent with wrapping-induced errors. These findings demonstrate that improper temporal sampling induces phase wrapping, compromising motion estimation and elasticity reconstruction in vibrator-based SWE.

papers.title: Extending Shear Wave Dispersion Beyond Spectral Limits via Wavelet-Guided Localization
papers.abstract: Dispersion analysis is widely used to study material behavior, but traditional frequency-wavenumber analysis degrades at high frequencies due to energy dissipation and low signal-to-noise ratio, leading to truncated dispersion curves. To address this limitation, this work proposes a high-frequency extension framework that decouples wave-packet localization from phase estimation using continuous wavelet transform (CWT)-anchored phase. A narrowband Morlet CWT is applied to localize the wave packet and determine its arrival time, followed by Hilbert transform to extract instantaneous phase at the identified temporal peak. This phase is converted into total transit time, spatially unwrapped, and linearly fitted to estimate high-frequency wavenumber and reconstruct phase velocity. Results demonstrate that the method produces stable phase evolution across spatial positions, enabling reliable wavenumber estimation. The reconstructed phase velocity remains consistent at high frequencies and successfully extends dispersion curves beyond conventional spectral limits, indicating strong potential for high-frequency dispersion analysis where traditional methods fail.

papers.title: Radial Energy Quantile Estimator for Robust Wavenumber Mapping Across Directional and Diffuse Shear Wavefields
papers.abstract: This work introduces the Radial Energy Quantile (REQ) estimator for robust local wavenumber mapping in harmonic shear wave elastography. REQ analyzes a windowed displacement patch in the spatial-frequency domain, computes the local two-dimensional power spectrum, radializes the spectral energy, and estimates wavenumber from a selected quantile of the cumulative radial energy distribution. The method is designed to handle wavefields that range from directional to reverberant or diffuse, where conventional estimators may fail or become geometry-dependent. Controlled-aperture simulations showed that the REQ quantile increases systematically with wavefield solid angle, consistent with the directional-to-diffuse transition. Homogeneous gelatin phantom experiments under directional and reverberant excitation showed stable shear wave speed estimates across frequency for both soft and stiff materials. These results support REQ as a geometry-aware spectral framework for harmonic elastography and provide a basis for future adaptive quantile selection in complex wavefields.

papers.title: Resolving Nodal Singularities in Reverberant Elastography via Weak-Integral Multi-Frequency Physics-Informed Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Reverberant shear wave elastography (RSWE) exhibits limited diagnostic sensitivity for sub-centimeter micro-tumors due to complex interference patterns and nodal blind spots. Conventional inversions and multi-frequency Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) struggle with severe artifacts, numerical singularities, and destructive inter-frequency gradient conflicts. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose the Weak-Form Multi-Frequency RSWE Network (WF-MF-RSWENet). Validated on Kelvin-Voigt fractional derivative numerical phantoms, our method reformulates acoustic equations into localized weak-integral forms, transferring high-order spatial derivatives onto analytical test functions. This fundamentally mitigates noise amplification and nodal singularities. Furthermore, a frequency-decoupled strategy anchors physical loss on a primary frequency, utilizing auxiliary frequencies as regularizers to avert gradient interference. Results demonstrate faithful viscoelastic recovery of micro-tumors. Our strategy suppresses maximum error to 2.90 kPa (11.6%), significantly outperforming conventional autocorrelation (65.0%) and strong-form PINNs (33.4%), yielding an rRMSE of 6.1%.

papers.title: Real-Time Optimization of Radial Energy–Quantile Estimator for Harmonic Shear Wave Elastography
papers.abstract: Radial Energy–Quantile (REQ) elastography estimates local wavenumber from a quantile of the angularly averaged radial spectrum, making it useful for directional and diffuse harmonic shear wavefields. However, real-time use is limited by the cost of repeated local spectral analysis. This work optimizes REQ for implementation on a Verasonics NXT research ultrasound platform while preserving agreement with the original estimator. Two acceleration strategies were developed for SWS mapping using simulations. A sparse batch implementation replaced point-by-point processing with batched computation, while a frequency-dependent decimated sparse batch method downsampled low-frequency complex harmonic wavefields before REQ reconstruction. Accuracy was assessed against baseline REQ, and runtime was measured. Sparse batch produced maps consistent with baseline, and decimated sparse batch maintained differences below 0.10 m/s at 300–400 Hz. At 400 Hz, offline runtime improved from 2542 ms/map to 526 ms/map and 42 ms/map. End-to-end performance increased from 0.03 fps to 2.0 and 5.76 fps, showing that frequency-aware algorithmic optimization can move REQ toward real-time elastography.

papers.title: Ex Vivo Feasibility of Harmonic Shear Wave Elastography for Central Nervous System Imaging
papers.abstract: In this study, we determine the initial feasibility of harmonic shear wave elastography in ex vivo brain samples and compare it with single-pulse shear wave elastography. We demonstrate improvements in SWS estimation relative to the single-pulse technique, show evidence for anatomical specificity of the estimated speed, and finally discuss the sources of the advantages of our technique and assess the drawbacks they create.

papers.title: Regime-Dependent Evaluation of Local Estimators in Harmonic Shear Wave Elastography
papers.abstract: Harmonic shear wave elastography (HSWE) enables frequency-resolved soft-tissue characterization through dispersion analysis. Shear wave speed (SWS) estimation is affected by physical constrains. We propose a regime-dependent framework to benchmark SWS estimators across quasi-static, modal, and free-space propagation regimes using dimensionless parameters related to wavelength, geometry, and attenuation. Phase gradient, 2D Cross-correlation, and spectral frequency domain estimators were compared Results showed strong regime dependence: PG and SFD were more stable at low frequencies, CC and SFD better handled modal interference, and all methods improved in free-space conditions, with SFD offering stable localized estimates.

sessions.title: MIS: Breast Cancer Diagnosis & Therapy Monitoring

papers.title: Longitudinal Multimodal RF-Based Ultrasound Segmentation of Breast Tumors During Neoadjuvant Chemotherapy
papers.abstract: Accurate segmentation of breast tumors in ultrasound imaging is essential for quantitative analysis and prediction of response to neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC). However, segmentation remains challenging due to speckle noise, low contrast, and therapy-induced changes in tumor morphology. A multimodal framework based on raw radiofrequency (RF) data was proposed. Composite three-channel representations combining B-mode images, Nakagami parametric maps, and RF signals were used. The dataset included longitudinal RF data from 42 patients undergoing NAC, with at least five timepoints per case, supplemented with baseline data. A transformer-based Mask2Former model was fine-tuned and evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation. The model achieved Dice = 0.6871 and IoU = 0.5749, with higher performance at early therapy stages and decreasing accuracy as tumor visibility diminished. These outcomes indicate the potential of RF-based multimodal analysis for tumor characterization and prediction of NAC response.

papers.title: Breast Lesion Classification in Trimodal Ultrasound Using Uncertainty-Aware and Evidential Fusion Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Ultrasound is widely used for breast lesion assessment. Combining B-mode morphology, shear wave elastography (SWE) stiffness, and color Doppler (CD) vascularity can improve diagnostic accuracy. However, most deep learning methods rely on single or bimodal inputs, manual annotations, BI-RADS labels, or handcrafted features, limiting scalability and real-world applicability. They assume fixed image counts and ignore modality-specific relevance and uncertainty. Therefore, we propose a fully automated, uncertainty-aware trimodal framework using multiple instance learning (MIL). The method utilizes modality-specific ConvNeXt-Tiny encoders to process wavelet-augmented inputs, while attention-based MIL aggregates variable numbers of images per patient. Then, an evidential deep learning (EDL) fusion mechanism models predictive evidence and uncertainty via Dirichlet parameters, with a quality-aware network adaptively weighting modalities. Evaluated on 793 patients with 5-fold CV, the method achieves an AUC of 0.902, outperforming conventional fusion approaches. It provides interpretable, uncertainty-adaptive weighting per modality and remains fully automated without requiring annotations.
