papers.title: Multimodal Breast Ultrasound Classification via Spatial-Frequency Dynamics and Clinical-Guided Feature Fusion
papers.abstract: This work proposes a deep learning framework for breast ultrasound lesion classification that jointly models imaging and clinical information through a three-branch architecture. Building upon multi-frame inputs, the method captures complementary spatial, temporal, and clinical features. Specifically, a spatial branch with hierarchical feature fusion enhances multi-scale representation, while a frequency-domain branch introduces a Sequence Frequency-Domain Extraction (SFDE) module to model temporal dynamics via spectral analysis of ultrasound sequences. In parallel, structured clinical variables are encoded using a lightweight residual MLP network. The proposed framework was extensively evaluated against state-of-the-art convolutional neural networks and lightweight vision transformers. It consistently outperformed all baselines across key metrics. Specifically, the proposed method achieved an AUC of 83.2%, surpassing the best baseline (NextViT, 77.9%) by 5.3%. The overall accuracy reached 81.2%, while the recall achieved 96.8%, indicating strong sensitivity in detecting malignant lesions. The F1-score reached 86.3%, demonstrating improved overall robustness.

papers.title: Dual-Branch Neural Network for TDLU Classification
papers.abstract: Terminal duct lobular units (TDLUs) are functional glandular substructures of the breast whose degree of involution correlates with breast cancer risk, making their assessment relevant for risk stratification. Reliable identification of TDLUs in ultrasound imaging, however, remains challenging due to low contrast and inter-patient variability. We propose a dual-branch convolutional neural network that integrates conventional B-mode ultrasound images with raw radio-frequency (RF) signal representations to improve automated TDLU detection. The model processes B-mode data and RF-derived features, specifically amplitude and phase, in separate branches and combines them through late fusion. It was trained and evaluated on a dataset of 500 annotated image patches extracted from clinical ultrasound examinations. While RF-only models showed limited performance, the proposed dual-branch architecture consistently outperformed the B-mode baseline, increasing accuracy from 0.901±0.020 to 0.934±0.007. Activation maps indicated that the model focuses on anatomically meaningful structures, suggesting that combining structural and signal-based ultrasound information improves TDLU classification.

papers.title: Multiparametric Ultrasound radiomic Projection Imaging for Monitoring Early Breast Cancer Response to neoadjuvant Chemotherapy
papers.abstract: Detection of tumor response trajectory after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) initiation is critical to assess efficacy. Quantitative ultrasound (US) imaging in a multiparametric framework has shown promise for early tumor response classification. However, existing approaches prioritize predictive accuracy over biological interpretability by mapping early NAC radiomic measurements to post-surgical pathological response. From a clinical standpoint, there is a need for a unified spatial representation that reflects NAC-induced tissue changes. We propose a multiparametric radiomic (MPR) projection imaging framework that integrates Ki-67 with baseline radiomics to generate spatial maps for characterizing early tumor response. Breast cancer patients scheduled for NAC underwent US exams at baseline and at early NAC time points using a clinical US scanner. Radiomic maps were analyzed from US data. MPR axes were constructed using baseline radiomic measures with molecular subtype stratification. Radiomic maps were then projected onto MPR axes to generate images. Analysis of MPR images revealed distinct trends across molecular subtypes. The classification model achieved a test AUC of 0.88.

papers.title: Joint Reconstruction of Speed-of-Sound and Acoustic Attenuation for Breast USCT via Waveform-Conditioned Deep Learning
papers.abstract: Breast Ultrasound Computed Tomography (USCT) is a non-invasive modality for tumor characterization, but simultaneous reconstruction of tissue biomarkers is traditionally slow or highly noise-sensitive. We propose a deep learning framework for rapid, noise-resilient Speed-of-Sound and Acoustic Attenuation mapping. For 2D acoustic simulations, a direct neural network maps Delay-and-Sum beamformed data to Speed-of-Sound and attenuation maps. This model achieves near real-time inference (0.35 seconds/image) and exceptional structural fidelity (maintaining >0.95 SSIM), even under severe 10dB SNR noise. Furthermore, while deterministic models struggle with the complexity of 3D data, we introduce a generative diffusion model that shows strong promise in recovering fine volumetric details from 3D acquisitions. Ultimately, this work demonstrates a highly accurate, noise-robust, and clinically viable reconstruction pathway for breast USCT.

papers.title: Shape Analysis of Breast Cancerous Forms in Ultrasound Images via Discrete Curves Manifold
papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging plays a crucial role in breast cancer diagnosis, in cases were mammography presents limitations, enabling clinicians to better visualize lesion structures and characteristics. The geometric manifold of discrete curves has been used in applications of biomedical image processing, primarily for the analysis of the morphology of cancer cells, but only rarely in ultrasound images. The utilization of manifold geometry framework, namely the discrete curves one, which is the set of all extracted curves forms concentrated in one geometric space, is aiming in the analysis of the structural characteristics of cancerous forms. The manifold of discrete curves is therefore considered a promising approach for the problem at hand, namely because of its ability to concentrate the boundaries of cancers in one geometric space, making easier the use of mathematical algorithms and statistical analysis.

sessions.title: MIS: Physical & Wave Methods

papers.title: Structure Tensor-Regularized Deep Learning for Inverse Problem Ultrasound Beamforming
papers.abstract: The inverse problem of ultrasound beamforming (IPB) reconstructs images by combining RF data fidelity with image-domain regularization, but iterative solvers are computationally expensive. This work investigates structure tensor regularization as a training constraint for deep learning-based IPB. The target reconstruction is associated with minimizing a data-fidelity term and a structure tensor regularizer, which promotes coherent local gradient orientation and structural continuity. An adjoint reconstruction is used as the network input, and a ResUNet predicts a residual correction to obtain the final image through an identity shortcut. The method was evaluated on simulated single-plane-wave cyst phantoms. Compared with one-plane-wave delay-and-sum beamforming, the proposed method improved CR from 12.98 dB to 25.62 dB and gCNR from 0.736 to 0.828, approaching 65-plane-wave DAS and iterative IPB-NLSTV. IPB-NLSTV required about 30 min per image in the current implementation, whereas the trained network only requires one forward pass.

papers.title: Rotational Hydrophone-Based Characterization of the Elevational Pressure Field of Imaging Transducers
papers.abstract: This work introduces a rotational hydrophone-based method to characterize the elevational pressure field of rotating 1D ultrasound transducers used in ICE and IVUS imaging. Hydrophone directivity typically limits measurement accuracy by reducing SNR and introducing angular sensitivity bias. By rotating the hydrophone around the transducer axis at a constant distance, the proposed approach ensures consistent measurement conditions. Compared to conventional 3D scanning with directivity compensation, it provides more robust measurements over a wider angular range and reduces reliance on correction models.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Grating Lobe Suppression in Ultrasound Imaging with Coherence-Guided Attention on Delay-Compensated Input
papers.abstract: Efficient sampling is important for portable and wearable ultrasound, but aggressive sparsity causes grating-lobe artifacts and image degradation. Raw RF sparse-to-dense interpolation is limited by wavefront variability across depth and scanning geometry. We propose a physics-informed deep learning framework using coherence-guided attention on delay-compensated (DC) channel data for grating lobe suppression. The model uses an HGNet-V2 encoder–decoder for sparse-channel interpolation. Field II simulations with randomized point and hyperechoic mass targets were generated over 288 radial scanning positions within a 90° field-of-view. Models were trained with random receive-channel decimation from 1× to 16× and tested under in-distribution and out-of-distribution sparsity. Compared with raw RF interpolation, DC input improved spatial consistency and enabled stable reconstruction at higher decimation rates. Adding coherence-factor attention further improved performance beyond 20× decimation, and scanning-radius tests showed improved robustness to geometry changes.

papers.title: Comparison of 3 Methods for Deconvolution for Refraction-Corrected 3D Ultrasound Reflection Tomography
papers.abstract: We compare three Richardson–Lucy deconvolution strategies for refraction-corrected 3D ultrasound reflection imaging. Method 1 compounds all 60 views and then deconvolves the resulting linear image using a constant PSF. Method 2 deconvolves each refraction-corrected view separately using a bead-phantom-derived spatially varying PSF, then compounds the deconvolved views and applies log compression. Method 3 is a hybrid effective-PSF approach: the 60 view-specific spatially varying PSFs are compounded to form a local effective PSF, and brick-wise spatially varying RL deconvolution is applied once to the compounded, non-log-compressed image before final log compression. Method 3 preserves the dominant spatially varying blur characteristics of the full view-wise method while avoiding 60 separate deconvolutions. Phantom and breast comparisons show that Method 3 provides image quality comparable to the spatially varying view-wise approach, including preservation of fine detail and point-target sharpening, while reducing computation time by approximately 60-fold. All reconstructions and timing measurements were performed on NVIDIA L40s GPUs, supporting practical clinical deployment.

papers.title: pCoRev: Physics-Informed Contrastive Learning for Unsupervised Reverberation Artifact Suppression in Medical Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Reverberation artifacts are challenging to suppress due to their similarity to tissue echoes and their non-stationary behavior, while supervised deep learning approaches are limited by the lack of paired artifact-free data. Notably, tissue signals remain coherent across steering angles, whereas reverberation artifacts exhibit angle-dependent variations. Motivated by this observation, this study aims to develop a physics-informed contrastive learning framework that exploits inter-angle coherence in unlabeled multi-angle data to achieve robust reverberation suppression while preserving anatomical structures.

papers.title: Physics-Embedded Deconvolution Flow for Ultrasound Scatter Inversion and Resolution Enhancement
papers.abstract: Ultrasound I/Q data are formed through a system-dependent point spread function (PSF), which spreads underlying tissue scattering responses and limits the apparent spatial resolution of the reconstructed image. Recovering latent scatter information from such degraded observations is highly ill-posed, as conventional deconvolution methods are sensitive to kernel mismatch, noise amplification, and handcrafted regularization. This study aims to develop a physics-embedded deconvolution framework that reconstructs a scatter-domain representation from ultrasound I/Q data while preserving consistency with the underlying image formation process.

papers.title: Inverse Problem for Reconstructing Despeckled Images with Sparse Linear Arrays
papers.abstract: Miniaturized and wearable ultrasound systems show strong promise to improve pulse-echo imaging and reduce its cost. However, they are often limited in their number of piezoelectric elements, making standard beamforming like delay-and-sum (DAS) ineffective due to strong grating lobes. In this work, we propose an inverse-problem approach using a frequency-domain model to directly reconstruct despeckled images, allowing efficient regularization. We simulate the acquisition of full synthetic aperture data using a sparse linear array of only 16 elements by downsampling the data acquired with a 128-element probe. We compare the proposed method using 16 elements with DAS using both numbers of elements for simulated and in-vitro data. Our method allows detection of inclusions and point reflectors when they are indistinguishable from background speckle when 16-elements DAS is used, thus showing strong potential for imaging under hardware constraints.

papers.title: Learned Transmit Combination for Two Stage beamformers
papers.abstract: Two stage beamformers, such as synthetic aperture sequential beamforming (SASB) (Ultrasonics 2013), achieve improved image quality through the coherent combination of low-resolution images (LRIs) from multiple transmits to create a high-resolution image (HRI). However, combining large numbers of LRIs may be difficult due to hardware limitations. Neural networks (NNs) have been applied to reduce the number of plane waves needed to create a high quality coherently compounded image. In this work, we describe a method using neural networks to non-linearly combine fewer LRIs, achieving comparable image quality. We validate our method on data simulated in silico in Field II. The performance of the method was quantified by assessing the improvement in resolution and contrast on an unseen test phantom for the same transducer and transmit configuration.

papers.title: Development of an Estimation Technique for 3D Distribution of Reflection Coefficients Using Acoustic Microscopy for Successive Observation of a Living and Identical Cell
papers.abstract: Acoustic microscopy using high frequency ultrasound with a center frequency of more than 100 MHz can observe the morphology of a single cell. As cell cytotoxicity of ultrasound is considered to be lower compared to that of optical measurement using laser, by taking this advantage, we have been developing a new measurement system using an acoustic microscopy for observation of the 3D structure of a living and identical cell based on acoustic properties such as reflection coefficient and acoustic impedance. In this study, we report an example of successive measurements of a single living osteoblast by focusing on the 3D distribution of the reflection coefficient.

papers.title: A Dedicated Sigmoid-Based Processing Pipeline for Improved Ultrasound Speckle Modeling in Fatiguing Biceps Brachii
papers.abstract: This study proposes a sigmoid-based pixel selection algorithm to improve speckle intensity distribution modeling in B-mode ultrasound images for muscle fatigue evaluation. Since non-speckle regions can distort statistical modeling, our pipeline isolates speckle using a sigmoid transformation to enhance hyperechoic areas, followed by Gaussian smoothing and thresholding. The approach was tested on 14 subjects performing isometric biceps brachii contractions with and without a superimposed vibration to increase muscle fatigue. The isolated speckle distribution was modeled using a Gamma function within selected regions of interest at task onset and end. Modeling performance is evaluated via the coefficient of determination and Kullback–Leibler divergence. Differences in Gamma parameters (onset/end) and fitting performances (preprocessed/raw) are assessed (two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, α=0.05). Results demonstrate that the proposed method substantially improves model fit. Furthermore, the Gamma scale parameter exhibited larger fatigue-related shifts under vibration, reflecting altered signal characteristics like mean intensity and signal-to-noise ratio.

papers.title: A Differentiable Ultrasound Simulator for Image inversion, scatter-Level Motion tracking, and physics-Based Augmentation
papers.abstract: We propose a differentiable ultrasound simulator implemented in PyTorch. The medium is a set of point scatterers, each with a position, an amplitude and optionally a class label. Image formation is composed of four stages whose parameters carry gradients: a Fresnel spatial-impulse-response stage, a transmit-sequence stage, a delay-and-sum beamformer, and envelope detection with log-compression. The learnable parameters are the scatterer positions and amplitudes, the transmit waveform centre frequency and bandwidth, the probe element pitch, the sound speed in the forward model and, separately, the sound speed in the beamformer, the attenuation coefficient, and the dynamic range. Two uses are shown. A clinical B-mode image is inverted into a scatter phantom whose simulated image reproduces the acquired one. The phantom is then re-rendered under acquisitions that differ from the original: plane-wave, focused and synthetic-aperture transmit sequences, different steering angles, centre frequencies, focal depths, a changed forward-model sound speed, dynamic ranges, envelope or RF filters, and different virtual-source positions of the focused transmit.

sessions.title: MTC: H-Scan Imaging, Tensor Imaging & Musculoskeletal Evaluation

papers.title: Impact of Sound Speed Errors on H-Scan Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: This work demonstrates that an incorrect sound speed assumption can severely impact H-scan ultrasound image quality and diagnostic interpretation, with phantom and in vivo data examples.

papers.title: Towards Optimization of Quantitative H-Scan Frequency Imaging Using a point-of-Care Ultrasound Device
papers.abstract: Handheld point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) systems have limited computational resources, creating challenges for quantitative imaging. H-scan ultrasound (US) is a technique for estimating relative scatterer size from frequency-dependent backscatter. Traditionally, data processing uses a large Gaussian filterbank, but parameter choices are often unoptimized. This study systematically varied Gaussian filterbank size and bandwidth in both phantom and mouse liver models to optimize H-scan US for efficiency. Results showed signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) improved up to filterbank size N = 16 and plateaued for larger sizes, allowing accurate scatterer discrimination and tissue differentiation with reduced computational burden. Overall, small filterbanks enable practical, quantitative H-scan US frequency imaging for handheld POCUS without loss of performance.

papers.title: Impact of Transducer and Tissue Motion on H-Scan Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: H-scan ultrasound (US) imaging is used to estimate relative scatterer size, but the impact of transducer and tissue motion on its measurements is unclear. This study used controlled compression in tissue-mimicking phantoms and tracked respiratory motion in mouse livers to measure effects on H-scan frequency. Using a Vevo F2 system and processing radiofrequency data with a Gaussian filter bank, researchers found significant frequency shifts up to 0.71 MHz (4.6%) with 6.5 mm compression in phantoms (p < 0.01) and 0.60 MHz (3.5%) between inhalation and exhalation in mouse livers (p < 0.05). Thus, motion impacts H-scan frequency analysis, and minimizing motion is crucial for reproducible in vivo measurements.

papers.title: Test-Retest Repeatability of the Steering Angle Dependence of First-Order Speckle Statistics As Metrics of Anisotropy in the Healthy and Pathological Patellar Tendon
papers.abstract: To address the need for objective monitoring of patellar tendon injury, we investigated quantitative ultrasound metrics that characterize microstructural anisotropy. This study assessed the test-retest repeatability of speckle statistics metrics in healthy and pathological patellar tendons. The injured and contralateral (uninvolved) patellar tendons of ten participants were imaged with a linear ultrasound probe while supine with knees rested in ~30° flexion. Long and short axis views were acquired. Subjects had two exams within a 1-7 day period and were imaged 3 times per view in each exam. Parameters of the Nakagami and homodyned K distributions were estimated from signals within the patellar tendon acquired at beam angles from -10 to 10 degrees, and the steering angle-dependence of these parameters was calculated. Intraclass correlation coefficients were calculated for the steering angle-dependence of the speckle statistics parameters both between-trial and within-trial. Between-trial repeatability was overall moderate (0.5-0.75] across metrics and conditions, and within-trial repeatability was good (0.75-0.9].

papers.title: Attenuation Coefficient Estimation of Vastus Lateralis Muscle Ultrasound Examinations with Different Isometric Contraction Conditions
papers.abstract: Quantitative ultrasound attenuation coefficient estimation (ACE) is a potential biomarker for muscle contractility, but standard methods suffer from high variance in heterogeneous tissue. This study investigates whether ACE can resolve dynamic states of the vastus lateralis under graded isometric loading (rest, 15%, and 30% maximum voluntary contraction) in 26 asymptomatic volunteers. Standard Spectral Difference (SD), Spectral Log Difference (SLD), and Tikhonov-regularized Spectral Log Difference (RSLD) were validated via k-Wave simulations and applied to in vivo RF data. Because absolute AC values varied broadly, analysis focused on relative changes. Results showed that unregularized methods (SD, SLD) failed to detect significant trends. In contrast, RSLD revealed a significant positive correlation between muscle loading and AC (r=0.49, p<0.001), with attenuation significantly higher at 30% MVC compared to rest (p<0.005). As the first study to track local AC response to MVC-graded isometric tensioning, we demonstrate that while dynamic ACE is a promising metric, regularized algorithms like RSLD are essential to reliably capture these changes in vivo.

papers.title: 3D Fiber Orientation Estimation Using an Extension of Backscatter Tensor Imaging
papers.abstract: The organization of fibrous tissue provides functional and structural information about musculoskeletal tissues. Backscatter Tensor Imaging (BTI) has been used to estimate fiber orientation in the myocardium using the spatial coherence (SC) of backscattered ultrasound signals received by a matrix array transducer but remained limited to assess the in-plane (IP) orientation of fibers only (i.e. the fiber angle in a plane parallel to the transducer surface). The objective of this work was to extend BTI to enable the estimation of the out-of-plane (OOP) angle by transmitting steered plane waves.

sessions.title: MBB: Volume Beamforming

papers.title: APCF-Enhanced 3D Ultrasound Imaging with Row-Column Arrays
papers.abstract: This work presents a 3D ultrasound imaging framework using a row-column addressed (RCA) array combined with adaptive phase coherence factor (APCF) beamforming. A 64×64 RCA probe is used with a single-transmit all-receive scheme to reduce system complexity while preserving spatial coherence. The acquired RF data are reconstructed using delay-and-sum and enhanced with APCF weighting. Results show significant improvements in image quality, including up to 50% reduction in lateral and elevational beamwidth, 14 dB sidelobe reduction, and 27 dB improvement in signal-to-clutter ratio. The method enables high-resolution volumetric imaging with reduced hardware complexity.

papers.title: Encoded Multi-Line Transmission for Volumetric Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: This work extends encoded multi-line transmission (MLT-Enc) to volumetric ultrasound imaging and evaluates its ability to suppress crosstalk while preserving image quality and acquisition efficiency. Simulated multistatic data were used to study three volumetric configurations: a fully sampled phased array, a row-column array (RCA), and a walking-aperture (WA) configuration. For the phased-array case, Hadamard-based polarity encoding was applied to a 4x4 volumetric MLT scheme producing 16 simultaneous steering beams per transmit event. Performance was assessed using simulated point targets and 3D anechoic-lesion phantoms, with SLT, conventional MLT, compounded plane waves, and compounded spherical waves used for comparison. MLT-Enc reduced off-mainlobe energy at 40 mm while maintaining comparable lateral and axial FWHM. In phantom simulations, MLT-Enc achieved the highest gCNR among the evaluated transmit strategies and substantially increased volume rate under matched steering-density assumptions. Results across RCA and WA cases further support the generalizability of encoded MLT for high-volume-rate 3D imaging.

papers.title: 3-Dimensional Unified Pixel Based Beamforming with Fully Sampled Matrix Array Transducers
papers.abstract: The unified pixel-based framework extends conventional virtual source models by incorporating multiple transmit path contributions, addressing limitations outside the focal region. While these methods have been explored primarily in two-dimensional imaging and linear arrays, their application to matrix arrays has received relatively limited attention. The objective of this work is to investigate the extension of unified beamforming to matrix array imaging. We develop a 3D implementation of the unified pixel-based beamformer. The transmit delay model is continuous across virtual source and non-virtual source regions. A beam-aligned coordinate framework with spatial mapping between local and global grids is developed. To address observed artefacts, we investigate compounding strategies that account for spatially varying contributions and weighting. We assess the beamforming strategy with data obtained from a 3D ultrasound research platform and calibrated 3.5 MHz 1024-element matrix array probe using focused emissions with focal lengths of 6 cm.

papers.title: Beamforming Strategies for Whole Brain 3D Ultrafast Imaging
papers.abstract: This work tackles 3D ultrafast ultrasound imaging of large organs such as the human brain, where PRF is reduced to image deeper, thus limiting the number of transmit events. A 3112-element ultrasound helmet, driven at 1MHz, was simulated using synthetic aperture (SA) imaging. Various sequences were tested to show the complexity of maintaining an ultrafast framerate in 3D transcranial imaging.

papers.title: Matrix Zero-Mean Apodization Design for 3D Null Subtraction Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Null Subtraction Imaging (NSI) improves spatial resolution with a ‘null’ signal created by a zero-mean (ZM) apodization and nonlinear processing. Extending the NSI method to volumetric ultrasound imaging using matrix arrays is a promising method to improve the limited spatial resolution associated with the small aperture. However, existing designs of matrix ZM apodization to create 2D ‘null’ beampatterns have not been systematically evaluated. Therefore, this work analyzes how to design effective matrix ZM apodizations that create a 2D ‘null’ and compares their performance on 3D NSI beamforming with examples. Researchers may refer to our examples to design proper ZM apodizations based on their array shape.

papers.title: Two-Way Hyper-Beam Row-Column-Addressed Array Imaging
papers.abstract: For real-time 3-D ultrasonic imaging, row-column-addressed (RCA) arrays are an attractive alternative to fully addressed 2-D arrays because they require fewer active channels, reducing hardware complexity and cost. However, their imaging performance is limited by the one-way focusing mechanism. Since the row and column elements are not on the same imaging plane, RCA arrays cannot achieve true two-way focusing, leading to degraded resolution and contrast. In addition, conventional linear compounding and delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming cannot fully overcome these limitations. To address this issue, this study proposes a two-way hyper-beamforming method to suppress sidelobes, narrow the mainlobe, and improve image quality.

sessions.title: MCA: Therapeutic delivery and bio-effects

papers.title: Regulation of Nonlinear Responses by Tailored Surface Tension of Monodisperse Microbubbles
papers.abstract: No direct experimental evidence links the surface tension of bubbles to nonlinear acoustic responses. This work aims to control MDMB surface tension by varying the contact time between bubbles and air, and to determine the relationship between nonlinear responses and surface tension. MDMBs were stirred in air-saturated saline for 20 s, 3 min, 13 min respectively before measurements. The initial surface tension of MDMBs agitated for different time was obtained by fitting the measured attenuation spectra to the linearized Rayleigh-Plesset model. Two transducers were used to transmit and receive signals, respectively. The initial surface tension of MDMBs significantly decreased as the stirring time increased from 20 s to 3 min then to 13 min. At a relatively low acoustic pressure, the nonlinear responses of MDMBs stirred for 20 s were significantly smaller than those stirred for 3 and 13 min. At a relatively high acoustic pressure, the nonlinear responses of MDMBs stirred for 20 s were significantly larger than others. These results showed that the initial surface tension could be regulated therefore improving non-linear responses for special ultrasound imaging and therapy modalities.

papers.title: Using Microbubbles to Enhance the Heating Effects of Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Mild hyperthermia (39-42°C) has been explored as a method for enhancing systemic anticancer therapies. High-intensity focused ultrasound can induce localized hyperthermia or tumor ablation; however, its small focal area limits the treatable region. Microbubbles (MBs) can enhance heating, enabling treatment of larger regions. This study investigates MB-enhanced heating (MBEH) in vitro using tissue-mimicking phantoms to evaluate the effects of acoustic pressure (p) and MB concentration (C) on temperature rise.

papers.title: Temporal and Nonlinear Characterization of Nanobubble Signals in Mouse Tumors
papers.abstract: Nanobubbles (NBs) are promising tumor contrast agents because they can circulate, accumulate, and potentially extravasate into tumor-associated spaces. This work used two complementary ultrasound strategies in vivo: high-frame-rate single-pulse plane-wave imaging (PWI) to monitor rapid NB transport after injection, and cross-amplitude modulation (xAM) to characterize nonlinear NB behavior. Undiluted phospholipid-shelled NBs were injected in mice bearing subcutaneous BxPC-3 tumors. PWI data were acquired on the Vevo F2, and NB-enhanced signals were isolated per breathing cycle using singular value decomposition, followed by power Doppler reconstruction. xAM was performed post-injection with transmit voltage varied from 10% to 100%. Power Doppler showed NB signals first mainly around the tumor, followed by increasing tumor-associated enhancement over time. xAM showed strong excitation dependence, with mean nonlinear signal intensity nearly tripling from 10% to 40% transmit voltage, then decreasing from 70% to 100% while localized enhancement persisted. These results show that PWI and xAM provide complementary characterization of NB signal dynamics and nonlinear behavior in tumors.

papers.title: Ultrasound Phase Change Contrast Agents for On-Demand, Low-Flow Monitoring of the Lymphatic System
papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging combined with phase change contrast agents (PCCA) is used to analyze the lymphatic flow, which normally could not be possible using lymphoscintigraphy due to its limitations in spatial and temporal resolution. When PCCAs interact with ultrasound pulses, they convert into microbubbles, which are monitored and tracked using ultrasound Imaging. To mimic the lymphatic structure, we created a 2 mm lumen made from agarose in which the PCCAs were flowed and interacted with ultrasound waves for both monitoring and activation. The flow rate inside the lumen was controlled using a syringe pump, and the velocity was measured using a flow sensor, which was found to be 1.0-2.0 mm/sec. Flow dynamics were estimated using Singular Value Decomposition, and Individual PCCA signals were detected using Hungarian assignment–based tracking to reconstruct trajectories and generate velocity maps. The average tracked velocities were within 10% compared to the velocity measured by the sensor. These findings support the feasibility of using PCCAs combined with US imaging as a noninvasive and quantitative method for real-time, on-demand, low-flow monitoring of the lymphatic system.

papers.title: Size-Sorted Mono-Sized Microbubbles for Blood-Brain Barrier Opening and 3D Super-Resolution Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: Microbubbles are essential for advanced ultrasound applications like blood-brain barrier (BBB) opening and super-resolution ultrasound (SRUS) imaging. Because microbubble acoustic response is highly size-dependent, the broad size distributions of clinically available agents limit procedural precision. This study evaluates mono-sized fractions of clinically relevant microbubbles (similar to Definity) to improve BBB opening and 3D SRUS imaging. Microbubbles were size-sorted via a microfluidic device to isolate a mono-sized population (4.6±1.0 µm diameter). We performed focused ultrasound-induced BBB opening in mice (1.05 MHz, 350 kPa) to compare mono-sized against poly-sized microbubbles for the delivery of a 3-kDa fluorescent dextran to the hippocampus. Additionally, 3D SRUS imaging was evaluated using a 32x32 matrix array probe on a cross-tube phantom and successfully reconstructed in vivo. Results confirmed the targeted delivery of dextran to the left hippocampus, indicating effective BBB opening. These initial in vivo studies demonstrate that mono-sized microbubbles have significant potential to enhance the precision of diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound.

papers.title: Sequence-Dependent Nonlinear Response of Microbubble Clouds to Therapeutic Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Therapeutic ultrasound with microbubbles depends on nonlinear radial oscillation, shell hysteresis, cloud coupling, and translation, yet cavitation feedback is often interpreted using isolated-bubble assumptions. This work investigates cloud response to pulse inversion (PI), amplitude modulation (AM), and asymmetric amplitude-modulation low-high (AMLH) excitation. A multi-bubble Keller-Miksis model coupled to a hysteretic Marmottant shell law was implemented, including translation and secondary Bjerknes interactions. The framework was tested for Definity, SonoVue, Optison, Sonazoid, and DSPC-type microbubbles at 1 and 0.5 MHz, with robustness checked against published ultrahigh-speed optical imaging. Scattered pressure from the full cloud was sequence-combined and analyzed over a pressure sweep. Subharmonic (SH) and nonlinear-frequency (NLF) changes were quantified relative to the first-burst fundamental. AM and AMLH produced stronger NLF growth than PI, approaching the first-burst fundamental at high pressure, while SH remained lower and more sequence-dependent. These results suggest that AM/AMLH can provide stronger nonlinear-feedback metrics for therapy monitoring.

papers.title: Softening of Fibrin Networks from ultrasound-Driven microbubble Action
papers.abstract: Chronic clots contain dense, retracted fibrin networks that restrict drug access to the clot core. These networks possess unique mechanical properties. We investigated whether microbubbles, known to enhance drug delivery in soft tissues, can be used to create drug access in dense fibrin mesh. Different densities and porosities of dense fibrin networks were exposed to bubbles undergoing stable cavitation at various ultrasound pressures. Bubbles were observed to penetrate over a threshold pressure and enhance matrix transport. It was found that fibrin mechanics play a crucial role in determining the bubble penetration event and its trajectory thereafter. Using atomic force microscopy, we analyzed the underlying physics of the interaction of bubble oscillations with the viscoplastic mechanics of fibrin networks.

sessions.title: MPA: Photoacoustic Imaging Systems

papers.title: High Sensitivity Photoacoustic Imaging with Integrated Photonic Ultrasound Transducers (IPUTs)
papers.abstract: Photoacoustic imaging requires highly sensitive, broadband ultrasound receivers, which is challenging for miniaturised piezoelectric transducers. Integrated Photonic Ultrasound Transducers (IPUTs) offer high sensitivity per unit area through optical readout and enable low-noise PA detection. This work presents the first PA experiments using a Silicon on Insulator IPUT array to image a laser excited wire target. Experimental signals closely match K wave simulations, and image reconstruction successfully recovers the target geometry, with an estimated noise equivalent pressure below 5 Pa, demonstrating the strong potential of IPUTs for high sensitivity PA imaging.

papers.title: Interleaved 3D Photoacoustic and Ultrasound Imaging Using Top-Orthogonal-Bottom-Electrode (TOBE) Arrays and Hadamard-Encoded Read-Out (HERO)
papers.abstract: Current photoacoustic (PA) imaging methods combine high-contrast optical imaging with fine resolution and deep penetration of ultrasound imaging. However, acquisition of massive-volume 3D PA images is currently challenging. Top-Orthogonal-Bottom-Electrode (TOBE) arrays are an emerging row-column transducer technology that offer the potential to scale to large arrays for imaging such massive volumes. The Hadamard-Encoded Read-Out (HERO) scheme can be used with TOBE arrays to read out from every element and produce massive volumes that are receive-focused everywhere, albeit with motion artifacts for moving tissues. The objective of this study is to demonstrate how photoacoustic transmissions can be interleaved with ultrafast volumetric ultrasound acquisitions to produce complete motion-compensated high image quality photoacoustic and ultrasound volumes.

papers.title: For Accessible Real-Time Multi-Spectral Photoacoustic Imaging: Open-Sourced System Architecture for OPOTEK Phocus & Verasonics Vantage Combination
papers.abstract: Real-time multi-spectral photoacoustic imaging (RT-mPAI) enables intraoperative functional guidance and thermal therapy monitoring. However, interfacing OPOTEK Phocus with Verasonics Vantage suffers from non-real-time host operating system (OS) instability, causing wavelength desynchronization. To overcome this, we present OPERA (OPOTEK-vERAsonics Architecture), an open-source framework for reliable RT-mPAI. OPERA features: 1) external microcontroller (MCU)-based trigger counting for OS-independent, deterministic pulse-to-wavelength tagging, 2) a decoupled real-time downstream computation, and 3) online pulse energy compensation. Since the Phocus-Vantage pairing is already widely implemented, OPERA has the potential to lower the barrier to entry and improve accessibility for RT-mPAI research by overcoming synchronization limitations only with an affordable external MCU and open-source software, instead of requiring costly equipment replacements. OPERA successfully demonstrated real-time spectral tissue characterization using an ex vivo porcine heart model in the context of ablation monitoring. The core code components are open-sourced on GitHub.

papers.title: Polarized Photoacoustic Imaging: a New Paradigm for label-Free Nerve Imaging
papers.abstract: Iatrogenic nerve injury remains a major surgical challenge as intraoperative nerve visualization is difficult because nerves often seem similar to adipose tissue, tendon, or blood vessels. Current imaging techniques rely on exogenous agents or multispectral photoacoustic (PA) imaging, which face many limitations. To address these challenges and limitations, we introduce Polarized Photoacoustic Imaging, a novel, label-free, single-wavelength approach exploiting the intrinsic optical anisotropy of fibrous neural tissue. We validated our method on porcine nerves across clinically relevant layered tissue environments (up to 4 mm of fat) and 3 different wavelengths. The results demonstrate a significant enhancement in nerve visibility without exogenous agents. Notably, our technique differentiated nerve from adjacent tendon beneath 3 mm of pork belly fat at 980 nm, achieving a nerve signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of 27 dB, exceeding the 1 dB SNR of standard PA imaging in the same experiment. This establishes a promising new paradigm for intraoperative nerve-preserving guidance.

papers.title: Model-Based Sparse Scanning Optimization for Non-Contact Photoacoustic Imaging
papers.abstract: Non-contact volumetric photoacoustic (PA) imaging using a laser Doppler vibrometer (LDV) maps critical structures such as vessels, or tumors without acoustic coupling. However, current single-channel LDV systems require sequential surface scanning, making dense volumetric acquisition too slow for intraoperative mapping and tracking. This work introduces a model-based sparse scanning optimization framework to select fewer, more informative sensing locations while preserving critical-structure visibility. The framework was evaluated in a realistic prostate digital phantom with blood vessels and in ex-vivo nerve imaging beneath pork fat using a single-channel LDV. Sensor selection was formulated using priority maximization, pairwise repulsion, boundary coverage, and sparsity, then solved using L-BFGS with box constraints. In simulation, 103 sensing points were reduced to 16 while achieving SSIM = 0.789 and PCC = 0.781 relative to dense scanning. In ex-vivo imaging, 100 points were reduced to 40 while preserving visible nerve localization, with SSIM = 0.61 and PCC = 0.75. This 2.5x scan-time reduction supports accelerated non-contact PA mapping and tracking for surgical guidance.

papers.title: Three-Dimensional Ultrahigh-Resolution Slit-Based Photoacoustic Array Hyperbeamformation Imaging
papers.abstract: Slit-based 3D photoacoustic array imaging, as realized by three-dimensional diffractive acoustic tomography (3D-DAT), enables volumetric imaging with a linear-array transducer via single-slit acoustic diffraction, providing near-isotropic resolution and a large field of view. However, conventional focal-line delay-and-sum (DAS) beamforming suffers from diffraction-limited resolution. In this work, we incorporate hyper-beamforming (HBF) into the 3D focal line reconstruction to greatly improve imaging resolution and contrast. In vivo mouse images reconstructed using DAS and HBF, respectively, in which HBF yields noticeably thinner vein structures and greatly improved imaging contrast.

sessions.title: MSR: Contrast and compare

papers.title: Fast-Acquisition Fast-Processing Label-Free Super-Resolution Renal Microvascular Imaging
papers.abstract: Super-resolution microvascular imaging has reshaped ultrasound vascular imaging research since the introduction of ultrasound localization microscopy. However, ultrasound localization microscopy requires contrast agent injections, long acquisitions, and computationally intensive localization and tracking, which limit its clinical translation. To move super-resolution microvascular imaging closer to clinical translation, a method that can overcome these limitations is needed. Here, we propose a fast-acquisition and fast-processing super-resolution microvascular imaging framework that enables contrast-free imaging of native blood flow.

papers.title: Contrast-Free Human Kidney Microvascular Imaging Using a Convex Array
papers.abstract: Contrast-free super-resolution ultrasound imaging using erythrocytes (SURE) enables visualization of microvascular structures without contrast agents and within short acquisition times. This study demonstrates the feasibility of imaging human kidney microvasculature in vivo using a convex array. A synthetic aperture sequence with 8 virtual sources and 64 active elements per emission was implemented on a Verasonics Vantage 256 system, achieving a frame rate of 625 Hz. A 5-second dataset was acquired, and motion was compensated. Tissue signals were removed using Singular Value Decomposition, followed by peak detection and directional SURE reconstruction using frequency-based separation. Compared to conventional Doppler imaging, the proposed method reveals finer vascular structures. These results demonstrate the potential of contrast-free SURE for rapid, non-invasive clinical assessment of renal microvasculature.

papers.title: Volumetric Ultrasound Localization Microscopy of in situ Kidney Vasculature Applied in a Longitudinal Model of Diabetic Kidney Disease
papers.abstract: We present the first longitudinal 3D ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) study of diabetic kidney disease (DKD) in a rat model. Seven rats were imaged weekly for six weeks using a 32×32 matrix array on a 1024-channel Verasonics system at 500 volumes/s. STZ-treated animals showed a 186% increase in blood glucose and ~18% cortical hypertrophy versus baseline, confirming disease induction and demonstrating ULM's potential for early, in vivo DKD detection.

papers.title: Freely-Moving Functional Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (fULM) for Cerebrovascular Imaging of Opioid Action
papers.abstract: Functional ultrasound localization microscopy (fULM) provides brain-wide microscopic hemodynamic imaging in freely-moving rats, but has so far been restricted to repeated-trial sensory paradigms that rely on sustained microbubble (MB) infusion and multi-cycle averaging. These constraints preclude pharmacological studies, where drugs act on small subregions and anesthesia or head fixation confounds drug responses. To bring freely-moving fULM into pharmacological neuroimaging, we performed serial imaging at baseline and 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 min after subcutaneous SR-17018, a G-protein biased μ-opioid receptor agonist, with vehicle-only controls, targeting bregma –6.5 mm to capture the periaqueductal gray (PAG). An analytical pipeline applies non-rigid motion correction to a baseline-derived template and quantifies hemodynamics via a relative flow-velocity metric (ΔV/V₀) insensitive to MB concentration variability. Following SR-17018 injection, PAG flow velocity rose by ~20% and remained elevated beyond 15 min before gradually declining, while controls showed no comparable changes, establishing freely-moving fULM as a practical tool for behaviorally-driven neuroscience.

papers.title: Coherent Nonlinear Ultrasound Localization Microscopy in Rat Liver and Spinal Cord
papers.abstract: Microvasculature and capillaries play a pivotal role in the diagnosis and treatment of various diseases. Recently, nonlinear ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) leveraging the acoustic nonlinearity to extract low-velocity microbubbles (MBs) has achieved super-resolution imaging at the microvascular and even capillary levels. To enhance imaging quality and MB extraction efficacy, coherent nonlinear ULM (CN-ULM) exploits the spatial and temporal coherence across different channel signals—an approach already validated in rat brain and kidney models. To investigate its broader clinical prospects, this work explores the application of CN-ULM in rat liver and spinal cord, aiming to provide high-resolution imaging evidence for evaluating microvascular health and related functional alterations.

papers.title: In Vivo Coronary Artery contrast-Free Erythrocyte Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Imaging in Mice
papers.abstract: This study presents the first in vivo demonstration of contrast-free coronary artery imaging in mice using erythrocyte ultrasound localization microscopy (eULM). A 35 MHz ultrafast ultrasound system combined with plane wave imaging enables detection of endogenous red blood cells. Image-based cardiac gating and optical flow motion correction compensate for rapid cardiac and respiratory motion. The reconstructed eULM images reveal coronary microvasculature with high spatial resolution, resolving vessels as small as 41.6 µm and improving sensitivity compared to ultrafast Doppler imaging. This approach provides a non-invasive, contrast-free solution for studying coronary microcirculation in small animal models.

papers.title: 3D Ultrasound Localization Microscopy Using Hadamard-Encoded Multipulse and Denoising with a 32×32 Matrix Array and a 256-Channel System: an In-Human Feasibility Study
papers.abstract: Three-dimensional ultrasound localization microscopy (3D ULM) enables micrometer-scale imaging of microvascular networks but faces challenges for clinical translation, including long acquisition times, low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), limited imaging depth, and insufficient microbubble (MB) contrast. To address these limitations, we developed a robust in-human 3D ULM framework on a 256-channel system with a 2D matrix array, improving MB SNR and contrast while enabling the use of higher MB concentrations for more reliable detection and faster imaging.In an IRB-approved study, 3000 volumes (~15 s) were acquired from a human kidney allograft using a Verasonics Vantage 256 system with a 3 MHz 2D matrix array. Diverging-wave imaging with Hadamard encoding enhanced MB SNR, followed by MB separation, 4D non-local means filtering, and MB localization/tracking to reconstruct the 3D microvasculature.The proposed method achieved high-quality visualization of microvessels over a depth range of 15–50 mm, with clear delineation of cortical vessels. Fourier shell correlation analysis estimated a spatial resolution of ~75 μm.

papers.title: Transthoracic Ultrafast Ultrasound Localization Microscopy of the Human Coronary Microcirculation Over the Entire Cardiac Cycle
papers.abstract: Up to 40% of patients with chest pain show no obstructive coronary lesion, pointing to coronary microvascular dysfunction (CMD). Direct in vivo visualization of the coronary microcirculation is still missing in clinical practice. Ultrasound Localization Microscopy (ULM) tracks individual microbubbles to image vessels below the diffraction limit, but in transthoracic cardiac imaging motion restricts microbubble detection to diastole. We propose a novel transthoracic ULM sequence and processing pipeline combining non-linear pulsing (pulse inversion at 1.9 MHz with second-harmonic demodulation at 3.8 MHz) with synchronous ECG. Inter-angle motion correction and coherence weighting further enhance microbubble echoes against residual tissue, and microbubbles are localized and tracked in the spatiotemporal domain to produce super-resolved density maps across the entire cardiac cycle. Preliminary in vivo data in a healthy volunteer show that microbubble tracks are recovered in the septal region at every phase of the cycle, lifting the diastole-only limitation and revealing arterioles and branching vessels of the human coronary bed.

papers.title: Flow-Informed Design and Functional Validation of Bioprinted Liver Microvasculature Using Volumetric ULM
papers.abstract: Bioprinted liver constructs require vascular architectures that reproduce hierarchical flow to achieve physiologically relevant perfusion, yet structural fidelity alone is insufficient without functional validation. Here, volumetric ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) is used to capture in vivo liver vascular topology and flow as a data-driven reference for bioprinted design and validation. ULM imaging was performed on murine liver using a 1024-element matrix array with high-frame-rate volumetric acquisition (~250 volumes/s). Extracted vascular hierarchies guided the design of an 8-branch bioprinted construct. Microbubble perfusion and 3D ULM reconstruction enabled volumetric flow mapping. ULM resolved three branching generations with ~45% diameter reduction across scales. While perfusion was preserved in primary and most secondary branches, flow deficits were observed in smaller tertiary vessels, indicating scale-dependent loss of patency. These results demonstrate that volumetric ULM enables flow-based validation of bioprinted vasculature and identification of perfusion limits for design refinement.

papers.title: Deep Learning-Based Microbubble Localization for Super-Resolution Microvasculature and Ultrasound Molecular Fusion Imaging
papers.abstract: Ultrasound localization microscopy (ULM) achieves super-resolution microvasculature imaging, while ultrasound molecular imaging (USMI) identifies disease biomarkers using targeted microbubbles (MBs). The combination of ULM and USMI enables simultaneous anatomical and molecular imaging for improved disease diagnosis. However, conventional USMI is limited by diffraction and cannot accurately distinguish adherent targeted MBs from free MBs, leading to mismatched resolution with super-resolution vascular imaging. This study introduces a unified deep learning framework applied to both super-resolution microvascular imaging and high-resolution ultrasound molecular imaging (HR-USMI). The deep learning model achieves robust classification and precise localization of targeted adherent MBs and free circulating MBs. By integrating a new imaging sequence with deep learning processing, we upgrade molecular imaging resolution to match microvascular scale. SRUS vascular data and HR-USMI molecular signals are acquired via a single MB injection, generating fused images that display high-resolution molecular signatures overlapped on super-resolution microvasculature.

papers.title: Characterising Tumour Angiogenesis and Growth for Early Detection of Mammary Carcinoma Using Super-Resolution Ultrasound
papers.abstract: Early detection of mammary carcinoma remains a critical clinical challenge. Super-Resolution Ultrasound (SRUS) offers a non-invasive means to characterise tumour vascularisation at microscopic resolution, yet its application to mammary carcinoma growth and angiogenesis remains largely unexplored. Ten subcutaneous 4-T1 mammary carcinoma tumours were imaged using a VisualSonics F2 Vevo system at four time points (days 4, 8, 11 and 14), and structural and functional vascular parameters — including vascularisation, tortuosity, density, blood flow uniformity, spatial entropy and heterogeneity — were estimated from SRUS density, velocity and angular maps. Structural parameters such as vascularisation and spatial vascular entropy showed a step change between days 4 and 8, with a minor drop at day 14, while functional parameters such as blood flow uniformity showed a similar early step change only. These findings suggest that combining structural and functional SRUS parameters has the potential to detect malignant mammary tumours early and estimate their stage.

sessions.title: MSD: Wearable Ultrasound

papers.title: Performance of Long Coded Excitation Under Crosstalk Constraints for Wearable Muscle Monitoring Using a Low-Cost Commercially Available Microcontroller for Signal Transmission
papers.abstract: Wearable ultrasound (WUS) enables non-invasive, real-time muscle monitoring for rehabilitation, sports science and neuromuscular diagnostics, but requires compact, low-cost hardware limited by low-voltage operation. Coded excitation can address this by enhancing SNR. Separated transmit and receive elements permit signal lengths (SL) beyond the time-of-flight (ToF), but this also introduces persistent crosstalk. This work hypothesizes that extending SL beyond ToF can practically overcome crosstalk-related limitations in wearable muscle monitoring. A Raspberry Pi Pico 2 W synthesized 5 MHz Maximum Length Sequences (MLS), transmitted via a PMN-PT transmitter and received by dual CMUT sensors. Results showed a non-linear crosstalk–SNR trade-off: intermediate MLS were limited by crosstalk, while longer MLS restored detectability as SNR gains exceeded these penalties. In vivo, extending from 8th- to 13th-order MLS improved SNR by 24.3 dB while maintaining frame rates above 600 Hz. These findings highlight long coded excitation as a promising strategy for resource-constrained WUS systems.

papers.title: Button-cell-Powered CMUT Receiver with Coded Excitation for Blood Vessel detection: Toward Wearable Continuous Blood Pressure Monitoring
papers.abstract: Capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducers (CMUTs) are promising for wearable health monitoring due to their high sensitivity, cost-efficiency, and integration with microelectronics. However, their need for high bias voltages limits low-power applications. This study demonstrates that a single-channel CMUT receiver, powered by two button cells (6V), combined with chirp excitation, can detect vessel-wall reflections at clinically relevant depths (2–5 cm) with sufficient SNR for arterial diameter tracking. A CMUT receiver with 20µm cells and an integrated ROIC (3.5mA) was tested with a piezo transmitter emitting a 1–4 MHz chirp. The setup was aligned with a blood vessel phantom in a water tank. Despite an 11 dB reduction in peak amplitude, the CMUT achieved an SNR of 32.5 dB, sufficient for detecting the tissue surface, vessel walls, and backwall at depths of 2–5 cm. Variations in flow due to pressure changes were also measurable, indicating potential for continuous blood pressure monitoring. This study highlights the feasibility of low-power CMUTs for wearable applications, paving the way for real-time, non-invasive blood pressure monitoring systems.

papers.title: Wearable Mechatronic Ultrasound Scanner for Longitudinal Intrapartum Patient Monitoring During Labor
papers.abstract: This work presents a compact wearable mechatronic ultrasound scanner for longitudinal intrapartum patient monitoring. Electronic fetal heart rate monitoring is widely used but indirectly assesses fetal status and does not directly evaluate fetal brain injury, while handheld B-mode ultrasound is episodic and operator-dependent. The cylindrical scanner is worn on the lower maternal abdomen above the pubic symphysis and secured by a belly band to keep the acoustic window coupled while preserving mobility. It provides three degrees of freedom: translation, pitch, and rotation. A custom transducer is immersed in castor oil within an acoustically transparent enclosure and interfaced to a Clarius platform. Motors, electronics, custom motor drivers, and frame-trigger synchronization record encoder positions in real time so each ultrasound frame can be registered to scanner pose for synthetic encoded scanning aperture reconstruction. The prototype demonstrated accurate coordinated 3-DOF motion, supporting volumetric scanning of structures relevant to fetal health and labor progress.

papers.title: Simulation-Aided Design of Wearable Mechatronic Ultrasound with Synthetic Encoded Scanning Aperture Focusing
papers.abstract: This work presents a simulation-aided design of wearable mechatronic ultrasound (MECHUS) with synthetic encoded scanning aperture focusing (SESAF). A 3D acoustic simulation model with a miniaturized convex array was developed to evaluate translation (-50 to 50 mm) and pitch (-20° to +20°) scanning. SESAF reconstructs elevation planes by compensating time-of-flight differences across scan events. Performance was assessed using elevation spatial resolution (FWHM) and mainlobe-to-grating-lobe ratio (MGR). Compared with no synthesis, SESAF improved elevation resolution at 120 mm depth by 19.7–77.2%. Adding pitch synthesis increased average MGR by 53.5–135.5% versus translation-only synthesis. These results support simulation-guided optimization of wearable ultrasound, which will further allow optimizations of spatial resolution, field of view, scanning sequence, and artifact suppression.

papers.title: A Cost-Effective Three-Element Probe and Front-End Electronics Design for Wearable Carotid Doppler Monitoring
papers.abstract: This work presents a cost-effective carotid Doppler monitoring approach using a custom three-element probe and front-end electronics design. Cardiac output monitoring is important in critical care, but array-based Doppler systems are costly and operator-dependent, while low-cost CW patches provide only relative flow tracking. The probe uses a central element for CW transmission and A-mode pulse-echo, and two tilted receive elements for vector Doppler. The receive angle was selected by Field II simulations for 1.5–3 cm carotid depths. CW signals were quadrature demodulated, clutter filtered, and analyzed by STFT; velocity components were combined to estimate the flow vector. A-mode echoes were averaged, and vessel walls were detected from the envelope to estimate diameter and CSA. Bench-top tests with a 2-cm-deep vessel-mimicking tube showed diameter errors within 3.5%, with cycle volume and average flow rate accuracies of 93.18% and 92.27%. A front-end board integrating an AFE, pulser, T/R switch, and FPGA is under fabrication for improved SNR and wearable deployment.

papers.title: Wearable Contact Lens Ultrasound Phased Array for High-Resolution, Noninvasive Retinal Neuromodulation
papers.abstract: A wearable contact lens–conformal ultrasound phased array is presented for noninvasive retinal neuromodulation. The device integrates a 64-element dual-ring piezoelectric array operating at 19.5 MHz on a flexible substrate, enabling high-resolution acoustic focusing (~100–150 μm). A custom FPGA-based system provides real-time beam steering and programmable stimulation patterns. Thermal testing under continuous operation (50 V, 20 h) shows stable performance with minimal temperature increase (~5°C). Acoustic characterization yields a peak pressure of ~0.31 MPa and a mechanical index of 0.068, well below ophthalmic safety limits. In vivo evaluation in a rabbit model demonstrates repeatable electrophysiological responses correlated with stimulation intensity without observable tissue damage. The results validate the feasibility of a wearable, biocompatible ultrasound platform for safe, spatially selective retinal stimulation, offering a noninvasive alternative to implantable prostheses for vision restoration.

papers.title: Hemodynamic Monitoring Using Simultaneous Real-Time Multichannel M-Mode and Doppler Imaging in a Miniature Wearable Ultrasound Device
papers.abstract: This work presents a miniature wearable ultrasound platform that performs simultaneous M-mode and Doppler imaging using time-delay spectrometry (TDS), addressing a gap in current wearable systems that rely on either high-voltage pulse-echo or single-frequency CW Doppler. TDS uses a 5 V wideband linear chirp to create a deterministic mapping between reflector depth and beat frequency, enabling real-time, depth-resolved displacement and velocity estimation from a single transmit. The architecture supports 4-channel acquisition at 400 Hz frame rate while drawing 200 mA from a battery. Validation on a calibrated string phantom showed a linear Doppler-shift vs string-velocity relationship (Pearson r = 0.999, p < 1e-13). On a pulsatile flow phantom, simultaneous M-mode wall motion and Doppler-derived wall velocity tracked the pump waveform across physiologic rates. To our knowledge this is the first wearable, single-element ultrasound system to deliver real-time, simultaneous M-mode and tissue Doppler under battery-powered operation, establishing a platform for continuous fetal and neonatal carotid hemodynamic monitoring.

sessions.title: MTH: Toward Intelligent and Responsive Ultrasound Therapies

papers.title: AI-Based Reverberation Detection to Enhance HIFU Delivery Safety Based on B-Mode Ultrasound Images with Overlays
papers.abstract: This work describes the development and characterization of a neural network for the identification of ultrasound reverberations in high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatments of the prostate. Reverberations need to be avoided in HIFU treatments as they negatively impact treatment safety and efficacy.

papers.title: Ultrasound Imaging-Based Blood Flow and Pressure Estimation for Potential Closed-Loop tFUS-Mediated Blood Pressure Reduction in Rats
papers.abstract: Transcranial focused ultrasound (tFUS) can modulate central autonomic circuits and represents a promising non-pharmacological approach for blood pressure (BP) control. However, fixed open-loop stimulation cannot adapt to rapid BP fluctuations. This study proposes an ultrasound imaging–based method for estimating dynamic BP to support potential closed-loop tFUS modulation. In rats undergoing tFUS-induced BP changes, ultrafast plane-wave imaging was used to monitor common carotid artery wall motion and blood flow at 2000 Hz using a Verasonics Vantage system with an L22-14vX transducer. Beamformed data were processed using spatiotemporal singular value Decomposition (SVD) filtering to extract blood flow, and an autocorrelation algorithm to track pulsatile wall displacement. Dynamic BP was estimated through a vascular pressure–area model. Results show that ultrafast imaging enables reliable real-time characterization of carotid vascular motion and allows BP estimation from ultrasound-derived mechanical metrics. These imaging-derived BP and flow features may serve as feedback signals for future adaptive, closed-loop tFUS-mediated BP regulation.

papers.title: Bayesian Optimization Framework for Efficient low-Intensity Focused Ultrasound Parameter Mapping
papers.abstract: Low-intensity focused ultrasound (LIFU) is an emerging non-invasive neuromodulation technique whose translational potential is currently limited by a poorly understood parameter space and by high intra- and inter-subject response variability. Conventional parameter mapping methods rely on grid searches, which are particularly inefficient with large parameter spaces, as in LIFU neuromodulation. Here we developed and validated a Bayesian-optimization (BO) approach for efficient, data-driven mapping of LIFU stimulation parameters.

papers.title: Focused Ultrasound neuromodulation via Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation Suppresses PTZ-Induced Epileptic Activity in Mice
papers.abstract: Epilepsy requires effective non-invasive therapeutic strategies. This study investigates ultrasound stimulation (US) targeting the transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve (taVNS) using a PTZ-induced seizure model with real-time EEG monitoring. FUS was applied to the auricular region, with acoustic characterization confirming focal pressure distribution. A structured protocol included baseline, PTZ-induced seizure, US, and post-US phases, with continuous EEG recording. In the PTZ_only group, seizure induction significantly increased epileptiform activity, reflected by higher spike density and total spike number, which remained elevated during sham conditions. In contrast, US-treated animals showed a clear reduction in spike activity during stimulation, with further suppression observed post-stimulation. Quantitative analysis confirmed a significant decrease in spike number compared to the PTZ condition, indicating effective seizure suppression. These findings demonstrate that US-mediated taVNS can reduce epileptiform activity and provide sustained neuromodulatory effects. This non-invasive approach shows strong potential for developing ultrasound-based therapies for epilepsy.

papers.title: A Pilot Study of Porcine Blood-Spinal Cord Barrier Modulation Using Focused Ultrasound and a Custom MRI Coil
papers.abstract: In this pilot study of blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB) modulation with focused ultrasound (FUS), 10 thoracic targets in 2 Yorkshire pigs were treated with 1.6-2.0 MPa FUS exposures in conjunction with intravenously administered circulating microbubbles. Sonications were performed using a 6144-element phased array (Arrayus Technologies; f0=525 kHz, 10 ms pulse, 1 Hz PRF). Contrast-enhanced (CE) T1w imaging was performed pre- and post-treatment with a custom, 12 channel spine-specific receive coil designed to accommodate the aperture, and post-treatment with a manufacturer-provided 18-channel body coil (Siemens). Exposures were repeated at 30 minutes followed by additional imaging. Following repeat treatment, barrier modulation was confirmed at 9/10 targets by Evans blue dye extravasation in necropsy. CE was visible at 8/10 targets, and percent enhancement was more prominent with the manufacturer-provided coil (19.8 ± 7.7%) than the custom coil (13.5% ± 7.8%). In future work, a ventral component of the custom coil will be investigated for improved detection of post-FUS CE.

papers.title: Development of an Awake Vibrotactile Stimulation Platform to Establish an Excitatory Baseline for Ultrasound-Mediated Neuromodulation
papers.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS) is an emerging tool for noninvasive neuromodulation, but variable baseline activity can obscure treatment effects. To establish a reproducible sensory-evoked baseline, we developed an awake, unrestrained whole-body vibrotactile stimulation platform for rats. The system used two speakers driven by a function generator and voltage source, with displacement characterized by accelerometry. Rats received no stimulation, 20 Hz, or 40 Hz stimulation for 1 hour, followed by DAPI/c-Fos/NeuN/GAD67 staining, atlas alignment, and QuPath quantification. The platform produced consistent 20 and 40 Hz stimulation, with displacements of 136.5 and 88.4 µm. Vibrotactile stimulation increased c-Fos+ cell density across cortical regions, with strongest activation in primary somatosensory cortex, including S1 forelimb. Although 20 Hz produced the greatest response, both frequencies significantly increased c-Fos+ cells in S1. These findings support vibrotactile stimulation as a reproducible in vivo control for defining sensory-evoked activity and evaluating FUS neuromodulation.

papers.title: A Feasibility Study and Computational Model for Ultrasound-Guided Directional Heat Transfer in Soft Tissue
papers.abstract: Thermal ablation relies on localized heating to destroy tumors, yet current approaches struggle to confine heat, especially near sensitive tissues. This work investigates whether ultrasound can steer conductive heat transfer to enable directional thermal spreading. A coupled acoustic–thermal COMSOL model was developed, where ultrasound-induced pressure modulates local density and, consequently, thermal conductivity. A 2D soft-tissue model (fat-mimicking properties) was simulated under two conditions: without and with ultrasound excitation. Experimental validation was performed using an agar phantom with an ultrasound transducer and a Peltier heat source. Results show that, without ultrasound, heat remains localized, while ultrasound induces directional extension along the propagation path. At a 38.5 °C threshold, axial thermal spread increased from 8.8 mm to 12.6 mm (43.2% enhancement). Experimental thermal imaging confirmed similar trends. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of ultrasound-assisted heat steering, offering a promising strategy for improving spatial precision in thermal therapies.

papers.title: Dual-Responsive Gelatin Microspheres for Ultrasound-Enhanced Enzyme-Mediated Drug Release in Cancer Therapy
papers.abstract: Gelatin microspheres (GMS) are attractive drug carriers due to their biocompatibility, biodegradability, and high drug-loading capacity. However, drug release from conventional GMSs relies on slow enzymatic degradation, limiting temporal precision and external control. To address this, we integrated ultrasound with collagenase to enhance release efficacy and spatiotemporal controllability. We developed ultrasound-mediated doxorubicin-loaded GMSs (UD-GMS) that enable stimulus-responsive drug release under clinically relevant conditions. Ultrasound increased GMS degradation by 37% and doxorubicin release by 3.35-fold compared with enzyme treatment alone, indicating a strong synergistic effect. Duty factor–dependent analysis revealed that cavitation, rather than thermal effects, predominantly governs release enhancement. In 3D 4T1 breast cancer spheroids, combined UD-GMS, collagenase, and ultrasound treatment reduced cell viability to 51.7%, demonstrating therapeutic potential. Overall, this study presents an ultrasound-regulated, enzyme-assisted drug delivery system that enables precise, externally controlled anticancer drug release.

sessions.title: TMS: Transducer Modeling and Simulation

papers.title: Ultra Wideband Integrated Photonic Ultrasound Transducer (IPUT) Design for Photoacoustic Intravascular Ultrasound Imaging
papers.abstract: This work designs an ultra wideband Integrated Photonic Ultrasound Transducer (IPUT) for photoacoustic intravascular ultrasound (IVPA), aiming to improve SNR and enable dense array integration compared with conventional piezoelectric readout. The target specification is a 1–10 MHz bandwidth with minimal sidelobes, a highly symmetric beam profile, and a 0.6 mm² sensing area. Broadband response is achieved by cascading multiple IPUT membranes with different radii so their impulse responses sum in time. A 2D axisymmetric COMSOL FEM model is used to simulate single membranes (3 um thick; 35–90 um radii) with 15–30 um Altuglas coating. An optimization algorithm selects the membrane counts per radius to maximize 1–10 MHz bandwidth while minimizing temporal length, and a subsequent layout optimization fits the membranes in 0.6 mm × 1 mm to achieve beam symmetry and suppress sidelobes. An example optimal design is presented with 23 membranes (42–64 um radii, 20 um coating) and achieves a flat −6 dB bandwidth of 1.7–9 MHz with Q < 1.5 and good centre symmetric, low sidelobe beam profiles.

papers.title: Optimization of Ultrasonic Field Reconstruction Distance for High-Fidelity Acoustic Hologram Lenses
papers.abstract: Selecting the optimal propagation distance is critical in acoustic holography, as fidelity and energy delivery depend on the balance between wavefront formation and diffractive loss. This study quantifies practical reconstruction limits for a 45 mm aperture (1.5 MHz) using the iterative angular spectrum approach (IASA) with 15x zero-padding to suppress numerical artifacts. Results show that stable reconstruction occurs between 8λ and 70λ, with an optimal peak at 15λ–30λ. At very short distances ~5λ, high-spatial-frequency and evanescent components prevent stable interference, while excessive distances lead to diffraction-induced degradation. Notably, the optimal distance consistently identifies near D/2, providing a key design benchmark for high-fidelity acoustic synthesis.

papers.title: How Cylindrically Curved Ultrasound Transducers Respond: a First-Principles Mathematical Derivation of Impulse Response
papers.abstract: This work presents a first-principles mathematical derivation of the impulse response of cylindrically curved ultrasound transducers. Starting from the Green’s function formulation of wave propagation, a closed-form solution is obtained for the two-dimensional case by explicitly resolving the governing integral and delta function. The approach is extended to three dimensions using line-element decomposition and geometric reparameterization. A key insight is that impulse response formation can be interpreted as the intersection between a spherical wavefront and the cylindrical aperture, producing distinct temporal regimes as the intersection evolves. Analytical predictions are validated against large-scale numerical summation and reveal curvature-specific effects not observed in planar geometries. The resulting framework provides both physical insight and a practical modeling approach for curved transducer design in radial and catheter-based imaging systems.

papers.title: Bias-Dependent Modified KLM Model for Bulk and Composite Relaxor Ferroelectrics
papers.abstract: The KLM model has been used for decades to describe piezoelectric transducers, but does not adequately describe the behavior of electrostrictive relaxor ferroelectrics. We developed and validated a modified KLM model with bias-dependent parameters to describe bulk and composite PMN-PT transducers.

papers.title: Broadband Ultrasound Transducer Using a Compliant-Interlayer-Coupled Dual-PZT Structure
papers.abstract: This study proposes a compliant-interlayer-coupled dual-PZT ultrasound transducer to broaden the bandwidth of conventional single-PZT designs. Single-PZT transducers are typically governed by one thickness-mode resonance, which limits the bandwidth required for short acoustic pulses and improved axial resolution in pulse-echo imaging. In the proposed stack, two PZT layers are coupled through a finite-stiffness compliant interlayer. The interlayer modulates stress transfer and displacement continuity between the two layers, allowing their thickness-mode responses to interact without making the stack behave as a single thicker PZT layer. A single-PZT stack was used as the reference model. The backing-side PZT layer was dominant under transmit excitation, whereas the water-side PZT layer showed a larger response under receive loading. The proposed structure produced a broader, flatter normalized voltage response, increasing the −6-dB FBW from 59.38% to 93.05%. These results suggest that the compliant interlayer broadens the passband by coupling two PZT thickness-mode responses.

papers.title: Superharmonic Response of Polydisperse microbubbles and Tissue Towards Improving dual-Frequency Hardware Design
papers.abstract: Superharmonic imaging is a contrast-enhanced ultrasound modality that combines low-frequency transmit (Tx) and high-frequency receive (Rx) to selectively capture the nonlinear microbubble response. Hardware optimization has been limited by costly and lengthy dual-frequency transducer development. To accelerate progress, we developed a simulation framework integrating the Marmottant model for polydisperse microbubble response with a custom angular spectrum method for ultrasound wave propagation. We simulated focused Tx waves at 1-4 MHz with peak negative pressures of 200-1600 kPa to depths of 2, 4, and 6 cm in a homogeneous medium. In silico results demonstrate strong consistency with established nonlinear ultrasound physics and microbubble dynamics from literature. Frequency-dependent and depth-dependent imaging performance was observed. Lower Tx frequencies (1-2 MHz) with mid-range Rx frequencies (10-20 MHz) achieved the highest CTRs. Preliminary in-vitro experiments in tissue-mimicking phantoms demonstrate good agreement with in-silico predictions, motivating the application of this framework for future DF transducer development and clinical imaging optimization.

papers.title: Nonlinear Dynamics of Piezoelectric MEMS Acoustic Transducers: Investigation of the Uncoupled Problem
papers.abstract: Piezoelectric MEMS resonators are electromechanical systems which may exhibit complex nonlinear dynamics, where geometric nonlinearities may dominate the response. In acoustic transducers, designs with multiple coupled cantilevers with short gaps are commonly employed, introducing additional dynamics complexity and leading to, e.g. parametric resonances, as reported in IUS’25. However, due to this coupling, the source of nonlinearity remains unclear. This work aims to investigate the contribution of each cantilever to the nonlinear dynamics of the full device by identifying roles of geometrical parameters to form a basis to understand the coupling effect.
